title: How We Built a 10-Language Digital Business Card Studio (With RTL Support)
description:
When we launched the RahaLune Digital Business Card Studio, it was a fully functional, client-side React application that allowed users to create a digital business card and generate a QR code.

There was just one problem: it was English-only. For a tool designed to help global professionals network, this was a massive barrier.

Today, we rolled out a major update. The entire Digital Business Card Studio is now natively translated into 10 languages, complete with full Right-to-Left (RTL) layout support.

Here is a behind-the-scenes look at how we handled the localization entirely on the client side.

1. The Translation Architecture

Because RahaLune is a 100% client-side app, we didn't want to rely on an external API to fetch translations. We wanted the site to remain instantaneous, even if a user switched languages multiple times in a single session.

We structured our translations using standard JSON files for each locale (en.json, fr.json, ar.json, ur.json, etc.). When a user selects a language from the header dropdown—or visits a localized URL like ?lang=fr—the app dynamically imports the corresponding JSON file and updates our React Context.

// Example of dynamic locale loading
const loadLocale = async (lang) => {
  const translations = await import(`./locales/${lang}.json`);
  setTranslations(translations.default);
};

This approach keeps the initial JavaScript bundle size small while ensuring subsequent language switches happen with zero network lag.

2. Handling the RTL Layout Challenge

Supporting languages like Arabic and Urdu wasn't just about swapping out strings—it required a complete mirror flip of the UI.

If you are building a web app with RTL support, the golden rule is to never hardcode directional CSS. Instead of traditional left and right properties, we migrated to CSS Logical Properties:

  • margin-inline-start instead of margin-left
  • padding-inline-end instead of padding-right
  • inset-inline-start instead of left

We also dynamically update the dir and lang attributes on the root <html> tag whenever the language state changes:

const isRTL = currentLanguage === 'ar' || currentLanguage === 'ur';
document.documentElement.setAttribute('dir', isRTL ? 'rtl' : 'ltr');
document.documentElement.setAttribute('lang', currentLanguage);

This single attribute change tells the browser to natively flip Flexbox containers, CSS Grid tracks, and text alignment. Our 3-step wizard, form inputs, and 3D phone preview all mirror seamlessly without maintaining duplicate stylesheets.

3. Fixing UI Breakage with Text Expansion

German and French translations are notoriously 20% to 30% longer than their English equivalents. In tight UI components—like our 3-step navigation tabs or theme color swatches—this immediately caused overflow and clipping bugs.

To make the UI resilient against text expansion, we applied a few defensive CSS patterns:

  • Replaced fixed widths with min-width and flexible flex-grow rules so buttons could expand gracefully.
  • Applied text-wrap: balance on headings and multi-line buttons to prevent awkward single-word orphans.
  • Allowed form labels enough vertical breathing room to wrap onto a second line without colliding with inputs.

4. The vCard (.vcf) Encoding Challenge

Generating a .vcf contact file that parses cleanly across both iOS Contacts and Android devices is notoriously finicky. When you introduce non-Latin scripts (like Arabic, Urdu, or accented European characters), improper character encoding results in garbled text (mojibake) when saved to a user's phone.

We had to explicitly enforce UTF-8 encoding (CHARSET=UTF-8) across fields like job titles, company names, and addresses, and test the generated files on physical iOS and Android devices across all 10 locales.

5. Client-Side SEO and hreflang Tags

Even in a Single Page Application (SPA), search engines need clear signals to index localized versions properly. Whenever the active language changes, we dynamically update the <title>, <meta name="description">, and Open Graph tags.

More importantly, we inject hreflang alternate links into the document <head> so crawlers understand the relationship between our localized URLs:

<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="https://rahalune-qr-studio.vercel.app/business-card?lang=en" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="https://rahalune-qr-studio.vercel.app/business-card?lang=fr" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="ar" href="https://rahalune-qr-studio.vercel.app/business-card?lang=ar" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="https://rahalune-qr-studio.vercel.app/business-card" />

This prevents duplicate content penalties and ensures that someone searching in French or Arabic lands directly on the localized version of the studio.

6. Maintaining 100% Client-Side Privacy

The core promise of RahaLune is zero-tracking privacy. We don't have a backend database, we don't store user contact details, and we don't run invasive analytics.

Scaling to 10 languages didn't compromise that architecture. Translation loading, .vcf file generation, and QR code rendering all execute locally inside the user's browser. Personal data never leaves their device.

Try It Out

We now have a Digital Business Card Studio that speaks 10 languages, handles RTL layouts natively, and remains 100% free.

If you want to see how the RTL layout flips the live 3D preview in real time, switch the language to Arabic or Urdu using the header dropdown:

👉 Try the Multi-Language Digital Business Card Studio

How do you handle i18n and RTL layouts in your React projects? Drop your thoughts or tips in the comments!

title: I built Diviso — a local-first AI agent that runs on your own machine, even on a phone
description:
Most AI agents I tried wanted an account, a subscription, and my data on someone else's server. I wanted the opposite, so I built Diviso.

It's a Python agent that runs entirely on your own machine. Point it at a local model through Ollama, or plug in OpenAI, Claude, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek or OpenRouter with your own key. No Diviso account, no server of mine in the middle.

What's inside

  • ReAct loop + a planner, with hard step and cost caps on every run
  • Persistent memory (SQLite + a plain MEMORY.md) and TF-IDF search over your local files
  • A small multi-agent team (Researcher / Coder / Reviewer)
  • Tools for Python, JavaScript and Bash, file edits, tests, read-only git, web fetch — all behind an approval gate and a workspace sandbox
  • MCP client, a guarded scheduler, checkpoint/resume after every step
  • CLI + a small web dashboard

The part I'm happiest with

The core is standard-library-only Python, so the same code runs on a GPU PC, an old laptop, and an Android phone under Termux. It detects your hardware and picks a lite / balanced / pro profile with model sizes that actually fit.

Honest limits

It's v0.1.0. No token streaming yet, and the cloud providers are implemented against their documented APIs — the offline test suite (74 tests, CI green) runs on a deterministic mock provider. Local Ollama is the main path I test by hand.

Repo: https://github.com/Neuzant/diviso-agent

Feedback very welcome — especially from anyone who runs it on weird hardware.

title: The stock client is already post-quantum
description:
I probed github.com's SSH service twice in one week, with the same tool and the same options. The first run, from my Ubuntu 24.04 laptop, said two post-quantum key exchanges worked only with the experimental Open Quantum Safe client. The second run, from a Debian 13 container, said the stock client and the experimental client negotiate identically.

GitHub had not changed anything. My client had. Debian 13 ships a newer OpenSSH, and that release already does what I was using an experimental build for.

This post is about that shift: stock OpenSSL and OpenSSH now negotiate post-quantum key exchange out of the box, which changes what a "stock versus experimental" comparison can tell you, and what a post-quantum audit should actually measure.

Part 4 of a series on building pqc-probe. Earlier: part 1, part 2, part 3.

What changed in the stock clients

Post-quantum key exchange arrived in the mainstream tools in a few releases:

Date Release Post-quantum key exchange
Apr 2025 OpenSSH 10.0 mlkem768x25519-sha256 becomes the default
8 Apr 2025 OpenSSL 3.5.0 default TLS key shares become X25519MLKEM768 and X25519
19 Sep 2024 OpenSSH 9.9 adds mlkem768x25519-sha256, enabled by default; adds the name sntrup761x25519-sha512
Apr 2022 OpenSSH 9.0 sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com becomes the default

The OpenSSL change is easy to miss because it is one line in the source. The 3.5 default group list begins with ?*X25519MLKEM768, and the * means the client sends an ML-KEM hybrid key share in every handshake, next to a classical X25519 one. A server that understands ML-KEM can complete a post-quantum handshake without a single extra round trip. OpenSSL 3.0, still common on long-term-support distributions, has no ML-KEM at all.

OpenSSH went further in 10.1, which by default warns the user when a connection is not using a post-quantum key exchange.

Same server, two client machines

GitHub's SSH service offers three post-quantum key exchanges: mlkem768x25519-sha256, sntrup761x25519-sha512 and its older name sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com. Here is what pqc-probe reported against it from each machine:

Ubuntu 24.04 laptop Debian 13 container
Stock SSH client OpenSSH 9.6p1 OpenSSH 10.0p2
mlkem768x25519-sha256 with the stock client not implemented completed
sntrup761x25519-sha512 with the stock client not implemented under this name completed
sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com with the stock client completed completed
Stock versus OQS client diff 2 algorithms "only experimental" none

The laptop's OpenSSH 9.6 predates 9.9, so it lacks ML-KEM and the newer sntrup name. It still completes a post-quantum exchange through the older @openssh.com name, which every OpenSSH since 9.0 uses by default. The Debian container's 10.0 does all three.

The report from the laptop was correct; it described the laptop. Read naively, though, it suggested that GitHub needs an experimental client for ML-KEM, which is not true for anyone on a current OpenSSH.

What the diff still tells you

A "stock versus experimental" diff measures the gap between two clients against one server. When the stock client was classical-only, that gap was a fair stand-in for "what the server supports beyond the mainstream". With post-quantum stock clients, it splits into two different findings, and pqc-probe now labels them apart:

  • Newer mainline, not experimental. An algorithm only the OQS client negotiates may simply be one your stock client is too old for. pqc-probe marks these with the first mainline release that has them, for example mlkem768x25519-sha256 (stock OpenSSH since 9.9). The fix is to update the client, not to adopt an experimental build.
  • Genuinely experimental. Names such as frodokem-976-shake-sha384 or the @openquantumsafe.org hybrids exist only in OQS builds. A server that offers them is running experimental software, which is worth knowing for a different reason.

For TLS the effect is stronger. A stock OpenSSL 3.5 client already completes X25519MLKEM768 wherever the server allows it, so an empty TLS diff no longer means the server is classical. When the stock client itself negotiated a post-quantum group, pqc-probe says so in the report (vanilla_pq_capable), because the diff then says little about the server.

What it means for an audit

A connection is post-quantum only when both ends support it. A server audit answers half the question; the clients that actually connect answer the other half.

  1. Measure the server with a current client. Use OpenSSL 3.5+ and OpenSSH 10+ (or pqc-probe's Docker image, which carries both). An old client makes a capable server look incapable.
  2. Know your client population. Long-term-support systems keep their versions for years: Ubuntu 24.04 ships OpenSSH 9.6, which has sntrup761 but no ML-KEM, and OpenSSL 3.0, which has no post-quantum key exchange at all. Build agents, deploy scripts, backup jobs and the SSH clients on your own servers count too. Until they are upgraded, a server's ML-KEM support does nothing for their TLS connections, and their SSH connections stay on the older sntrup761 exchange.
  3. Record the client with the result. A finding such as "ML-KEM not negotiated" is meaningless without the client version that produced it. pqc-probe's JSON reports include the client versions for exactly this reason.

The practical consequence: "our servers support post-quantum key exchange" and "our connections are post-quantum" are two different claims, and only the second one protects traffic today against harvest-now, decrypt-later collection.

The comparison is shrinking, and that is good news

When I started pqc-probe, the interesting output was the diff: what the experimental client could do that the stock one could not. For the most common algorithms, that gap has largely closed. ML-KEM hybrids are in stock OpenSSL and OpenSSH, on by default, and negotiated without anyone asking for them.

That moves the useful question from "can it be done?" to "is it being done, by every client that matters?" The answer now depends far more on how old your clients are than on anything exotic on the server, and the cheapest post-quantum upgrade available to most teams is a routine package update.

Next in the series: shipping two liboqs builds in one container, and two GCC 14 bugs found on the way.

title: How to Preserve Webhook Signatures During Retries in Python
description:
Handling incoming webhooks from payment processors, source control platforms, and SaaS providers requires strict payload integrity. When receiving a webhook, your application usually verifies a cryptographic signature—such as GitHub's X-Hub-Signature-256 or Stripe's signature header—to confirm that the request actually came from the provider and has not been altered in transit.

However, unexpected downstream outages or temporary database connection errors often require your system to buffer and retry these incoming webhooks. A common bug occurs during this retry cycle: applications parse incoming JSON into native dictionaries, store that parsed data, and later serialize it back into a string or bytes when replaying the request.

This guide explains the underlying problem of payload mutation during webhook persistence and demonstrates how to use rawhook_webhook_retry_helper.py to capture, verify, and store raw payloads without invalidating cryptographic signatures.

The Problem: Serialization Drift and Stream Exhaustion

Cryptographic signatures are computed across the exact sequence of bytes transmitted across the wire. If a single byte changes, verification fails. When handling webhooks, two architectural issues frequently disrupt signature verification:

1. Payload Mutation Through Re-Serialization

When an application receives raw bytes and parses them into memory using standard JSON decoders, several transformations occur:

  • Key Reordering: Dictionary keys in parsed structures do not guarantee the original wire order.
  • Floating-Point Drift: Numeric types like 10.0 or scientific notation might be parsed and re-encoded differently (e.g., 10 or 1.0e1).
  • Whitespace and Escaping: Indentation, spaces after colons, newline placement, and Unicode escape sequences (such as \u0026 versus &) are lost or altered upon re-serialization.

If you attempt to recalculate or forward a re-serialized JSON payload, its SHA-256 digest will differ from the original digest, rendering signatures invalid.

2. WSGI Stream Exhaustion

In Python WSGI servers, request bodies are delivered via an input stream stored in environ['wsgi.input']. Because network streams are readable only once, consuming the stream to compute a signature or write an audit log empties the stream. Downstream web framework components then attempt to read from environ['wsgi.input'] and receive empty bytes, failing with empty request body errors.

Install & Usage

The tool is implemented in a single self-contained Python file. It has no external dependencies and uses only Python standard library modules (argparse, sqlite3, hmac, hashlib, http.client, io, and urllib.parse). You do not need to run pip install for any third-party packages.

Installation

Save the source code directly as rawhook_webhook_retry_helper.py in your project directory:

# Verify the script executes cleanly using the Python interpreter
python rawhook_webhook_retry_helper.py --help

Usage as a Python Library

You can import the module directly into your existing Python backend to capture WSGI inputs, verify signatures against raw bytes, and persist records in SQLite.

from rawhook_webhook_retry_helper import (
    capture_wsgi_environ,
    verify_signature,
    RawHookRecord,
    RawHookStorage,
    TamperDetectedError,
)

# 1. Capture raw payload and headers from a WSGI environment
# This rewinds environ['wsgi.input'] so your framework can still read it
raw_body, headers = capture_wsgi_environ(environ)

# 2. Verify signature before processing
secret = b"webhook_secret_key"
signature_header = headers.get("x-hub-signature-256", "")

is_valid = verify_signature(
    raw_body=raw_body,
    secret=secret,
    header_value=signature_header,
    scheme="github",
)

if is_valid:
    # 3. Store raw bytes safely in SQLite for retry handling
    storage = RawHookStorage(db_path="webhooks.db")
    record = RawHookRecord(
        record_id="evt_1001",
        target_url="/internal/webhook/handler",
        method="POST",
        headers=headers,
        raw_body=raw_body,
    )
    storage.save(record)

How It Works

The tool relies on four core components to guarantee that raw bytes remain intact throughout the ingestion and persistence pipeline.

1. Rewindable Stream Wrapper

To resolve WSGI stream exhaustion, RewindableStreamWrapper reads the input stream up to the declared CONTENT_LENGTH, stores the raw bytes in an internal memory buffer, and re-populates the environment with a seekable io.BytesIO instance:

class RewindableStreamWrapper:
    """
    Prevents framework-specific stream exhaustion (e.g. WSGI environ['wsgi.input']
    or ASGI receive streams). Reads the raw stream into an internal memory buffer,
    computes integrity checksums, and replaces the stream with a rewindable buffer
    so downstream framework consumers can still read it cleanly.
    """

    def __init__(self, original_stream: Any, content_length: Optional[int] = None) -> None:
        self.raw_bytes = b""
        if hasattr(original_stream, "read"):
            if content_length is not None and content_length >= 0:
                self.raw_bytes = original_stream.read(content_length)
            else:
                self.raw_bytes = original_stream.read()
        elif isinstance(original_stream, (bytes, bytearray)):
            self.raw_bytes = bytes(original_stream)
        else:
            raise TypeError("original_stream must provide a read() method or be raw bytes")

        self.buffer = io.BytesIO(self.raw_bytes)

2. Tamper-Evident RawHookRecord

When initializing a RawHookRecord, the class enforces binary input (bytes or bytearray). It automatically computes a SHA-256 checksum over the byte sequence. If the payload is modified while in transit or in memory, tamper_check() detects the mismatch and raises a TamperDetectedError:

computed_sha = hashlib.sha256(self.raw_body).hexdigest()
if content_sha256 is None:
    self.content_sha256 = computed_sha
else:
    self.content_sha256 = content_sha256
    if self.content_sha256 != computed_sha:
        raise TamperDetectedError(
            f"Integrity check failed: expected {self.content_sha256}, calculated {computed_sha}"
        )

3. Native Signature Verification

The script supports GitHub (sha256= or sha1=) and Stripe timestamped signatures (t=...,v1=...). It handles timestamp extraction and compares signatures using hmac.compare_digest to prevent timing attacks:

def compute_github_signature(raw_body: bytes, secret: bytes) -> str:
    """Computes standard sha256=<hex> HMAC signature."""
    mac = hmac.new(secret, raw_body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return f"sha256={mac}"

For Stripe signatures, the verification logic inspects tolerance windows and computes HMAC over the concatenated timestamp and raw body:

payload = f"{ts}.".encode("utf-8") + raw_body
expected_mac = hmac.new(secret, payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

for sig in signatures:
    if hmac.compare_digest(expected_mac, sig):
        return True

4. Binary BLOB Storage in SQLite

Headers and payloads are stored directly in SQLite without translating JSON data into string encodings that could mutate formatting. Headers are parsed into a case-insensitive map, serialized to colon-delimited lines, and the payload is saved as a raw BLOB using sqlite3.Binary:

cursor.execute(
    """
    INSERT OR REPLACE INTO webhooks (
        record_id, target_url, method, headers_raw,
        raw_body, content_sha256, created_at, retry_count, status, last_error
    ) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
    """,
    (
        record.record_id,
        record.target_url,
        record.method,
        headers_serialized,
        sqlite3.Binary(record.raw_body),
        record.content_sha256,
        record.created_at,
        record.retry_count,
        record.status,
        record.last_error,
    ),
)

Limitations

Before deploying this script, note the limitations present in its current implementation:

  • Built-in Scheme Support: verify_signature only implements verification schemes for GitHub and Stripe formats. If your provider uses a different header structure or signing format, you must write custom verification code.
  • Header Serialization: Header storage serializes headers into single-line key:value pairs separated by newline characters (\n). Multi-line header values or values containing literal newline characters will have those characters stripped.
  • In-Memory Buffering: RewindableStreamWrapper loads the entire raw request into an in-memory io.BytesIO buffer. While suitable for standard webhooks, it is not designed to stream multi-gigabyte payloads.
  • In-Memory SQLite Concurrency: When using :memory: databases, state is isolated to the specific database connection created at instantiation and cannot be shared across multiple processes.

FAQ

Can I re-serialize JSON payloads using json.dumps instead of saving raw bytes?

No. Standard JSON encoders do not guarantee preservation of original key ordering, whitespace padding, or Unicode escape patterns. Any change to the serialized byte string invalidates HMAC verification computed against the original transmission.

What happens if a payload is modified after being saved?

When tamper_check() runs, or when a record is loaded and verified, RawHookRecord compares the SHA-256 digest of self.raw_body to the stored content_sha256. If the bytes do not match, it raises a TamperDetectedError.

Does RawHook require installing external database drivers or HTTP libraries?

No. The implementation relies entirely on Python's built-in standard library, utilizing sqlite3 for local persistence and hmac/hashlib for signature verification. No third-party packages need to be installed.

Full version, tests and changelog: RawHook Webhook Retry Helper on PyForge.

title: Python Day 7: Positional-Only, Keyword-Only Arguments and Return Statement
description:
1. Positional-Only Arguments (/)

In Python, / is used as a positional-only argument separator.

It means that the parameters written before / must be passed using their position. We cannot pass them using parameter names (keyword arguments).

Example:

def calculate(a, b, /):
    print(a + b)

calculate(10, 20)  # 30
calculate(a=10, b=20)  # TypeError

TypeError: calculate() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments

Here, a and b must be passed as positional arguments.

2. Keyword-Only Arguments (*)

In Python, * can be used as a keyword-only argument separator.

It means that the parameters written after * must be passed using their parameter names.

Example:

def calculate(a, *, b):
    print(a + b)

calculate(a=10, b=20)  # 30
calculate(10, b=20)    # 30
calculate(10, 20)      # Error

TypeError: calculate() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given

Here:

  • a can be passed as either a positional or keyword argument.
  • b must be passed as a keyword argument.

Difference Between / and *

Symbol Meaning
/ Parameters before it are positional-only
* Parameters after it are keyword-only

Remember:

  • / separates positional-only parameters.
  • * separates keyword-only parameters.

Return Statement in Python

The return statement is used to send a value from a function back to the place where the function was called.

Example:

def play():
    teamA = 300
    teamB = 290

    if teamA > teamB:
        return "Winner Trophy"
    else:
        return "Runner Trophy"

hand = play()
print(hand)


Output:

Winner Trophy

title: Fixing PyInstaller --onefile tmpfs Issues by Switching to --onedir and Clarifying Size Myths
description:
Anatomy of the --onefile vs. --onedir Bundle and the Size Myth

When you pass --onefile to PyInstaller, the build tool does not strip dead code, prune unused shared libraries, or shrink your Python interpreter. Instead, the bootloader appends a compressed archive (typically using zlib or LZMA) containing the exact same set of .pyc bytecode files, .so/.dll shared objects, and data assets that a --onedir build places into a directory tree. If your bundle contains a 600 MB scientific or machine learning stack, --onefile still carries all 600 MB of underlying payload inside that single executable. Any file-size reduction you observe on disk comes from archive compression ratios minus a small bootloader stub, whereas at runtime the uncompressed bytes must be written out anyway—meaning --onefile often inflates temporary storage pressure rather than saving space.

The physical cause of tmpfs failures lies in how a --onefile binary boots. When launched, the C bootloader reads the embedded archive, decompresses each entry, and writes the unpacked files into a temporary directory—commonly under /tmp or TMPDIR—before loading the embedded Python runtime from those extracted files. Because tmpfs stores files in page cache backed by system RAM and swap rather than a persistent block device, every decompressed byte occupies volatile memory pages or hits a strict tmpfs size cap (such as a container's default 64 MB /dev/shm or tight /tmp mount). As decompressed bytes accumulate in tmpfs, free memory pages shrink or the mount hits its quota; once exhausted, the write syscall fails with ENOSPC (no space left on device) or the kernel's out-of-memory (OOM) killer terminates the process.

Startup latency follows a parallel mechanical chain. Under --onefile, cold start requires sequential decompression and filesystem writes of potentially hundreds of megabytes into the temporary directory on every invocation, followed by dynamic linker symbol resolution and Python imports. Under --onedir, the files already sit unpacked on disk or in an existing directory, so launching skips the full-bundle decompression-and-extraction pass and goes straight to loading shared libraries and executing Python code. However, --onedir is not universally faster: if a network filesystem has high metadata latency across thousands of small files, or if a warm tmpfs page cache already holds the extracted payload while cold storage is slow, those local I/O dynamics can shift the balance.

Decision Dominance: Choosing Between --onedir and --onefile

  • Optimal default for tmpfs-constrained and production runtimes: --onedir. By eliminating runtime self-extraction into volatile temporary storage, --onedir avoids ENOSPC quota exhaustion and avoids duplicating payload bytes across both archive/page cache and extracted files in RAM-backed tmpfs. It is strictly more reliable than --onefile when temporary space is bounded or memory is tight.
  • When --onedir stops working: When the deployment target only permits distributing a single standalone binary file with no directory bundle or archive wrapper allowed, or when the target filesystem has severe per-file open/stat overhead across thousands of tiny dependency files and cannot be pre-staged.
  • Typical choice errors and their mechanism: Engineers frequently pick --onefile assuming single-file packaging shrinks the application, when in reality compression only trades CPU decompression time for a smaller transfer artifact while expanding back to full size in tmpfs at runtime. Another common mistake is pointing TMPDIR at a larger tmpfs mount without checking total system RAM: expanding tmpfs capacity without sufficient backing RAM/swap simply allows a giant extraction to push the host closer to OOM eviction.
  • Selection rule: If /tmp or TMPDIR is backed by memory-capped tmpfs, or if cold-start speed and predictable memory headroom matter more than a single-file artifact -> use --onedir. Only use --onefile when a single-file executable is a hard distribution requirement and the target environment has ample temporary storage and RAM headroom to absorb full decompression on every launch.

Why --onefile Breaks on tmpfs: Extraction, Memory, and Execution Constraints

When a PyInstaller --onefile executable launches, a compiled C bootloader opens its own binary image, locates the trailing archive appended during build, decompresses entries (typically zlib or LZMA), and writes every extracted file into a temporary directory under TMPDIR or /tmp before starting the embedded Python runtime. When that target directory sits on a tmpfs mount, those writes do not hit a disk block layer; they allocate kernel page cache backed by physical RAM and swap. Switching to --onedir eliminates this runtime extraction phase because the bootloader loads pre-unpacked .pyc bytecode, shared libraries, and data files directly from disk rather than materializing a second copy in volatile memory.

A common assumption is that --onefile shrinks an application because it produces a single file. It does not prune unused modules, strip dead bytecode, or shrink shared libraries; it packages the same dependency graph as --onedir inside a compressed container plus a bootloader stub. Any file-size reduction comes strictly from archive compression minus bootloader overhead, while runtime execution still inflates the uncompressed payload.

Core Failure Mechanics on tmpfs

  • Mount cap exhaustion (ENOSPC): Each extracted file written to a size-capped tmpfs mount consumes filesystem blocks out of the mount's configured capacity limit. Once uncompressed bytes plus filesystem metadata exceed that cap, the kernel rejects further write syscalls with ENOSPC, aborting bootloader extraction before Python starts.
  • Page-cache and RAM pressure (OOM killer): Because tmpfs stores file contents in memory pages rather than persistent blocks, extracting a large scientific or AI bundle expands anonymous/page-cache memory usage while the Python process simultaneously allocates heap for interpreters and loaded .so libraries. When total memory and swap demand crosses the cgroup or system limit, the kernel out-of-memory (OOM) killer terminates the process.
  • Noexec and permission enforcement: Bootloaders unpack shared libraries and helper binaries into the temp directory and invoke dynamic linking or execution against those extracted paths. If the tmpfs mount carries noexec or restricted permissions, loading shared objects or executing extracted binaries fails at the kernel/loader boundary even when free space and RAM remain available.
  • Cold-start extraction latency: Every cold launch of a --onefile binary repeats archive scanning, decompression CPU work, and temp-directory file creation before symbol resolution and module imports even begin. A --onedir build bypasses decompression and write amplification on launch, moving straight to opening existing files.

Five Deployment Scenarios Where --onefile Fails

Deployment Scenario Physical Constraint Causal Failure Chain Observable Effect
Restricted container /tmp Capped tmpfs on /tmp with tight container memory limit Bootloader decompresses bundle into /tmp -> page cache fills capped tmpfs or pushes cgroup memory to limit -> write returns ENOSPC or cgroup OOM kills task Immediate startup crash with extraction write error or silent exit code 137
Shared-memory /tmp mapped to /dev/shm /tmp symlinked or bound to small /dev/shm segment Unpacked shared libraries and data exceed small shared-memory cap -> page allocation hits segment ceiling -> archive unpack halts mid-stream Partial temp folder and failed PyInstaller bootloader extraction error
Hardened Linux runtime with noexec /tmp tmpfs mounted with noexec (and sometimes nosuid/nodev) Bootloader writes .so or binary payloads to /tmp -> dlopen or execve hits noexec mount flag -> kernel blocks code execution Dynamic linker or permission/execution failure during runtime initialization
High-concurrency worker autoscaling Multiple --onefile workers starting simultaneously on one host Concurrent processes decompress duplicate bundles into tmpfs -> multiplied page-cache footprint and CPU decompression contention -> memory exhausts host RAM/swap Cascading OOM kills and multi-second startup spikes across workers
Low-RAM embedded or edge Linux node Limited physical RAM with little or no swap Decompressed payload plus Python/ML runtime heap exceeds physical page frames -> memory reclaim cannot free pinned/active pages -> kernel OOM killer triggers Process killed mid-import or right after extraction completes

--onedir vs. --onefile: Effectiveness and Edge Cases

--onedir is the optimal default for server, container, and edge deployments. By keeping files unpacked in a directory, it removes per-launch decompression work, avoids duplicate byte materialization inside tmpfs, and makes memory consumption much more predictable. It also matches actual on-disk payload reality: a 600 MB scientific or AI stack is roughly 600 MB of actual code, libraries, and data either way, so --onefile is trading startup time and runtime memory/temp overhead for single-file convenience rather than shrinking the real application footprint.

Even --onedir stops working cleanly under specific edge conditions. If a distribution pipeline strictly mandates a single standalone binary with zero supporting directories or wrapper scripts, --onedir does not meet that packaging constraint. In addition, when a --onedir bundle containing thousands of small files sits on a high-metadata-latency network filesystem without pre-staging, repeated open and stat round-trips across many tiny files can slow startup, whereas a warm tmpfs page cache or slow cold storage can invert relative I/O costs between the two modes.

Typical Choice Errors and Selection Rule

  • Treating --onefile as a footprint shrinker: Teams often pick --onefile expecting a smaller app, overlooking that archive compression only packs the same underlying dependencies on disk while unpacking them back into memory or temp storage at runtime.
  • Raising tmpfs size without RAM/swap headroom: Increasing a tmpfs TMPDIR limit lets extraction write more bytes into page cache, which removes ENOSPC only to push total memory usage past physical RAM and swap into an OOM kill.
  • Pointing TMPDIR at a noexec mount: Redirecting TMPDIR to another tmpfs volume without checking mount flags can still block shared-library loading if noexec is set.

Decision rule: If /tmp or TMPDIR is backed by a memory-capped tmpfs, or if cold-start speed and predictable RAM headroom matter more than a single file, use --onedir; use --onefile only when a hard single-file requirement applies and temp storage plus RAM/swap have enough headroom for full per-launch extraction.

Fixing PyInstaller --onefile tmpfs Issues by Switching to --onedir and Clarifying Size Myths

When a Python service or CLI tool built with PyInstaller --onefile starts failing inside containers, restricted Linux pods, or low-memory nodes, the culprit is almost always how the bootloader handles temporary storage on tmpfs. Switching from --onefile to --onedir is the right fix in most server and container environments. It eliminates per-launch extraction onto memory-backed temporary filesystems, cuts cold-start overhead, and preserves predictable memory headroom without actually costing you real-world application size.

A common misconception is that --onefile shrinks your application. It does not prune unused imports, strip dead bytecode, or drop shared libraries from your dependency graph. It takes the exact same set of .pyc files, .so or .dll shared objects, and data files that --onedir places into a folder, compresses them into a trailing archive (typically zlib or LZMA), and attaches a C bootloader stub. If your scientific or AI stack unpacks to 600 MB, all 600 MB of underlying code and libraries still exist inside the single binary. The single executable looks smaller on disk only because the archive is compressed minus the bootloader stub's bytes; the moment it runs, those compressed bytes must be decompressed and written back out in uncompressed form.

Why --onefile Breaks on tmpfs

Unlike a persistent block device such as an ext4 or XFS disk partition, tmpfs stores files in volatile page cache backed by physical RAM and swap. When a --onefile binary launches, its C bootloader reads its own trailing archive, decompresses entries in sequence, and writes the unpacked files into a temporary directory under TMPDIR or /tmp before starting the embedded Python runtime.

  • Mount cap exhaustion (ENOSPC): Writing uncompressed shared libraries and assets into a size-capped tmpfs mount allocates page cache entries against that mount limit. Once the unpacked payload plus filesystem metadata hits the cap, the kernel rejects subsequent write syscalls with ENOSPC, aborting startup before Python imports even begin.
  • RAM and swap pressure (OOM killer): Every byte written to tmpfs consumes memory pages alongside the Python interpreter heap, NumPy or PyTorch allocations, and mapped shared libraries. When combined page cache and process memory cross a cgroup limit or host RAM-plus-swap capacity, memory reclaim cannot free enough clean pages fast enough, and the Linux OOM killer terminates the process (often surfacing as exit code 137).
  • Hardened mount permissions (noexec): Security-hardened containers frequently mount /tmp or TMPDIR with noexec (often paired with nosuid and nodev). Even when free space and RAM are plentiful, extracting .so libraries or helper binaries into a noexec mount causes dynamic linking (dlopen) or execution (execve) to fail with permission errors because the kernel blocks code execution from that mount.
  • Concurrent worker spikes: Scaling out multiple --onefile workers on one host triggers simultaneous archive decompression and page-cache growth across processes, compounding CPU load and pushing shared RAM/swap into contention or OOM kills.

Comparative Trade-Offs: Reliability, Startup Latency, and Operational Overhead

Choosing between --onedir and --onefile is an operational trade-off between single-artifact convenience and runtime determinism. Once unpacked, both modes load shared objects and execute Python bytecode in the same general runtime model, but --onefile pays an extraction tax on every cold start while competing for tmpfs memory.

  • Containerization and memory predictability: In Docker or Kubernetes, --onedir copies a pre-unpacked directory into the container image layer once at build time. At runtime, shared libraries and data files are read straight from the container filesystem rather than duplicated into a memory-capped tmpfs /tmp or /dev/shm. That keeps memory usage much more predictable under tight cgroup limits.
  • CI/CD and artifact distribution: --onefile wins on raw distribution simplicity when you must ship a single standalone file over a basic upload step, copy it to an air-gapped target, or hand a single binary to users without packaging a tarball or zip archive. --onedir requires archiving and unpacking a directory (such as a .tar.gz) in your build and deploy pipeline, adding a small packaging step in CI/CD so runtime hosts do not have to unpack on every launch.
  • Filesystem permissions and hardening: Because --onedir lives in a known application directory (for example, /opt/app) rather than extracting executables into /tmp at runtime, it avoids noexec failures on /tmp and makes file ownership and read/execute permissions explicit at deploy time.
  • Cold-start speed: Every --onefile cold launch must scan the archive, run decompression CPU cycles, and create temporary files before Python starts importing modules. --onedir skips full-bundle extraction and goes straight to opening existing files and resolving symbols, making cold starts faster in standard local and container setups.

Edge Cases and Failure Modes of --onedir

--onedir is not immune to environmental bottlenecks. If you place a large --onedir bundle containing thousands of small .pyc and dependency files onto a high-metadata-latency network filesystem (such as certain remote NFS or shared mounts) without pre-staging locally, repeated open and stat calls during Python startup can introduce noticeable latency—sometimes enough to invert the usual startup advantage over a warm tmpfs cache. It also falls short whenever a distribution policy strictly forbids a directory bundle or wrapper script.

Engineers running into --onefile tmpfs errors frequently make three mechanical mistakes: treating --onefile as if it shrinks runtime memory or dependency size; enlarging a tmpfs TMPDIR limit without adding backing RAM or swap (which simply shifts failures from ENOSPC to OOM kills); or pointing TMPDIR to another tmpfs path without checking whether noexec is set.

Decision Rule

If /tmp or TMPDIR sits on a memory-capped tmpfs, or if cold-start speed and predictable RAM headroom matter more than shipping a single file, use --onedir. Use --onefile only when a strict single-file requirement applies and the target host has enough temporary storage, non-noexec permissions, and RAM/swap headroom to absorb full decompression on every launch.

Why --onedir Beats --onefile on tmpfs and What --onefile Actually Shrinks

When a PyInstaller --onefile binary fails on tmpfs, the failure is not a quirk of PyInstaller being picky about temporary folders—it is a resource collision between archive decompression and memory-backed filesystem allocation. Switching to --onedir is the right move for servers, containers, and edge runtimes because it eliminates per-launch self-extraction, keeps memory consumption predictable, and exposes the true uncompressed size of your application rather than hiding it behind a zip or LZMA wrapper.

A common myth is that --onefile shrinks the application. It does not prune unused imports, strip dead bytecode, or drop heavy scientific or AI libraries from the dependency graph. It packs the exact same .pyc files, shared libraries (.so or .dll), and data assets into a compressed archive appended to a C bootloader stub. On disk, the single binary looks smaller only because archive compression (such as zlib or LZMA) squeezes repetitive bytes minus the bootloader overhead. At runtime, the bootloader still decompresses that payload and writes the full unpacked tree to disk before embedded Python starts. A 600 MB scientific or numerical stack is still 600 MB of code and libraries once materialized.

How --onefile Breaks tmpfs and Inflates Startup Latency

Unlike a persistent block device such as ext4 or XFS, tmpfs stores files in volatile kernel page cache backed by physical RAM and swap. When a --onefile process launches, its C bootloader reads the trailing archive, decompresses entries sequentially, and issues write syscalls into TMPDIR (often /tmp) before Python imports begin. Each causal failure chain traces directly to that extraction step:

  • Mount cap exhaustion (ENOSPC): Sequential decompression writes uncompressed files plus filesystem metadata into tmpfs page cache -> allocated pages reach the tmpfs size cap -> subsequent write syscalls fail with ENOSPC -> startup aborts before Python initializes.
  • RAM and swap pressure (OOM killer, exit code 137): Decompressed tmpfs pages expand concurrently with the Python heap, numerical or ML array allocations, and mapped shared libraries -> total anonymous and page-cache memory crosses the cgroup or host RAM-plus-swap ceiling faster than page reclaim can free clean or movable pages -> the Linux OOM killer terminates the process with exit code 137.
  • Hardened mount enforcement (noexec): Security-hardened hosts mount /tmp or TMPDIR with noexec (often alongside nosuid and nodev) -> the bootloader extracts .so libraries or helper binaries into that directory, then calls dlopen or execve -> the kernel blocks execution on the noexec mount despite free space and free RAM -> dynamic linking or binary launch fails immediately.
  • Concurrent worker spikes: Multiple --onefile workers start on the same host simultaneously -> parallel decompression multiplies CPU load while multiple tmpfs directories expand page cache at once -> host memory pressure spikes and triggers cascading OOM kills or multi-second startup stalls.
  • Cold-start overhead: Every cold launch repeats archive scanning, decompression CPU cycles, and temp-file creation before module imports even start, whereas --onedir opens pre-extracted files directly.

Decision Framework and Migration Checklist for Moving to --onedir

Between the two modes, --onedir is the superior default whenever you control the runtime environment, care about cold-start speed, or run inside memory-constrained containers and edge nodes. It places pre-unpacked files in an explicit directory (such as /opt/app) with deterministic ownership and permissions, avoiding tmpfs bloat and /tmp noexec traps.

--onedir stops working cleanly under two clear conditions: first, when distribution policy or packaging rules strictly require a single standalone executable with no supporting directory or wrapper; second, when a bundle containing thousands of small files is placed directly on a high-latency network filesystem (such as remote NFS) without local staging, where thousands of open and stat round-trips can make startup slower than unpacking into a warm local cache.

Engineers frequently make three avoidable mistakes when troubleshooting --onefile tmpfs failures. First, they assume --onefile reduces runtime RAM or trims unused dependencies, ignoring that unpacked artifacts still enter memory or page cache. Second, they enlarge the tmpfs size cap without adding backing RAM or swap, which merely trades an ENOSPC write error for an OOM kill when memory fills. Third, they point TMPDIR at another tmpfs mount without checking whether noexec is set, leaving dlopen and execve blocked.

Selection rule: If /tmp or TMPDIR sits on a memory-capped tmpfs, or if cold-start latency, predictable cgroup memory headroom, and explicit file permissions matter most, use --onedir. Use --onefile only when a strict single-file requirement applies and the target host provides enough temporary storage, non-noexec permissions, and RAM-plus-swap headroom for full decompression on every launch.

If --onefile must stay in place temporarily, contain the blast radius by setting TMPDIR to a non-noexec persistent or local scratch path with verified free space, sizing RAM and swap above peak unpacked payload plus runtime heap, and staging concurrent worker starts rather than launching dozens in lockstep.

  • Switch the build spec to --onedir: Update your PyInstaller build command or .spec file from --onefile to --onedir and inspect the actual uncompressed directory size and largest dependencies.
  • Package and transfer as an archive: Bundle the output directory (for example, with tar.gz) in CI/CD so artifacts move cleanly between build stages, registries, or release hosts.
  • Install into a non-tmpfs directory with explicit permissions: Extract the bundle into a persistent path such as /opt/app (or bake it into the container image layer at build time) with explicit read/execute permissions and ownership rather than relying on /tmp.
  • Avoid high-latency network mounts for raw --onedir trees: If deploying to network storage, copy or unpack onto local disk or container storage before execution rather than serving thousands of small files over a high-latency share.
  • Verify cold-start latency and cgroup memory under concurrency: Benchmark startup time and peak RSS/cgroup memory with realistic worker concurrency, confirming tmpfs usage stays flat and exit code 137 OOM kills disappear.

title: React useReducer – Interview Questions & Answers
description:
Q1. What is useReducer in React?

  • useReducer is a React Hook used to manage state using a reducer function and actions.
  • It is useful when state logic becomes complex or when multiple actions update the same state. 
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);

state – current state value.
dispatch – function used to send an action.
reducer – function that decides how state changes.
initialState – initial value of the state.

Q2. What is a reducer function?
A reducer is a function that takes two arguments:

  1. Current state
  2. Action It returns the updated state.

syntax:

function reducer(state, action) {
    return newState;
}

Example:

function reducer(state, action) {
    switch (action.type) {
        case "Increment":
            return state + 1;

        case "Decrement":
            return state - 1;

        case "Reset":
            return 0;

        default:
            return state;
    }
}

Q3. What is dispatch?
dispatch is a function used to send an action to the reducer.
Q4. What is an action in useReducer?
An action is an object that describes what we want to do with the state.
Q5. What is the purpose of action.type?
action.type identifies which action was dispatched.

Q6 Practical coding interview – Counter using useReducer
This is one of the most common coding questions for React interviews.
Requirements

  • Increment
  • Decrement
  • Reset
  • Increment by 5 
import React, { useReducer } from 'react';

function reducer(state, action) {
    switch (action.type) {
        case "Increment":
            return state + 1;

        case "Decrement":
            return state - 1;

        case "IncrementByFive":
            return state + action.payload;

        case "Reset":
            return 0;

        default:
            return state;
    }
}

function App() {
    const [count, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, 0);

    return (
        <>
            <h1>{count}</h1>

            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "Increment" })}>
                Increment
            </button>

            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "Decrement" })}>
                Decrement
            </button>

            <button onClick={() => dispatch({
                type: "IncrementByFive",
                payload: 5
            })}>
                +5
            </button>

            <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: "Reset" })}>
                Reset
            </button>
        </>
    );
}

export default App;

title: Introducing ONCSS: A Lightweight CSS-in-JS Library for Modern JavaScript Applications
description:
I've been working on ONCSS, a CSS-in-JS library designed to make styling modern web applications simple, flexible, and developer-friendly.

Instead of writing separate CSS files for every component, ONCSS lets you define styles directly in JavaScript using a familiar object-based API.

Why ONCSS?

ONCSS provides a css() function that generates and injects CSS dynamically.

Here's a quick example:

import css from "oncss";

const button = css({
  backgroundColor: "#2563eb",
  color: "#fff",
  padding: "10px 20px",
  borderRadius: "8px",

  "&:hover": {
    backgroundColor: "#1d4ed8",
  },

  "@media (min-width: 768px)": {
    padding: "14px 28px",
  },
});

function Button() {
  return <button className={button}>Click me</button>;
}

Features

  • Object-based CSS styling
  • Nested selectors and pseudo-classes
  • Responsive media queries
  • Custom breakpoints
  • Dynamic keyframes and animations
  • Global styles
  • CSS at-rules: @media, @container, @layer, @supports
  • Custom aliases and CSS property transformations
  • Configurable style injection
  • TypeScript support
  • Server-side rendering support

Installation 

npm install oncss

Built for flexibility

ONCSS also supports customization through configuration options such as classPrefix, breakpoints, aliases, injectStyle, and custom property handlers.

It also provides CSSFactory for collecting generated styles during server-side rendering.

I'm building ONCSS as an open-source project and would appreciate feedback from developers who work with React and modern JavaScript styling.

Check it out:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/devnax/oncss
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/oncss

If you try it, I'd love to hear what you think and what features you'd like to see next.

title: How to Choose a Programming Language for a New Web Application
description:
Every new project starts with the same argument. Someone on the team wants to use the language they picked up last month, someone else says "just use what we know," and a third person has read a benchmark on the internet that settles everything, or so they claim. An hour later nothing is decided and the kickoff meeting is over.

Here's the thing nobody says out loud: for most web applications, there isn't one correct language. There are several decent ones and a handful of bad fits. Your job is to avoid the bad fits and not lose sleep over picking the absolute best. This post walks through how I'd think about it, in the order I'd think about it.

Start with what the app actually needs to do

Before comparing languages, write down what you're building in plain terms. A content-heavy marketing site, a real-time chat tool, an internal dashboard, an online store and a data-heavy analytics product all push on different things.

A few questions help here:

  • Is it mostly pages and forms, or does it need live updates, such as notifications, chat or collaborative editing?

  • Will it do heavy calculation, process large files, or run machine learning models?

  • How many users do you expect in year one, and is that number realistic or hopeful?

  • Does it need to talk to a lot of third-party services or existing systems?

  • Will there be a mobile app later that shares the same backend?

If the honest answer is "it's mostly forms and a database," you have a lot of freedom. If it's real-time or compute-heavy, your options narrow quickly.

Frontend and backend are separate decisions

This trips up beginners a lot. In the browser you don't really get a choice: it's JavaScript, or something that compiles down to it, like TypeScript. Frameworks such as React, Vue or Svelte sit on top of that.
The backend is where you actually pick. That's the part running on a server, handling data, logins, payments and business rules. Here the common contenders are:

JavaScript or TypeScript (Node.js). Handy if your team already writes JavaScript on the frontend, because one language across the stack means fewer context switches and easier hiring. It handles lots of simultaneous connections well, which suits real-time features and APIs.

Python. Readable, quick to write, and the obvious choice when your product leans on data analysis or machine learning. Frameworks like Django and FastAPI are mature and well documented. Raw speed isn't its strongest trait, though for most apps that never becomes the bottleneck.

PHP. It gets mocked more than it deserves. A huge portion of the web still runs on it, hosting is cheap and everywhere, and Laravel is genuinely pleasant to work with. For content sites and standard business apps it remains a practical option.

Java or C#. Common in larger organisations and for systems where structure, strict typing and long-term maintainability matter. They take longer to get started with, but they scale well in big teams and codebases.

Go or Rust. Great when performance and efficiency are the point, such as high-traffic services or infrastructure tools. Both have steeper learning curves, and the hiring pool is smaller than for the others.

None of these is "best." Each is best at something.

The factors that matter more than benchmarks

People love comparing speed numbers. In practice, a few less exciting factors tend to decide whether a project goes well.

What your team already knows. A team that's comfortable in a language will ship faster and write fewer bugs than a team learning a trendier one on the job. Learning is fine when you have time for it. A deadline isn't the time.

Hiring and long-term support. Think about who will maintain this in three years. Popular languages mean a bigger talent pool and more answers when someone gets stuck. A niche language can be wonderful and still become a staffing headache.

The ecosystem. Look at the libraries, frameworks and tools available for what you need. Authentication, payments, email, file uploads and admin panels are all problems you don't want to solve from scratch. The language with a ready-made, well-maintained solution saves you weeks.

Community and maturity. Active communities mean fixed bugs, regular security patches and plenty of tutorials. Check when the main framework last had a release and how quickly security issues get handled.

Scalability, honestly assessed. Almost any mainstream language can scale if the architecture is sound. Most apps that struggle under load do so because of database queries and design choices, not the language itself. Don't pick something exotic to solve a problem you may never have.

Cost. Developer salaries, hosting and tooling all vary. A language that's cheap to run but expensive to hire for (or the reverse) changes the real budget.

Common mistakes worth avoiding

Chasing hype is the big one. A new language or framework can look amazing in demos and still lack the libraries, documentation and people you'll need when something breaks at 11pm.

The second is over-planning for scale. Building for ten million users when you have ten usually means building something slower to deliver and harder to change. Start with something your team can ship, and refactor when real growth shows you where the pressure is.

The third is ignoring the future shape of the product. If you already know a mobile app, a public API or machine learning features are coming, make sure your choice doesn't make those painful.

A simple way to decide

If you're stuck, try this short process:

  1. Write down your core requirements and your biggest risks.
  2. List two or three languages that fit those requirements.
  3. Score each on team familiarity, ecosystem, hiring and long-term support.
  4. Build a small proof of concept for the riskiest feature in your top choice.
  5. Decide, write down why, and move on.

Step four is underrated. A weekend spent prototyping the hardest part tells you more than a month of reading comparison articles.

When it helps to bring in outside input

Sometimes the right call is to talk it through with people who build web applications every day. If you're a business owner without a technical team, or a team weighing a big architectural decision, an experienced development partner can pressure-test your assumptions before you commit budget. A custom web development team such as iWebwiser is the kind of option you can look at if you want help matching your requirements to a technology stack and building the application around it.

Whoever you speak with, ask them to explain why they recommend a given stack. A good answer references your needs, not their preferences.

Final thoughts

Choosing a programming language for a web application isn't a one-way door. It matters, but less than most debates suggest. Pick something that fits the problem, that your team can work with confidently, and that has a healthy ecosystem behind it. Then spend your energy on what actually decides whether an app succeeds: understanding your users and shipping something useful.

What did you pick for your last web project, and would you pick it again? Share it in the comments.

title: When you replace a library, you also take over everything it did
description:
DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants the text of privacy law. Its search runs on the CPU, so it needs no GPU.

The usual way to run an embedding model in Python is sentence-transformers. DPOLens doesn't use it: with PyTorch's CPU build it installs about 1 GB, against about 200 MB for ONNX Runtime, the tokenizers library and NumPy. So DPOLens calls the model through ONNX Runtime directly, and does the tokenising and pooling itself, in about forty lines.

Those forty lines did their job. What they didn't do was what the library does without being asked. When a new instance starts for the first time, it embeds every clause of the law it carries, and while load-testing the community version, I found that this was the heaviest thing DPOLens ever did. In a container limited to 1.5 CPUs, about what a small server offers, it took nearly 23 minutes and peaked at 3.4 GB.

Two fixes made it 5.1× faster with 65% less memory, and the vectors came out the same. If you've swapped sentence-transformers for raw ONNX Runtime to slim an image, you probably have both problems too.

The setup

DPOLens's meaning search uses multilingual-e5-small. A new instance embeds GDPR, the UAE's data protection law and a sample company policy: 1,350 clauses, from 19 to 512 tokens long, 63 in the middle. The vectors go into Postgres with pgvector, so this happens once, before the instance answers anything.

Every run below embedded those 1,350 clauses inside the published DPOLens 0.1.0 image, the release before the fixes, from a fresh copy of the same database, with 4 GB of memory and a Docker CPU limit: 1.5 CPUs, 2.5 (what the community version gives this step), or none, which on my laptop is 10 cores.

What the library was doing: sorting by length

A model reads a batch as one rectangle. Every string is padded to the longest in its batch, and the padding costs as much work as the text.

sentence-transformers sorts its inputs by length before it batches them, so each batch holds strings of about one length. My forty lines didn't. They embedded 64 clauses at a time in the order they're stored, so a 20-token paragraph next to a 512-token article was read as 512 tokens. I counted: the clauses hold 110,000 real tokens, and the model read 304,000. Almost two thirds of its work was padding.

Padding costs memory too, and more than its share: the memory for attention grows with the number of strings in a batch times the square of the longest. A batch of 64 strings at 512 tokens was the heaviest shape 0.1.0 could make, and in stored order, every batch with one long article had that shape. Sorting alone doesn't prevent it, since the library still batches by count, so the fix also caps each batch by that measure, in the spirit of --max-batch-tokens in Hugging Face's Text Embeddings Inference:

# How much one batch may hold, as its clauses times the square of the longest,
# which is how the memory for attention grows: 64 clauses of 64 tokens, 16 of
# 128, or one of 512.
BATCH_BUDGET = 64 * 64 * 64

def batches(tokens: Sequence[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    found: list[list[int]] = []
    batch: list[int] = []
    for at in sorted(range(len(tokens)), key=lambda position: tokens[position]):
        # Sorted, so this string is the longest the batch would hold.
        if batch and (len(batch) + 1) * tokens[at] ** 2 > BATCH_BUDGET:
            found.append(batch)
            batch = []
        batch.append(at)
    if batch:
        found.append(batch)
    return found

Sorted and capped, the model reads 114,000 tokens instead of 304,000, and the longest clauses go one at a time. Budgets from half this one to eight times it were no better.

What nobody was doing: reading the CPU limit

The second problem isn't the library's.

Inside a container limited to 2.5 CPUs on a 10-core machine, Python's os.cpu_count() says 10, and ONNX Runtime, left to choose, starts a thread for each of them. A Docker CPU limit isn't a set of cores but a share of time, so ten threads took turns on two and a half CPUs' worth of it.

dpolens index build now reads the limit from /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max and rounds it up, so 2.5 CPUs get three threads. With no limit, it takes os.process_cpu_count(), which follows CPU affinity but not a time limit. Picking a fixed number doesn't work: three threads were the best with 2.5 CPUs, and with no limit they took 143 seconds, slower than 0.1.0's 129 with all ten.

The results

With 2.5 CPUs, each fix on its own, then both:

Change Seconds Peak memory
0.1.0 632 3,486 MiB
Threads 468 3,488 MiB
Sorted 257 1,427 MiB
Both 174 1,426 MiB
As shipped 163 1,213 MiB

The two sorted rows in the middle used a budget four times the one that shipped. Threads changed the time and nothing else. Sorting changed both.

Then 0.2.0, which shipped both, against 0.1.0 at each limit:

CPU limit Before After Faster
1.5 CPUs 1,375 s 267 s 5.1×
2.5 CPUs 632 s 163 s 3.9×
None 129 s 53 s 2.4×

The gain is largest where the machine is smallest, which is where a 23-minute first start gets noticed. The peak after, 1,213 MiB at every limit, is exactly what loading the model takes before embedding anything: embedding the whole law now adds nothing measurable to it.

Same vectors, same search

Padding is masked, so in theory it changes nothing. I checked anyway. 885 of the 1,350 vectors were bit-identical to 0.1.0's, and the rest differed by at most 0.00000011 in any component, the rounding of a batch with a different shape. Every published evaluation set scored the same recall@5, recall@10 and MRR, and a test now checks that each clause's stored vector is the one it gets embedded alone.

One more: memory that wasn't given back

Measuring the first start also caught DPOLens's worker, which embeds an organisation's policies, loading its own copy of the model for jobs with nothing left to embed, and keeping it. Closing the model wasn't enough either: glibc keeps freed memory for the process, so a process that held 875 MiB with the model loaded still held 440 after closing it, and 93 after malloc_trim(0). The worker now loads the model only when there's work, and gives the memory back after. It doesn't change what an instance needs, but it frees about 900 MB between jobs.

What I took from it

  • A library is more than its API. Forty lines replaced sentence-transformers and kept the image about 800 MB smaller, and they also dropped the sorting the library does without saying so.
  • Sort before you batch, then cap by shape. A batch's memory grows with its strings times the square of the longest, so that's what to limit.
  • A container's CPU limit isn't its core count. os.cpu_count() and ONNX Runtime both see the whole machine. Read /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max, and don't hard-code a number instead.
  • Check the vectors, not only the clock. The same search results are the only reason the change could ship.

Everything here was measured on one laptop, with one model, over clauses whose lengths vary a lot: text of one length would gain little from sorting, and your seconds will differ. The batching is in index.py, the thread count in encode.py, and every measurement, including the options I didn't take, in #68. Both fixes shipped in DPOLens 0.2.0. To run an instance yourself, start with Get started. DPOLens is open source, under the Apache License 2.0.

First published on dpolens.com. DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants privacy law and an organisation's own policies, clause by clause: github.com/alkhatibdev/dpolens.

title: SQL Challenge : How to Find Customers Whose Spending Increased Using LAG()
description:
When working with customer purchase data, looking at individual orders doesn't always tell us the full story.


Sometimes, we need to compare a customer's current purchase with their previous purchase to understand whether their spending is increasing or decreasing.

For example:

  • Did the customer spend more on their latest order?
  • Has their purchase amount increased compared to the previous order?
  • Which customers are spending more over time?

We can solve this using the SQL window function "LAG()".

In this tutorial, let's see how to use "LAG()" with "PARTITION BY" and "ORDER BY" to compare customer purchases in Oracle SQL.

The Problem

Suppose we have a table called "customer_orders" containing customer IDs, order dates, and purchase amounts.

Sample Table: customer_orders

customer_id| order_date| amount
C101| 01-Nov-2026| 1000
C101| 05-Nov-2026| 1500
C101| 10-Nov-2026| 1200
C102| 02-Nov-2026| 500
C102| 08-Nov-2026| 800
C102| 12-Nov-2026| 1000

Your Challenge

Write an SQL query to:

  1. Display customer ID, order date, and purchase amount.
  2. Find the previous purchase amount for each customer using "LAG()".
  3. Compare the current purchase amount with the previous purchase.
  4. Display only records where the purchase amount increased.
  5. Keep each customer's purchase history separate.
  6. Arrange the results by customer ID and order date.

Can you write the query before looking at the solution?

SQL Solution (Oracle)

We can use a subquery with the "LAG()" function to solve this problem.

SELECT
customer_id,
order_date,
amount,
previous_amount
FROM (
SELECT
customer_id,
order_date,
amount,
LAG(amount) OVER (
PARTITION BY customer_id
ORDER BY order_date
) AS previous_amount
FROM customer_orders
)
WHERE amount > previous_amount
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;

Expected Output

customer_id| order_date| amount| previous_amount
C101| 05-Nov-2026| 1500| 1000
C102| 08-Nov-2026| 800| 500
C102| 12-Nov-2026| 1000| 800

Notice that:

  • C101 spent 1500 compared to 1000 on the previous order.
  • C102 spent 800 compared to 500 on the previous order.
  • C102 then spent 1000 compared to 800 on the previous order.

The record for C101 on 10-Nov-2026 is not displayed because the purchase amount decreased from 1500 to 1200.

Why Does This SQL Query Work?

Let's understand the important parts.

  1. LAG(amount)

"LAG()" retrieves a value from a previous row without requiring a self-join.

Here, it retrieves the previous purchase amount.

  1. PARTITION BY customer_id

This separates the purchase history of each customer.

For example, C101's orders are compared only with other C101 orders. The same applies to C102.

  1. ORDER BY order_date

This determines the order in which purchases are compared.

The earliest purchase comes first, followed by the next purchase.

  1. WHERE amount > previous_amount

This condition returns only those records where the current purchase amount is greater than the previous purchase amount.

  1. Why use a subquery?

In Oracle SQL, we cannot directly use an analytic function in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

The subquery first calculates the previous purchase amount. The outer query then filters the results.

One Thing to Remember

  • "LAG()" retrieves a value from a previous row.
  • "LEAD()" retrieves a value from a following row.
  • "PARTITION BY" separates calculations into groups.
  • "ORDER BY" determines the sequence of rows.
  • Window functions are useful for analyzing changes over time.

Your Turn: Try This Next!

How would you modify this query to find customers whose spending decreased compared with their previous purchase?

Hint: Check the comparison operator in the WHERE condition.

Share your SQL query in the comments!

Where Can You Use This in Real Projects?

This type of SQL query is useful in:

  • Customer purchase analysis
  • Sales trend reporting
  • E-commerce analytics
  • Customer spending comparisons
  • Business intelligence dashboards
  • Data analytics projects

Learning window functions like "LAG()", "LEAD()", "ROW_NUMBER()" and "DENSE_RANK()" can help you solve many practical SQL reporting and interview problems.

More SQL tutorials and practical challenges:
https://www.sankalandtech.com/
