Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Many developers assume that creating a foreign key also creates an index on the column. In SQL Server it does not. A primary key or unique constraint automatically gets an index; a foreign key does not. Missing foreign key indexes are one of the most common causes of slow deletes, slow joins and unexpected blocking.

Example 

CREATE TABLE dbo.PayrollLine (
    PayrollLineId BIGINT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    PayrollRunId  INT NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT FK_PayrollLine_PayrollRun REFERENCES dbo.PayrollRun (PayrollRunId),
    EmployeeId    INT NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT FK_PayrollLine_Employee REFERENCES dbo.Employee (EmployeeId),
    Amount        DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL
);

Here PayrollLineId is indexed (primary key), but PayrollRunId and EmployeeId are not.

Problem 1: deleting or updating parent rows

When you delete a row from dbo.PayrollRun, SQL Server must check that no PayrollLine rows still reference it. Without an index on PayrollLine.PayrollRunId, that check scans the entire child table, once per deleted parent row. On a table with millions of lines, deleting one payroll run can take minutes and hold locks on the child table the whole time, blocking other users.

Problem 2: joins and lookups

Almost every query that reads children by parent, such as "all lines for this run" or "all payments for this employee", filters or joins on the foreign key column. Without an index, those queries scan as well.

Problem 3: cascading actions

With ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a parent deletes its children automatically. Without an index, finding those children means scanning, and the cascade can lock large parts of the child table.

Find foreign keys without a supporting index

This query lists foreign keys where no index starts with the foreign key's first column (good enough for most single-column keys):

SELECT
    OBJECT_NAME(fk.parent_object_id)                         AS child_table,
    fk.name                                                  AS foreign_key,
    COL_NAME(fkc.parent_object_id, fkc.parent_column_id)     AS fk_column,
    OBJECT_NAME(fk.referenced_object_id)                     AS parent_table
FROM sys.foreign_keys fk
JOIN sys.foreign_key_columns fkc
     ON fkc.constraint_object_id = fk.object_id
    AND fkc.constraint_column_id = 1
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM sys.index_columns ic
    WHERE ic.object_id  = fkc.parent_object_id
      AND ic.column_id  = fkc.parent_column_id
      AND ic.key_ordinal = 1
)
ORDER BY child_table, foreign_key;

Create the index 

CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_PayrollLine_PayrollRunId
ON dbo.PayrollLine (PayrollRunId);

CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_PayrollLine_EmployeeId
ON dbo.PayrollLine (EmployeeId);

If queries usually filter on the foreign key plus another column, put both in the index (foreign key first) and INCLUDE commonly selected columns, so one index serves both the constraint check and the queries.

Are there exceptions? A tiny child table, or one whose parent rows are never deleted and which you never query by parent, may not need the index. Those are rare; indexing foreign keys is the right default.

Bonus: untrusted foreign keys

If a foreign key was disabled, or created or re-enabled WITH NOCHECK, SQL Server marks it as not trusted. The optimizer then cannot rely on it, for example to skip a join it knows is unnecessary.

-- Find untrusted foreign keys
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS table_name, name
FROM sys.foreign_keys
WHERE is_not_trusted = 1;

-- Re-validate (checks existing rows, so run it in a quiet period)
ALTER TABLE dbo.PayrollLine WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT FK_PayrollLine_PayrollRun;

Quick checklist

  • Remember: foreign keys are not indexed automatically.
  • Run the query above and index foreign keys used in deletes or joins.
  • Combine the foreign key with common filter columns where it helps.
  • Re-validate untrusted foreign keys with WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT.

Related reading:

  • SQL Server Index Tuning for Beginners
  • SQL Server Statistics Explained
  • How to Read a SQL Server Execution Plan

More SQL Server guides on my blog, SQL & Cloud Lab.

title: Figma to Next.js: my process for pixel-perfect, responsive builds
description:
“Pixel-perfect” is easy to promise and hard to deliver, especially on mobile. Here’s the process that keeps my builds close to the design from 360px phones to wide monitors.

1. Read the design before writing code

I go through every frame and list missing pieces: hover and focus states, empty states, error messages, and breakpoints the designer didn’t draw. Asking these questions on day one saves days of rework.

2. Turn Figma styles into design tokens

Colours, font sizes, spacing and radius from Figma become Tailwind theme tokens. That way a button is the same everywhere, and a brand colour change happens in one place.

3. Components first, pages second

  • Buttons, inputs, cards and navigation are built and checked first
  • Sections (hero, features, testimonials) are built from those components
  • Pages are assembled from sections, which makes them consistent and fast to build

4. Compare side by side

I check the build against Figma at the same viewport width, then test real devices. Fluid typography and container queries handle the in-between sizes designers rarely draw.

5. Animate with restraint

Animations use only transform and opacity, respect the reduced-motion setting, and never delay the main content. The page should feel smooth, not slow.

Have a Figma file ready? Send the link and I’ll review it and point out anything missing before we start.

Originally published at sagarbharvadiya.com.

title: Raise MaxIdleConnsPerHost to Prevent Go HTTP/1.1 Connection Churn and High CPU Under Load
description:
Executive Summary and the Hidden Default Trap

Leave Go's http.DefaultClient untouched on a busy HTTP/1.1 service and you hand away up to 8x of your throughput while burning client CPU for nothing. In our benchmarks, comparing default settings against tuning MaxIdleConnsPerHost to match actual in-flight concurrency exposed a brutal cliff: when concurrent requests surge, http.Transport keeps only 2 idle connections per host, forcing every excess request to dial a fresh TCP connection, tear it down later, and push the Linux kernel into expensive ephemeral port searches.

The mechanism is straightforward and unforgiving. Because HTTP/1.1 lacks stream multiplexing, ten or fifty parallel requests to the same upstream service require parallel TCP sockets. Once MaxIdleConnsPerHost hits its cap of 2, extra connections cannot sit idle in Go's pool; they churn through open and close cycles. Every new outbound connection asks the kernel to assign an ephemeral local port from a finite slice—typically 32768-60999 on Linux—while closed sockets enter a mandatory 60-second TIME_WAIT cooldown. As free ports shrink and sockets pile up in TIME_WAIT, kernel port-allocation routines scan wider ranges and contend on locks, turning network setup into client-side CPU starvation.

Why a Legacy Default Breaks High-Concurrency Services

A limit of 2 idle connections per host made sense when Go's standard HTTP client was shaped around classic web browsing and light scraping against a few hosts. Inside a modern Kubernetes cluster, internal microservices hammer the same upstream endpoints over HTTP/1.1 with bursty fan-out traffic. The default transport treats those bursts as transient noise rather than steady concurrency, so sockets get discarded right when the next wave of goroutines needs them.

Teams routinely misdiagnose this failure as a slow downstream server or flaky pod networking. In reality, the client is choking on its own connection churn: impact (concurrent HTTP/1.1 spikes past 2 sockets per host) → internal process (constant TCP handshakes, TIME_WAIT accumulation, and kernel ephemeral port scans) → observable effect (up to an 8x throughput drop, rising client CPU, latency spikes, and occasional address already in use or timeout errors). Upgrading a hop to HTTP/2 can mask the trap via stream multiplexing, which is why pure HTTP/1.1 paths get hit hardest.

  • Optimal baseline fix: Set MaxIdleConnsPerHost to your expected peak concurrent requests in flight to that host, rather than leaving it at 2, and pair it with a sensible global MaxIdleConns cap so idle sockets do not accumulate unbounded memory across many hosts.
  • Typical choice error and why it fails: Leaving MaxIdleConnsPerHost at 2 starves HTTP/1.1 reuse and triggers port churn; blindly setting it to an enormous number like tens of thousands avoids churn only up to memory and file-descriptor limits, after which idle connection retention bloats memory or leaves stale sockets under connection resets.
  • When the fix stops working: Raising MaxIdleConnsPerHost stops helping once concurrency exceeds your configured pool ceiling, when upstream keep-alives close faster than requests arrive, or when shared node port exhaustion and CPU contention are already saturated by neighboring workloads.

Decision rule: If your service talks HTTP/1.1 with concurrency greater than 2 per host → set MaxIdleConnsPerHost to expected peak in-flight requests per host and cap total pool footprint with MaxIdleConns; if you are signed out, signing into a Google Account lets you keep this investigation and your follow-up notes saved for later.

Mechanics of Connection Churn and Kernel Port Contention

When a Go service talks to another over HTTP/1.1, there is no stream multiplexing on a single socket like HTTP/2 gives you. If ten goroutines fire requests to the same host at once, Go needs separate TCP connections to carry them concurrently. That is where MaxIdleConnsPerHost defaulting to 2 turns into a quiet trap. When a burst of twenty requests finishes and returns sockets to the idle pool, the runtime keeps only two alive for that host and closes the rest. On the very next burst, those extra connections are gone, forcing fresh three-way TCP handshakes instead of reusing warm sockets.

Closing those surplus sockets does not immediately free the local networking resources they used. Because HTTP/1.1 connections are routinely torn down or reset between bursts, closed sockets on the client side enter the TIME_WAIT state for a mandatory 60-second window under TCP rules. Every new outbound connection asks the Linux kernel for an ephemeral source port—typically drawn from the narrow 32768 to 60999 range (just over 28,000 ports total). Under heavy churn, thousands of ports sit locked in TIME_WAIT at once, shrinking the pool of immediately reusable local addresses while new requests keep demanding fresh ones.

As free ephemeral ports get scarce, port allocation stops being a cheap lookup and becomes a CPU tax right inside the kernel. To pick an unused source port for a new socket, the kernel's port allocator scans candidate ports and acquires table locks across active and TIME_WAIT entries. The fewer free ports remain, the longer those search loops run and the more lock contention builds up under high concurrency. The causal chain is brutal: high HTTP/1.1 concurrency past the cap of 2 forces open-and-close churn, which packs the ephemeral port table with TIME_WAIT sockets, which stretches kernel port scans and lock waits, burning client CPU cycles, spiking tail latency, and—when the usable port space runs dry—triggering address already in use failures or connection timeouts.

In real Kubernetes clusters, this failure mode is notorious for fooling engineers into blaming the upstream service. Because pods share node IP addresses and aggregate outbound traffic across containers, a noisy neighbor or a chatty microservice can chew through local port capacity while CPU time is quietly eaten in kernel socket allocation rather than user-space application logic. In benchmarks where HTTP/1.1 concurrency pushes hard against that default limit of 2, leaving it untouched can cost up to 8x throughput compared to sizing the pool for actual in-flight work.

Comparing the main tuning options makes the trade-offs clear:

  • Leaving MaxIdleConnsPerHost at 2: Minimal idle memory footprint, but catastrophic under HTTP/1.1 bursts because excess connections are evicted, driving handshake churn, TIME_WAIT buildup, kernel port-scan CPU overhead, and up to an 8x throughput drop.
  • Setting MaxIdleConnsPerHost to expected peak in-flight concurrency per host (paired with a bounded MaxIdleConns): Optimal for high-concurrency HTTP/1.1 clients. Keeping enough warm sockets per host prevents repeated handshakes and cuts ephemeral port churn, while a global MaxIdleConns ceiling bounds total memory and file descriptors across many target hosts.
  • Setting MaxIdleConnsPerHost excessively high (such as tens of thousands) or leaving MaxIdleConns unbounded: Eliminates eviction for a single host in theory, but creates real risk by holding open large numbers of idle sockets, inflating memory retention and file descriptor pressure, and leaving more connections vulnerable to silent drops or resets behind NATs and load balancers.

Decision rule: If your service uses HTTP/1.1 and peak concurrent requests to a host are greater than 2, set MaxIdleConnsPerHost to your expected peak in-flight requests per host and set a sensible global MaxIdleConns cap; if traffic is low-concurrency HTTP/1.1 or multiplexed over HTTP/2, keep the default or a modest per-host value and focus tuning elsewhere.

Even the right pool configuration stops saving you when external limits take over. If live concurrency spikes past your configured per-host cap, the overflow still opens and closes new sockets. If upstream servers or middleboxes close idle keep-alive connections faster than requests arrive, sockets go stale and still force reconnects. And if a Kubernetes node's ephemeral port range or CPU is already saturated by co-located pods, tuning one client's transport will not manufacture free ports out of thin air.

Five High-Throughput and High-Concurrency Scenarios

Go's http.Transport sets MaxIdleConnsPerHost to 2 because the standard library default was shaped around low-concurrency clients rather than high-density service-to-service traffic. Under HTTP/1.1, a single TCP connection carries one request at a time—there is no stream multiplexing—so ten concurrent requests to the same upstream host require ten separate TCP sockets. When a burst finishes and those sockets return to the transport, Go keeps at most two idle per host and closes the rest. Each closed socket enters the kernel's 60-second TIME_WAIT state, holding its local ephemeral port (typically inside Linux's 32768-60999 range, roughly 28,232 ports) hostage while the next wave forces fresh three-way handshakes, longer kernel port scans, and table lock contention.

1. Bursty Microservices Traffic

Internal services rarely see a flat line of calls; they get hit by cron waves, queue drains, or retry storms that jump from two in-flight calls to eighty in a few milliseconds. Because HTTP/1.1 cannot pipeline independent concurrent responses over two sockets, the client opens seventy-eight extra TCP connections during the spike. Once responses finish, seventy-eight sockets are evicted and torn down instead of staying warm.

Repeatedly opening and closing sockets under bursty waves drives up client CPU in two places: user-space goroutine/socket allocation and kernel port selection. As thousands of closed connections pile up in TIME_WAIT across short intervals, the kernel's port allocator has to scan further through occupied or cooling port entries and contend on table locks for every outbound handshake. Observable symptoms look like server slowdowns—p99 latency jumps and client CPU spikes—even when the upstream handler itself is barely breaking a sweat.

Decision rule: If bursty HTTP/1.1 traffic pushes per-host concurrency above 2, set MaxIdleConnsPerHost to expected peak in-flight requests per host and cap global pool memory with MaxIdleConns. Leaving it at 2 causes constant churn; setting MaxIdleConnsPerHost to tens of thousands without bounding MaxIdleConns wastes memory on idle file descriptors across dozens of hosts. This fix stops working when bursts exceed your configured MaxIdleConnsPerHost ceiling or when upstream keep-alive timeouts expire between bursts and force reconnects anyway.

2. High-QPS Fan-Out Calls

An API gateway or aggregator that fans out one incoming request into twenty or fifty parallel HTTP/1.1 calls against a shared backend or cache tier multiplies connection churn by its fan-out factor. At several thousand queries per second, even a modest fan-out means thousands of outbound TCP handshakes every second if the idle pool caps reuse at two sockets per host.

Physically, every new outbound connection demands a free local ephemeral port paired with the target IP and port. Under sustained high-QPS fan-out, sockets cycle through SYN_SENT, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT, and TIME_WAIT faster than the 60-second TCP timer can clear them. The shrinking pool of free ports turns local port assignment from a quick hit into a heavier kernel search and lock-acquisition tax, burning CPU cycles that should be serving requests and pushing throughput down—up to an 8x drop in worst-case high-concurrency benchmarks.

Decision rule: If fan-out concurrency to a host regularly exceeds 2 at high QPS, match MaxIdleConnsPerHost to peak concurrent fan-out requests for that host and set a finite MaxIdleConns. A common mistake is assuming HTTP/2 is active everywhere because a client supports it; if a proxy or upstream downgrades or speaks plain HTTP/1.1, the 2-socket ceiling hits immediately. The tuning loses effectiveness once client CPU or NIC softirqs are already saturated by other workloads on the machine.

3. Short-Lived Connection Spikes

Autoscaling events, batch jobs, or sudden campaign launches create sharp, short-lived spikes where hundreds of goroutines open connections to an endpoint over a few seconds and then go quiet. Even if the spike lasts only ten seconds, the sockets closed at the end of it still sit in TIME_WAIT for up to sixty seconds per TCP specification.

That mismatch between a ten-second traffic spike and a sixty-second TIME_WAIT hold window is where short-lived spikes quietly hurt the next wave. If a second spike hits forty seconds later, a large slice of the local ephemeral port space is still locked in TIME_WAIT. The kernel spends extra CPU scanning port tables for available ports, and if the spike is sharp enough to exhaust free ports for that destination tuple, new connections fail outright with address already in use errors or stall into timeouts.

Decision rule: If short-lived spikes drive brief bursts above 2 concurrent HTTP/1.1 requests per host, raise MaxIdleConnsPerHost to cover the spike's peak concurrency rather than average traffic. A frequent error is sizing the pool for average QPS and ignoring spike peaks, which leaves the burst overflow to churn sockets and pollute the TIME_WAIT table. This adjustment stops helping if requests arrive faster than upstream servers can accept connections or if connection lifetimes are too short to reuse pooled sockets before they close.

4. Cross-Zone Service Meshes

In a multi-zone cluster or service mesh, a client pod in zone A frequently talks to endpoints across zones, often passing through sidecars, ingress/egress proxies, or zone-aware load balancers. When HTTP/1.1 is used between the Go client and the next hop—whether that hop is a local sidecar or a remote backend—MaxIdleConnsPerHost = 2 still limits reusable idle sockets to two per target host.

Cross-zone hops add round-trip time to every TCP handshake and tear-down cycle, stretching connection setup latency across availability zones while churn continues to consume local ephemeral ports and kernel CPU. Worse, teams often blame cross-zone network jitter or sidecar proxies when p99 latency spikes, missing that the client is discarding dozens of reusable connections after every burst and paying both handshake RTT and kernel port-search overhead.

Decision rule: If cross-zone HTTP/1.1 traffic sees more than 2 concurrent requests per host, raise MaxIdleConnsPerHost to match peak in-flight calls to each host and set an explicit MaxIdleConns. People often misdiagnose this as a cross-zone routing or sidecar bug and tweak mesh retries, which actually worsens churn by multiplying connection attempts. The fix breaks down if an intermediate proxy or firewall silently drops idle connections earlier than Go's idle timeout, leaving stale sockets in the pool that fail on reuse.

5. NAT and Ephemeral-Port-Constrained Containers

Containerized workloads—especially on Kubernetes nodes running many pods behind shared node IPs or SNAT/NAT gateways—operate inside tight port budgets. While a single pod might look small in isolation, multiple containers sharing a host IP or NAT mapping draw from constrained source port pools and share the same host kernel.

When a Go service leaves MaxIdleConnsPerHost at 2 under HTTP/1.1 concurrency, rapid connection churn floods the kernel with outbound socket allocations and TIME_WAIT entries. In constrained container setups, port exhaustion happens much sooner: available ports shrink, the kernel burns extra CPU searching for free ports under lock contention, and pods start hitting connection timeouts, refused connections, or address already in use errors—often blamed on "flaky container networking" or noisy neighbors rather than client socket churn.

Decision rule: If a containerized HTTP/1.1 service runs with per-host concurrency above 2 under tight port or NAT limits, set MaxIdleConnsPerHost to expected peak concurrent requests per host and bound total idle sockets with MaxIdleConns. A classic mistake is leaving defaults untouched while scaling replica counts up, which multiplies total churn across the node's shared port space. Raising these limits will not rescue a pod if noisy neighboring containers have already exhausted the shared ephemeral port pool or starved the node of CPU.

Diagnostic Telemetry and Root-Cause Verification

When p99 latency climbs and throughput tanks across internal HTTP/1.1 services, teams almost always blame the upstream pod first. That instinct backfires when Go's http.Transport leaves MaxIdleConnsPerHost at 2: concurrent requests exceeding two sockets open fresh TCP connections, close excess sockets after bursts, and strand local ports in 60-second TIME_WAIT states. What looks like an overloaded server or flaky service mesh is often a local kernel port allocator burning CPU cycles and lock contention inside the calling container or host.

OS and Kernel Indicators: Port Scans, TIME_WAIT Accumulation, and System CPU

The clearest fingerprint of MaxIdleConnsPerHost churn shows up at the kernel socket layer rather than inside application handler logs. Because HTTP/1.1 cannot multiplex parallel requests over one socket, bursty concurrency forces repeated three-way handshakes and socket closures, pulling ephemeral ports out of the Linux local range (commonly 32768–60999) into TIME_WAIT.

  • TIME_WAIT socket counts and ephemeral port exhaustion errors: Inspecting socket tables (such as ss -tan state time-wait or /proc/net/sockstat) reveals thousands of lingering sockets tied up for the 60-second TCP cool-down. As free ports shrink, kernel port-allocation routines scan deeper and contend harder on table locks, driving client system CPU up; if churn outpaces port turnover, bind/connect fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL ("address already in use") or connection timeouts.
  • Elevated kernel/system CPU paired with idle upstream handlers: When Go goroutines spend time inside kernel socket allocation and lock contention rather than business logic, CPU profiles and node metrics show rising kernel-space work while upstream CPU and request queues stay calm. In Kubernetes, noisy neighbor pods sharing a node IP aggregate outbound port consumption, magnifying port-scan cost and starving other pods even when the target service is healthy.

Go Runtime and net/http Instrumentation

Kernel counters prove that sockets are churning, while Go-level telemetry confirms that MaxIdleConnsPerHost eviction—not DNS stalls, packet loss, or upstream slowness—is driving the reconnect loop.

  • httptrace connection reuse vs. fresh dials: Instrumenting outgoing requests with httptrace.ClientTrace lets you separate GotConn with Reused: true from ConnectStart/ConnectDone and DNSStart/DNSDone. A low reuse ratio during bursts alongside flat, fast DNS lookups rules out DNS resolution delays and points straight to pool eviction or stale keep-alive closes.
  • Goroutine and socket lifecycle telemetry: Tracing or runtime/pprof profiles during load spikes expose tight loops around net/http.(*Transport).getConn, dialConn, and socket teardown, alongside climbing open file descriptors or rapid FD churn. If server response times stay flat once a connection is established but total throughput drops up to 8x under concurrency, connection setup and teardown—not server processing—is eating the budget.

Separating Pool Churn from Upstream Saturation, DNS, and Network Drops

Misreading these signals leads to expensive wild-goose chases. Raising pool limits when the real bottleneck sits elsewhere wastes memory or masks a deeper fault.

  • Server saturation: Upstream saturation shows up as rising server-side queue/service time and higher latency even on already-open, reused connections, whereas MaxIdleConnsPerHost churn degrades throughput and spikes client CPU even when upstream handlers respond quickly once connected.
  • DNS issues: DNS problems inflate DNSStart-to-DNSDone spans and produce name-resolution errors without necessarily generating massive TIME_WAIT counts or socket-allocator lock contention.
  • Network drops and middlebox resets: Packet loss or load-balancer/NAT idle timeouts cause retransmissions, SYN/RST anomalies, and read/write timeouts or reset errors on reused sockets—whereas pure MaxIdleConnsPerHost = 2 churn stems from deliberate client-side eviction after bursts above two concurrent requests.

Diagnostic Decision Rule and Where Pool Tuning Stops

If telemetry shows HTTP/1.1 per-host concurrency above 2, low httptrace connection reuse, rising TIME_WAIT or port-allocation CPU overhead, and healthy upstream/DNS behavior, set MaxIdleConnsPerHost to expected peak per-host in-flight concurrency and set a finite global MaxIdleConns to cap total idle sockets and memory across hosts. Keeping the default of 2 preserves handshake churn; setting MaxIdleConnsPerHost or MaxIdleConns arbitrarily huge risks memory bloat, file-descriptor pressure, and keeping sockets open past middlebox idle timeouts where silent drops cause stale-socket errors.

This fix stops working when live concurrency bursts past the configured MaxIdleConnsPerHost ceiling (overflow sockets still open and close), when upstream servers or proxies close idle keep-alives faster than requests arrive, when traffic runs over HTTP/2 multiplexing where per-host TCP connection counts behave differently, or when co-located Kubernetes workloads have already exhausted node ephemeral ports or CPU.

Tuning Guidelines, Trade-Offs, and Production Safeguards

Fixing HTTP/1.1 connection churn requires sizing Go's http.Transport pool around actual peak per-host concurrency rather than leaving MaxIdleConnsPerHost at its legacy default of 2. Because HTTP/1.1 lacks stream multiplexing, N simultaneous in-flight requests to a single upstream host require up to N separate TCP sockets. When traffic bursts to 40 concurrent calls and then subsides, a limit of 2 forces the client to close 38 idle sockets. Those closed sockets enter the TCP TIME_WAIT state for roughly 60 seconds, holding local ephemeral ports from ranges such as 32768-60999 out of circulation and forcing the kernel to scan port tables and contend on locks as new connections open.

Sizing Connection Pools and Comparing Transport Strategies

Different transport configurations resolve socket churn with sharply different resource costs. Raising MaxIdleConnsPerHost to match peak per-host in-flight concurrency is optimal for high-concurrency HTTP/1.1 microservices because it keeps established sockets warm across bursts, eliminating repeated three-way handshakes and keeping ephemeral ports out of TIME_WAIT. Setting it to an arbitrary huge number is inferior because idle file descriptors and socket buffers stay pinned in memory across every host contacted, even when traffic to most backends is sparse. Switching downstream hops to HTTP/2 is effective where supported end-to-end because stream multiplexing shares fewer TCP connections across concurrent requests, yet it can mask a misconfigured http.Transport whenever a proxy, sidecar, or upstream downgrades a route back to HTTP/1.1.
Strategy Mechanism and Effect Verdict and Failure Mode
Match MaxIdleConnsPerHost to Peak In-Flight Retains burst-sized HTTP/1.1 sockets in the idle pool instead of closing them into 60-second TIME_WAIT, cutting port scans and client CPU. Optimal for HTTP/1.1 bursts. Fails if live concurrency spikes past the cap or upstream keep-alives expire early.
Unbounded or Very High Per-Host Cap Keeps large numbers of idle sockets open per host, increasing file-descriptor counts and kernel socket buffer memory retention. Suboptimal. Wastes memory and file descriptors across many hosts or triggers silent middlebox socket drops.
HTTP/2 Multiplexing Carries concurrent streams over fewer TCP connections, reducing new socket creation and ephemeral port churn on HTTP/2 paths. Situational. Fails to protect routes that fall back to HTTP/1.1 or traverse proxies that split/downgrade traffic.

Apply a direct selection rule when configuring http.Transport: if a workload sends HTTP/1.1 traffic with per-host concurrency greater than 2 and exhibits rising system CPU or TIME_WAIT growth, set MaxIdleConnsPerHost to expected peak per-host in-flight requests and pair it with a finite global MaxIdleConns ceiling. If per-host concurrency stays at or below 2 and latency is steady, keep the default and focus optimization elsewhere.

Timeouts, Keep-Alive Alignment, and Where Tuning Breaks Down

Pool sizing only works if socket lifetimes align with the network path between client and server. If IdleConnTimeout is set longer than an upstream server, load balancer, or NAT gateway keep-alive window, the middlebox silently drops or resets idle sockets while Go still treats them as reusable. Reusing a dead socket triggers failed reads or writes, retries, and fresh connection setup that re-injects churn and TIME_WAIT pressure. Setting DialContext timeouts, TLSHandshakeTimeout, and ResponseHeaderTimeout keeps stalled handshakes or slow upstreams from holding sockets and goroutines open during cascading latency spikes.

  • Typical choice error - sizing for average QPS instead of burst concurrency: A service averaging 10 requests per second with 25-request bursts leaves MaxIdleConnsPerHost too low. Overflow sockets close after each burst, enter 60-second TIME_WAIT, shrink available ephemeral ports in the 32768-60999 range, and drive kernel port-search CPU overhead on subsequent spikes.
  • Typical choice error - raising MaxIdleConnsPerHost without bounding MaxIdleConns: Clients talking to dozens or hundreds of service endpoints accumulate idle sockets across all targets, inflating memory usage and file-descriptor pressure under high service density.
  • Typical choice error - tuning client retries before fixing pool limits: Retrying failed or slow calls under load multiplies outbound connection attempts, accelerating ephemeral port depletion and address already in use failures.
  • When the chosen fix stops working: Raising MaxIdleConnsPerHost stops helping when live concurrency exceeds the configured limit, when upstream keep-alive timeouts are shorter than request intervals so sockets cannot be reused, or when co-located Kubernetes pods on a shared node exhaust the node's ephemeral port pool or CPU budget regardless of one pod's pool setting.

Production Safeguards and Verification

Never treat a raised MaxIdleConnsPerHost as a complete fix without observing both Go transport behavior and host kernel state. Inspect connection reuse with httptrace.ClientTrace to verify that requests reuse existing connections rather than re-dialing, and track file-descriptor counts alongside client system CPU so socket retention does not quietly displace application memory. On Linux and Kubernetes nodes, monitor TIME_WAIT socket counts and ephemeral port consumption across pods sharing a node IP; if port exhaustion persists across workloads, inspect node-level port allocation and pod density rather than endlessly enlarging per-client pools.

title: Building a Reusable WebGPU & Rust Engine: Part 7 — From Reusable Engine Template to Real Project
description:
Previous Parts in This Series

Windowing & Pipeline Architecture

Loading Custom Geometry & WGSL Shaders

Implementing a 3D Camera System & Hot-Reloading Shaders

Implementing Depth Buffering and a Post-Processing Pass

Implementing Lighting Systems

HDRI Environment Lighting & Dynamic Shadows

Before jumping into the final pieces, a quick reflection on building this series: I leaned heavily on AI assistance to help write the Rust and WebGPU boilerplate across these seven parts, and the biggest lesson I learned is that AI only works if you strictly own the architecture. Without a clear hierarchy and decoupled modules, generated code quickly turns into a tangled mess you can no longer read or debug by hand. Keeping a clean structure is what lets me move fast with AI while still understanding every piece of how the engine works.

Almost all the core rendering features are finally ready to use. In this final part of the template phase, I want to add the last—and most important—piece that turns a rendering demo into an actual usable tool: a data-driven scene system and a lightweight editor UI.

[1]. Data-Driven Scenes with JSON
To make the engine truly reusable across different projects, the engine binary itself shouldn't hardcode meshes, lights, or camera positions.

My plan is straightforward: use a JSON file to describe the entire scene.

  • Decoupled Assets: Lights, camera parameters, object transforms, and material attributes live as lightweight JSON data. Heavy 3D geometry files (.glb / .gltf / .obj) are referenced purely by file path links rather than baked into the engine.

  • Engine as a Functional App: By separating scene data from engine code, the compiled Rust binary acts as a standalone functional tool that loads any scene file on demand.

[2]. Why We Need an Editor UI (winit + egui)

If you want to load a JSON scene, you also need an easy way to edit and export one without hand-typing transforms and light coordinates in a text editor.
The cleanest solution is integrating an immediate-mode UI using winit + egui. Of course, adding a UI layer immediately increases architectural complexity. Even when working with AI assistance, having a strict, clear hierarchy is essential—otherwise, the codebase grows fast and you lose control over how systems talk to each other.
To keep everything manageable, I enforce strict separation of concerns across three layers:

  1. Rendering Modules: Core GPU systems (lighting, materials, environment, post-processing) stay isolated in their own dedicated modules.
  2. Scene Layer: Handles serializing, loading, and exporting the JSON scene graph and asset references.
  3. UI Layer (egui): Lives in its own module and simply reads/modifies scene state.

Keeping the GUI Layout Simple
For the interface itself, I am sticking to a classic, minimal 3-panel layout:

  1. Top Bar: Global actions (Load Scene, Export JSON, Play/Reset, View modes).
  2. Left Panel (Outliner): Scene hierarchy showing cameras, lights, and loaded meshes.
  3. Right Panel (Inspector / Attributes): Properties for whichever object is currently selected.

You can always expand an editor UI endlessly, but keeping the layout simple makes it fast to build and easy to maintain.

[3]. Architecture Review: Everything in Our Template
Before moving on to a real project, here is a complete review of the core components now wired together inside the engine template:

1, Window & Event Loop (winit): Cross-platform window creation, input handling, and frame lifecycle management.

2, Core GPU State Container:

  • Hardware & Swapchain: Surface, Device, Queue, Window, and main RenderPipeline + layout.

  • Camera System: View/projection matrices, uniform buffers, and interactive controls.

  • Depth & Shadows: Depth texture/view, shadow maps (textures, views, faces/arrays), and the dedicated shadow pipeline/layout.

  • Post-Processing: Offscreen bind groups, layouts, uniform buffers, and the full-screen post-processing pipeline.

  • Controllers: Dedicated modules for analytical lights, HDRI environment baking, and the egui integration.

3, Shaders (WGSL): Vertex shaders for mesh geometry and PBR fragment shaders for physically based shading.
4, Asset Loaders: Support for loading .obj and .glb / .gltf meshes into GPU vertex and index buffers.
5, Unified Analytical Lighting: 16-byte aligned GPU uniform buffers supporting Directional, Point, and Spot lights.
6, HDRI / Image-Based Lighting (IBL): Equirectangular-to-cubemap conversion, diffuse irradiance, prefiltered specular maps, and BRDF LUTs.
7, Scene Serialization & GUI: JSON scene import/export paired with the egui outliner and attribute inspector.

[4]. What’s Missing (Future Roadmap)
A reusable template doesn't need every advanced AAA feature on day one—it just needs a clean foundation you can extend when a real project demands it. A few systems I plan to add later as the engine evolves:

  • Temporal & Denoising Passes: Expanding the post-processing stack with temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) and denoising filters.
  • Advanced Rendering Architecture: Evolving the render pass scheduler (such as deferred rendering / G-Buffer passes or render-graph abstractions) as scene complexity scales.
  • Hierarchy & Rigging Support: Adding a parent-child transform hierarchy and basic skeletal/rig support for animated characters and mechanical assemblies.

Wrapping Up the Template — And Starting the Next Build

With JSON scene loading, asset linking, and an egui inspector in place, the template phase is officially complete. Instead of endlessly tweaking an empty engine in isolation, it is time to freeze the core architecture and use it to build an actual project.

Thanks for reading! Check out my industrial Rust projects available on the Microsoft Store:
Download on the Microsoft Store
Download from Gumroad

title: The scan failed on the vendor's own agent
description:
Originally published at tothenoc.substack.com

Our image was clean. The package that failed came from the cloud's own repository.

Before a hardened image goes public on Google Cloud, Google runs its own validation on it. Part of that is a vulnerability scan of every package, including the Go standard library compiled inside binaries.

Two of our images failed it: AlmaLinux 10 and Rocky Linux 10.

The finding was not in anything we added. It was google_osconfig_agent, Google's own management agent, installed from Google's own repository. It was built with Go 1.25.5. The scanner wanted at least 1.25.13 (CVE-2026-39821).

First idea: wait for a new package. I checked the repositories. Stable still had the same build. Unstable and the next upstream tag were built with Go 1.26.3, still under the line (the fix there is 1.26.6). Waiting would not fix it, not in days.

Second idea: remove the agent. No. Without it, patch management and inventory from the console stop working for the customer. A hardened image with half of the cloud features missing is not what somebody pays for.

What we did: the agent is open source. In our build, after hardening, we compile it from the upstream tag with a current Go (1.27.4, checksum pinned), with the same flags as Google's own packaging, and replace only that one binary. Toolchain and source are removed after. A note in /usr/share/doc on the image says what was replaced and from which commit.

Then a gate. Before an image is accepted, every Go binary on it is checked for the Go version it was built with. Under the line, the build fails. It did not stay a one-off: the same gate later stopped builds on AWS, on agents from the base image.

The boot test also checks that the agent runs and reports our rebuilt version. Both images passed validation and are public now.

The point is not who wrote the binary. Anything you install from a vendor repository is still your image, and the scanner does not care where the package came from.

If you run Go binaries you did not build, on a machine with Go installed one command tells you what compiled them:

go version /usr/bin/<binary>

The images, per distribution:

  • AlmaLinux 9: AWS | Google Cloud
  • AlmaLinux 10: AWS | Google Cloud
  • Rocky Linux 9: AWS | Google Cloud
  • Rocky Linux 10: AWS | Google Cloud
  • Debian 13: AWS | Google Cloud

-- Alexandru

title: PocketBase Tutorial: Run a Backend From One Binary
description:
Quick answer

PocketBase is a single Go binary that gives a small app a database, an admin dashboard, user auth, file storage, and a REST API, with no separate database server to install. You download one file, run pocketbase serve, and the backend is live on your machine. This post builds a small orders backend for a shop in Karachi with four real orders, and fixes the 403 error that stops the first record.

A small shop in Karachi takes orders over the phone and writes each one in a paper notebook. The owner wants a simple backend: save an order, list the orders, total them by city. The usual route means a database, an API server, and auth to wire up and keep running: a week of setup for an afternoon job. PocketBase folds the whole stack into one file, and this post shows the full loop: start it, create a collection, save four orders, and read them back.

What I would check before using it

My first check is whether the app is a small app. PocketBase runs as one process on one server. A shop backend or a prototype fits it well. A system that needs several servers sharing one database does not, and that is where I would look at a hosted service instead. The Supabase Explained: The Open-Source Firebase Alternative post covers that side.

My second check is the database underneath. PocketBase stores everything in SQLite, one file inside the pb_data folder, so a backup is copying a file. Heavy write traffic on one file is the limit, which a small shop will never reach. The SQLite Explained: The Database That Lives Inside Your App post explains that design.

My third check is who can read and write what. A new collection starts with empty rules, which means only superusers can touch it, as the demo below shows with a real 403. That default is safe, but opening the rules for public reads is a deliberate step.

My fourth check is who runs the server. There is no monthly bill and no vendor to lock you in, but backups, updates, and uptime are your job. If nobody on the team will own that, the hosted backend in the Firebase Explained: A Backend Without Building a Backend post is the honest alternative.

My verdict, as judgement: adopt PocketBase for a small app or prototype that fits on one server. Keep a hosted backend when the app must scale across servers or nobody will own operations. The recommendation flips the moment the app outgrows a single server.

Four orders, one binary, and a 403 error

Four orders belong to one small shop: Ayesha in Karachi, Rs 12,400; Bilal in Lahore, Rs 7,800; Hina in Karachi, Rs 9,600; Usman in Islamabad, Rs 15,200. The plan: an orders collection, four records saved through the API, and a list back.

First, download the binary from the releases page. The version below is the latest at the time of writing; an older version number returns a plain 404.

$ curl -L -o pocketbase.zip https://github.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/releases/download/v0.40.6/pocketbase_0.40.6_linux_amd64.zip
$ unzip -o pocketbase.zip
$ ./pocketbase --version
pocketbase version 0.40.6

Start the server. It listens on port 8090, and the log shows where the API and dashboard live.

$ ./pocketbase serve --http 127.0.0.1:8090
2026/11/21 03:04:24 Server started at http://127.0.0.1:8090
├─ REST API:  http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/
└─ Dashboard: http://127.0.0.1:8090/_/

Before the API accepts anything, create a superuser, the admin account for the backend.

$ ./pocketbase superuser upsert admin@shop.local shopadmin123
Successfully saved superuser "admin@shop.local"!

Log in as that superuser to get a token, and save it in a variable for the Authorization header on admin calls.

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/_superusers/auth-with-password \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"identity":"admin@shop.local","password":"shopadmin123"}'

The token is saved here into TOKEN. Next, create the orders collection: city is a select with three values, and total is a number, so a wrong value is rejected.

{
  "name": "orders",
  "type": "base",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "customer", "type": "text", "required": true},
    {"name": "city", "type": "select", "required": true,
     "values": ["Karachi", "Lahore", "Islamabad"]},
    {"name": "items", "type": "text", "required": true},
    {"name": "total", "type": "number", "required": true}
  ]
}

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections \
    -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d @create-collection.json
{"id":"pbc_3527180448","name":"orders","type":"base", ... "created":"2026-11-21 03:04:46.657Z"}

Here is the thing that goes wrong: creating a record without the token fails, because empty rules mean superusers only.

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/orders/records \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"customer":"Ayesha","city":"Karachi","items":"kurta, dupatta","total":12400}'
{"data":{},"message":"Only superusers can perform this action.","status":403}
HTTP 403

The fix is the Authorization header with the superuser token. With it, the same request works.

$ curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/orders/records \
    -H "Authorization: $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"customer":"Bilal","city":"Lahore","items":"sneakers","total":7800}'
{"city":"Lahore","collectionId":"pbc_3527180448","collectionName":"orders","customer":"Bilal","id":"ifjpo74pv3nnvij","items":"sneakers","total":7800}

The other three records went in the same way. Listing the collection back returns all four, and the numbers check out: Karachi Rs 22,000, and the four orders add to Rs 45,000.

$ curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections/orders/records" -H "Authorization: $TOKEN"
page 1 perPage 30 totalItems 4
Bilal | Lahore | sneakers | Rs 7800
Ayesha | Karachi | kurta, dupatta | Rs 12400
Hina | Karachi | handbag, wallet | Rs 9600
Usman | Islamabad | jacket, shalwar kameez | Rs 15200
grand total: Rs 45000

That is a working orders store: one binary, one data folder, a dashboard at /_/ , and a REST API the shop app can call. The FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed post shows the same job done by building the API by hand in Python.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, creating a record without logging in. The symptom is HTTP 403 with the message "Only superusers can perform this action." The fix is to log in as a superuser first and send the token in the Authorization header. If the public should write, that is a rule change, not a missing header.

Second, sorting the list by created. The symptom is HTTP 400 with "Something went wrong while processing your request." when the request includes sort=created, while sort=total works. The fix is to sort by a field on the collection, such as total, or to leave the sort off.

Third, downloading a release that no longer exists. The symptom is curl saving a 9 byte file that says Not Found. The fix is to check the latest release tag first, then build the download URL from that tag.

Fourth, sending a number as a string. The symptom is silent: a total of "7800" in quotes was accepted and stored as 7800, so the record looks right while the client has a type bug. The fix is to send numbers as numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does PocketBase need a separate database server? No. It stores everything in an embedded SQLite database inside the pb_data folder, so nothing else needs installing.

Is PocketBase free to use? Yes. It is open source under the MIT license, and you run it on your own server, so there is no monthly fee.

Can I use PocketBase in production? Yes, for small apps that fit on one server. Keep the pb_data folder backed up, keep the binary updated, and put the server behind HTTPS.

How is PocketBase different from Supabase or Firebase? PocketBase is a single self-hosted binary with its database built in, while Supabase and Firebase are hosted services. Self-hosting means no monthly bill and full control, but you own backups and uptime.

Does PocketBase include user auth and realtime updates? Yes. It ships with auth collections for users, including email and OAuth login, and realtime subscriptions so a client can watch records change.

What to remember

  • One binary is the whole backend: database, dashboard, auth, storage, and API.
  • Create a superuser first, then log in for a token.
  • New collections start with empty rules: superusers only.
  • No token means a 403; the fix is the Authorization header.
  • Data lives in pb_data, so back up that folder.

Where this leaves you

PocketBase earns its place the afternoon a small app needs a real backend and nobody wants to spend a week building one. The demo proved the parts that matter: one binary started the server, a superuser and a token unlocked the API, the 403 made the auth rule visible instead of failing silently, and four real orders came back with a grand total of Rs 45,000. Try it on your next small project, keep the rules tight, and back up pb_data from day one.

Further reading

  • PocketBase docs
  • PocketBase records API
  • PocketBase on GitHub
  • Supabase Explained: The Open-Source Firebase Alternative
  • Firebase Explained: A Backend Without Building a Backend
  • SQLite Explained: The Database That Lives Inside Your App
  • FastAPI Explained: Python APIs at Full Speed

Waqas Shahid is a software engineer from Karachi with more than 12 years of experience, including 6+ years in engineering leadership. He writes The Practical Developer.

title: Why Background Token Refreshes Overwrite Your Google Antigravity Session (and How Session Guards Fix It)
description:
If you juggle two or three Google accounts with Google Antigravity (agy), you eventually notice an odd bug after switching accounts manually. You switch to Account B, start a coding session, and an hour later Antigravity silently flips back to Account A.

No crash happened, and nobody ran a login command. Another agy process running in a forgotten terminal or IDE workspace simply refreshed its hourly OAuth token and wrote the updated credentials back into the shared local state under ~/.gemini.

Here is why that race happens, how the open-source terminal switcher agy-swap isolates switches and harvests background refreshes without clobbering your active account, and how to run two completely separate accounts side by side when you need concurrent agents.

Why switching accounts by hand often reverts an hour later

Both the standalone agy CLI and the Antigravity IDE read and write shared credential files under ~/.gemini alongside your system keychain entry. Suppose Terminal 1 started earlier under Account A, and an hour later you sign out and sign into Account B in Terminal 2 (or inside the IDE).

Terminal 1 still holds Account A's OAuth refresh token in memory. When Terminal 1's access token expires, it calls Google OAuth, receives a new access token for Account A, and writes that session straight back to disk. Whatever you switched to in Terminal 2 gets overwritten on disk without warning.

On macOS, frequent reads and writes against the login keychain by credential helpers can also trigger repeated OS password prompts right in the middle of a coding loop.

What one safe account switch updates locally

Instead of asking you to sign out in a browser, agy-swap saves each OAuth session once (agy-swap add) and performs atomic updates guarded by advisory file locks (flock on Unix, LockFileEx on Windows) with automatic rollback if any write step fails:

  1. Writes the target account's OAuth session (file permissions 0600) under ~/.gemini for agy CLI, IDE, and Jetski.
  2. Mirrors the active session into the OS keychain via /usr/bin/security on macOS, secret-tool on Linux, or Windows Credential Manager.
  3. On macOS and Linux, updates the signed-in email label inside state.vscdb when sqlite3 is installed so the IDE UI stays consistent.
  4. Drops a reload marker on macOS and Linux so the background agy --hub service restarts cleanly under the new account without forcing you to close the IDE window.

Harvesting background token refreshes with --sync-session

Updating the active session atomically solves half the problem. The other half is stopping older agy processes in other directories from overwriting that switch later.

When agy-swap configures its launcher guard (either automatically or through agy-swap install-agy), it installs lightweight wrappers at ~/.local/bin/agy and ~/.gemini/bin/agy, moving the real binary to ~/.local/libexec/agy (or .agy.real) and updating size and modification metadata in agy.version.json so the IDE trusts the launcher.

Whenever a wrapped agy process exits or completes a refresh, agy-swap --sync-session inspects the refreshed session token on disk:

  older workspace `agy` refreshes Account A token
                      │
                      ▼
        wrapper runs `agy-swap --sync-session`
                      │
          matches `refresh_token` in vault
                      │
        ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
        ▼                           ▼
updates Account A row         keeps Account B active
 inside `vault.json`         as your selected session

Because tokens are matched by refresh_token against saved accounts rather than blindly trusting whichever account happened to write last, Account A receives its fresh token cleanly inside your vault while Account B stays active across your workspace.

If switching ever reverts unexpectedly, agy-swap doctor checks both ~/.local/bin/agy and ~/.gemini/bin/agy to verify that every shell invocation passes through the wrapper.

Checking 5-hour, weekly, and Gemini 4 Argon pools before hitting HTTP 429

Quota starvation is usually what drives people to switch accounts in the first place. Antigravity meters three separate quota pools rather than one global counter:

  • Gem (Gemini) enforces both a 5-hour rolling window and a 7-day weekly cap, and agy-swap displays whichever remaining percentage is tighter.
  • C/G (Claude and GPT) shares an independent 5-hour rolling window and 7-day weekly cap alongside Gemini.
  • Argon (Gemini 4 Argon) tracks a separate weekly ceiling on Pro plans and renders in its own detail panel so an exhausted Argon pool never marks standard Gemini or Claude/GPT quota as LIMITED.

The TUI refreshes your active account every 20 seconds (or roughly 10 seconds after agy writes logs) and idle accounts every 2 minutes, converting reset timestamps to your local timezone with clock skew compensation. From scripts or agent loops, you can inspect and rotate accounts directly:

# Inspect 5-hour windows, weekly ceilings, and local reset timestamps
agy-swap limits --refresh --verbose

# Rotate automatically to the next account with Claude/GPT quota left
agy-swap next --family claude

# Put a noisy account on a 6-hour cooldown for Claude/GPT
agy-swap limit set 1 6h --group claude

# Bind a repository profile with sticky, balanced, or round-robin ranking
agy-swap profile set work work-account --family claude --policy sticky --threshold 15
agy-swap bind set /path/to/repo work --mode recommend
agy-swap run now

See the Quota Limits Guide for status badge behavior (READY, LOW, GEMINI ONLY, CLAUDE/GPT ONLY, LIMITED, VERIFY) and agy-swap verify recovery steps when Google returns HTTP 403.

Running two separate accounts simultaneously in two terminals

Directory bindings and agy-swap run now select an account before launching in your shared Antigravity session, which covers jumping between work and personal repos one at a time. When you actually need two standalone agy CLI agents running at the exact same moment under two different Google accounts on macOS or Linux, launching a second process without isolation still collides in the shared OS keychain.

Creating an isolated HOME directory with the file-backed keyring marker avoids that collision (Parallel Sessions Guide):

AGY_BIN="$HOME/.local/libexec/agy"
[ -x "$AGY_BIN" ] || AGY_BIN="$(command -v agy)"

PROFILE_HOME="$HOME/.agy-homes/account-b"
mkdir -p "$PROFILE_HOME/.gemini/antigravity-cli/cache"
touch -t 203601010000 "$PROFILE_HOME/.gemini/antigravity-cli/cache/antigravity-keyring-unavailable"

HOME="$PROFILE_HOME" AGY_SWAP_SKIP_SYNC=1 WSL_INTEROP=1 "$AGY_BIN"

Setting WSL_INTEROP=1 alongside antigravity-keyring-unavailable instructs agy to keep its OAuth credentials inside $PROFILE_HOME/.gemini instead of touching your global macOS Keychain or Linux Secret Service, while AGY_SWAP_SKIP_SYNC=1 stops the isolated instance from firing global session sync.

Local-first storage details without hand-waving

agy-swap runs strictly on your workstation with zero telemetry, analytics, or crash-reporting endpoints:

  1. Saved account tokens live in vault.json inside your config directory with file permissions 0600. By default, vault.json is not encrypted so headless shells and non-interactive --sync-session hooks never hang waiting for a passphrase.
  2. Desktop users who want hardware or OS keystore protection can export AGY_SWAP_VAULT=keychain (using native Security.framework on macOS, Windows Credential Manager, or Linux Secret Service) and run agy-swap account migrate.
  3. Secret archives (agy-swap backup export --include-secrets) encrypt payloads using AES-GCM with 600,000 PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 iterations, and tokens are redacted from logs and CLI output.

The full network endpoint list and backup recovery behavior are documented on the Security page.

Getting started

On macOS with Homebrew:

brew install aklkbqx/agy-swap/agy-swap

Linux and Windows installers (SHA-256 verified) plus shell completion and Starship/tmux/zsh statusline setup instructions are on the project website, and the Go source code is MIT-licensed at github.com/aklkbqx/agy-swap.

title: Beginner's Roadmap: What to Learn to Become an AWS Cloud Engineer or DevOps Engineer
description:
Which topics, programming language, and networking concepts a beginner should learn to get a job as an AWS Cloud Engineer or DevOps Engineer."
tags: aws, devops, beginners, cloud

Starting a cloud career can feel overwhelming. There are hundreds of AWS services, many tools, and lots of advice online. This guide is a simple roadmap for beginners: which topics to learn, which programming language to pick, and which networking topics matter, in a sensible order.

Cloud Engineer vs DevOps Engineer: What's the Difference?

  • AWS Cloud Engineer: designs, builds, and manages infrastructure on AWS, covering servers, storage, networking, security, and cost.
  • DevOps Engineer: automates how software is built, tested, deployed, and monitored, using CI/CD pipelines, containers, and Infrastructure as Code.

The two roles share about 70% of their foundation. Learn the common base first, then specialize.

Step 1: Learn the Foundations (Weeks 1–4)

  1. Linux basics: most servers on AWS run Linux. Learn the command line, file permissions, users and groups, package managers (yum/apt), services (systemctl), and process and log management.
  2. Basic networking: covered in detail below.
  3. Cloud computing concepts: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, the shared responsibility model, pay-as-you-go pricing, and scalability vs elasticity.
  4. Git and GitHub: commits, branches, pull requests, merging. Every DevOps workflow starts here.

Step 2: Core AWS Services (Weeks 4–10)

Learn these in order and practice each one hands-on in the AWS Free Tier:

Area Services to learn
Global infrastructure Regions, Availability Zones, Edge Locations
Identity and security IAM (users, roles, policies), MFA, Security Groups, NACLs
Compute EC2, Auto Scaling, Elastic Load Balancer (ALB/NLB), Lambda
Storage S3 (versioning, bucket policies, lifecycle), EBS, EFS
Networking VPC, Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, Route 53, CloudFront
Databases RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB
Monitoring CloudWatch, SNS, CloudTrail
Cost control AWS Budgets, Billing Alarms, Cost Explorer

Tip: don't just read. Build a small project for each area, for example a static website on S3, a highly available web app with ALB and Auto Scaling, or a CloudWatch alarm that sends an SNS email.

Step 3: Which Programming Language Should You Learn?

Short answer: start with Python.

  • Easy syntax for beginners
  • Boto3, the official AWS SDK for Python, lets you automate AWS services
  • Widely used for AWS Lambda functions, automation scripts, and DevOps tooling
  • Huge community and learning material

Alongside Python, also learn:

  • Bash/Shell scripting: essential for Linux automation, EC2 user data scripts, and CI/CD steps.
  • YAML and JSON: not programming languages, but you will write them daily (CloudFormation, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions, Docker Compose, IAM policies).
  • Go (optional, later): many DevOps tools (Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform) are written in Go, but you don't need it to get a first job.

Here is a tiny Boto3 example that lists your S3 buckets:

import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3")
response = s3.list_buckets()

for bucket in response["Buckets"]:
    print(bucket["Name"])

Step 4: Networking Topics You Must Know

Networking is the topic beginners skip, and it is the one interviewers ask about most. Learn:

  1. IP addressing: IPv4 and IPv6, public vs private IPs
  2. CIDR notation and subnetting: for example, what 10.0.0.0/16 means and how to split it into subnets
  3. OSI and TCP/IP models: a basic understanding of the layers
  4. Common ports and protocols: HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), SSH (22), RDP (3389), DNS (53), TCP vs UDP
  5. DNS: how domain names resolve, plus record types (A, CNAME, MX, NS) and Route 53
  6. NAT, gateways and routing: how private instances reach the internet
  7. Firewalls: Security Groups (stateful) vs NACLs (stateless)
  8. Load balancing: how traffic is distributed, plus health checks
  9. VPC concepts: subnets, route tables, Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, VPN, Direct Connect
  10. Troubleshooting tools: ping, traceroute, curl, nslookup/dig, netstat

If you understand VPC well, you will understand most of AWS.

Step 5: DevOps Skills (Weeks 10–20)

Once the AWS and networking basics are solid, add:

  1. CI/CD: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, or AWS CodePipeline, CodeBuild and CodeDeploy
  2. Containers: Docker (images, containers, Dockerfile, Docker Hub), then ECS and ECR on AWS
  3. Kubernetes: pods, deployments, services, then Amazon EKS
  4. Infrastructure as Code: Terraform (most popular) and AWS CloudFormation
  5. Configuration management: Ansible basics
  6. Monitoring and logging: CloudWatch, Prometheus, Grafana
  7. Code quality and security: SonarQube, secrets management, least-privilege IAM
  8. Build tools: Maven or npm, depending on your stack

Step 6: Certifications and Learning Platforms

Certifications prove your knowledge to recruiters:

  1. AWS Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02): the best first step
  2. AWS Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03): the most valuable for cloud roles
  3. AWS Developer Associate or SysOps Administrator Associate: good for DevOps paths
  4. AWS DevOps Engineer Professional: later, once you have experience

Free and low-cost places to learn: AWS Skill Builder, AWS Cloud Quest, AWS Educate, AWS Free Tier for hands-on labs, and the AWS Builder Center community.

Step 7: Build Projects (The Most Important Step)

Employers hire people who can show real work. Build and document projects such as:

  • A three-tier web application on AWS (ALB, EC2, RDS or Aurora)
  • A CI/CD pipeline with Jenkins or GitHub Actions deploying to EC2 or Kubernetes
  • A Dockerized app pushed to ECR and run on ECS
  • Infrastructure created entirely with Terraform
  • A monitoring setup with CloudWatch alarms and SNS notifications

Put them on GitHub, write about them on dev.to or AWS Builder Center, and share on LinkedIn.

Suggested 6-Month Learning Plan

Month Focus
1 Linux, Git, basic networking, cloud concepts
2 IAM, EC2, S3, VPC, Cloud Practitioner exam
3 Load balancing, Auto Scaling, RDS, CloudWatch, Python basics
4 Bash and Python automation, Docker, CI/CD (Jenkins/GitHub Actions)
5 Terraform, Kubernetes/EKS or ECS, projects
6 Solutions Architect Associate prep, portfolio, resume, interviews

Final Advice for Beginners

  • Learn one thing at a time and practice it hands-on.
  • Don't try to memorize every AWS service. Master the core ones.
  • Set billing alarms before you start so you don't get surprise charges.
  • Document what you learn. Writing articles is one of the best ways to learn.
  • Be consistent. One hour every day beats ten hours once a week.

Cloud and DevOps careers are open to anyone who is willing to learn and build. Start small, stay consistent, and keep building.
