title: Why Oracle Database Users Disappear: Understanding CDB_USERS and DBA_USERS in Oracle 19c
description:
A Practical DBA Troubleshooting Guide for Local Users, Common Users, CDBs and PDBs

Technology: Oracle Database 19c

Environment: Oracle Multitenant Architecture

Technical Focus: Database User Management, SQL, Troubleshooting and Security

When you manage Oracle Database 19c, you might see that a database user does not appear when you query DBA_USERS.

At first, this result might make you think the database user is missing.

In Oracle multitenant architecture, this outcome does not always mean the user was deleted or never created.

The account could live inside a Pluggable Database (PDB), while you are connected to the Container Database root, CDB$ROOT.

Knowing this difference matters for database administration, application access control, troubleshooting and security.

1. Understanding Oracle Multitenant Architecture

Oracle Database 19c runs an architecture.

In this design, a Container Database (CDB) can hold Pluggable Databases (PDBs).


Oracle Database 19c

+-- CDB$ROOT

|   |

|   +-- Common users and CDB administration

|

+-- PDB$SEED

|   |

|   +-- Template for creating PDBs

|

+-- LABPDB

|

+-- Application schemas

+-- Local database users

+-- Application tables

+-- Database objects

CDB$ROOT is the main container of the CDB.

CDB$ROOT stores Oracle system. Handles database-wide administration tasks.

A Pluggable Database is a database container that holds application schemas, user accounts and data.

Each PDB can keep its local user accounts.

PDB$SEED is a system template used when you create PDBs.

PDB$SEED is usually read-only.

A database session works inside a current container.

The container you are connected to determines which database users, schemas and objects you can see.

If you are connected to the CDB root, do not assume that querying DBA_USERS will show all users in every PDB.

2. Understanding Common Users and Local Users

Oracle setups separate common users from local users.

A common user can live in containers within its defined scope.

In a CDB, common users usually get the C## prefix unless you change the naming rule.

Common users can get privileges that apply across containers, based on how the privileges were granted.

A common user does not automatically own all database objects.

A local user belongs to one PDB.

For example, the user LAB_READER may exist in LABPDB but not in CDB$ROOT.

You can. Manage a local user inside its PDB, if you have the right admin rights.

Oracle gives you a COMMON column in its user dictionary views.

Common | Meaning |

|--------|---------|

| YES Common user |

| NO Local user |

For example:


SELECT username,

common,

account_status

FROM dba_users

WHERE username = 'LAB_READER';

If you run the query in the right PDB, a local user will normally have:


COMMON = NO

3. The Problem: User Not Found in DBA_USERS

Consider a DBA checking whether an application account exists.

The DBA connects to the CDB root and executes:


SELECT username,

account_status

FROM dba_users

WHERE 'LAB_READER';

Illustrative result:


no rows selected

Conclusion should not be made immediately that the user has been deleted.

The database session may be connected to the container.

The next step should be to confirm where the current session is connected.

4. Step 1. Identify the Current Container

Oracle SQL*Plus provides a command to identify the current container.


SHOW CON_NAME;

Example output:


CON_NAME

------------------------------

CDB$ROOT

Result indicates that the current session is connected to the CDB root.

Alternatively, use:


SELECT SYS_CONTEXT(

'USERENV',

'CON_NAME'

) AS current_container

FROM dual;

Query can be useful in tools that do not support SQL*Plus SHOW commands.

Why should DBAs check this first?

Because a query may return information depending on the current container.

Before troubleshooting missing users or objects, confirm the current container.

Simple step can prevent account recreation, privilege changes and confusion.

5. Step 2. Check Available PDBs

From an administrative session in the CDB root, execute:


SHOW PDBS;

Displays the PDBs known to the database, together with their open mode.

A SQL alternative is:


SELECT con_id,

name,

open_mode

FROM v$containers

ORDER BY con_id;

output:


CON_ID  NAME       OPEN_MODE

------  --------   ----------

1       CDB$ROOT   READ WRITE

2       PDB$SEED   READ ONLY

3       LABPDB     READ WRITE

The CON_ID column identifies the database container.

Typical identifiers are:

  • 1: CDB root

  • 2: PDB seed

  • 3 and higher: PDBs and supported container types

An important point is that the container ID must be obtained from the database rather than assumed.

For example, LABPDB is shown as container 3 here for demonstration.

Your environment may use another container name or ID.

6. Step 3. Locate the User Using CDB_USERS

The dictionary view is useful for investigating database users across containers.

From the CDB root, a privileged session can execute:


SELECT con_id,

username,

common,

account_status

FROM cdb_users

WHERE username = 'LAB_READER'

ORDER BY con_id;

Illustrative result:


CON_ID  USERNAME     COMMON  ACCOUNT_STATUS

------  -----------  ------  --------------

3       LAB_READER   NO      OPEN

What does this result mean?

Result indicates that:

  1. The account exists in container ID 3.

  2. It is an user (COMMON = NO).

  3. Its account status is OPEN.

Result demonstrates why the account did not appear in the earlier root-level DBA_USERS query.

The account was associated with a PDB than the root.

security consideration

Oracle restricts access to data dictionary views.

A common user querying CDB_USERS from the root may see the containers allowed by its privileges and CONTAINER_DATA configuration.

Therefore, a missing row in CDB_USERS is not always proof that a user does not exist.

If the expected account's absent, verify:

  • The database sessions current container.

  • Dictionary query privileges.

  • Applicable container-data visibility.

  • Whether the relevant PDB is open and accessible.

  • Whether the query uses the username.

For this reason, it is helpful to perform troubleshooting using an authorized administrative account.

Do not grant privileges simply to make a troubleshooting query succeed.

7. Step 4. Verify the User Inside Its PDB

After you have found the PDB, connect directly to that PDB or change to it with an account that has the needed privileges.

Example:


ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = LABPDB;

This change to the session is administrative. Needs the right privileges.

Confirm the session:


SHOW CON_NAME;

output:


CON_NAME

------------------------------

LABPDB

Now execute:


SELECT username,

account_status,

common

FROM dba_users

WHERE username = 'LAB_READER';

Expected example output:


USERNAME     ACCOUNT_STATUS  COMMON

-----------  --------------  ------

LAB_READER   OPEN            NO

The user becomes visible because the session is now connected to the PDB that holds the account.

lesson

DBA_USERS is not malfunctioning.

The query result depends on the container.

When fixing user accounts in Oracle 19c, always check if the account is local to a PDB.

8. Reproducible Laboratory Demonstration

This example lets administrators see how things work in a test environment.

Warning: This section has a command that changes the database. Use it in a lab that is meant for testing. Do not create accounts or change containers in production without the approval.

Step 1. Connect to the lab PDB

With an admin session, switch to the lab PDB:


ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = LABPDB;

Verify the current container:


SHOW CON_NAME;

Step 2. Create a schema‑only user

To demo without storing a password in the article, create a schema-only account:


CREATE USER LAB_READER NO AUTHENTICATION;

A schema- account does not have a normal password and cannot log in by itself.

The schema‑only account is useful because we want to show user metadata, not test authentication.

The USER command requires the appropriate administrative privilege.

Step 3. Verify the account in the PDB 


SELECT username,

account_status,

authentication_type,

common

FROM dba_users

WHERE 'LAB_READER';

Check that the account appears.

For a schema- account, the AUTHENTICATION_TYPE column should identify NONE.

The account should also be marked as local.

Step 4. Switch to the root 


ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = CDB$ROOT;

Step 5. Query DBA_USERS 


SELECT username,

account_status

FROM dba_users

WHERE 'LAB_READER';

For this local-only account, the expected result in the root is:


no rows selected

Step 6. Query CDB_USERS 


SELECT con_id,

username,

common

FROM cdb_users

WHERE username = 'LAB_READER';

With sufficient dictionary access and container visibility, this query should identify the PDB that holds the account.

The exact output depends on the environment, user privileges and container configuration.

Step 7. Record the result

Capture the SQL outputs. Compare the two views.

The difference demonstrates the importance of understanding container context in an environment.

Any cleanup, such as dropping the laboratory account, should be performed after confirming that it is the intended disposable test account and that cleanup is authorized.

9. DBA_USERS vs CDB_USERS. Key Differences

The following table summarizes the important differences.

| Feature DBA_USERS | CDB_USERS |

|---|---|---|

| User information | Current container | multiple containers |

| CON_ID column | No | Yes |

Local users in other PDBs | Not displayed | Visible when permitted |

| Current container matters | Yes | Yes |

Dictionary privileges required | Yes | Yes |

| Suitable for Container‑level account checks | CDB‑wide account investigation |

When should DBA_USERS be used?

Use DBA_USERS to check account information inside the container that is currently connected to your database session.

Examples include:

  • Confirm whether a user exists in a PDB using DBA_USERS.

  • Check an accounts status with DBA_USERS.

  • Review authentication configuration via DBA_USERS.

  • Investigate local application accounts using DBA_USERS.

When should CDB_USERS be used?

Use CDB_USERS to identify user accounts across containers from the CDB root when the session has the visibility.

Examples include:

  • Find which PDB contains an username using CDB_USERS.

  • Compare account metadata across PDBs with CDB_USERS.

  • Review common users through CDB_USERS.

  • Support multitenant account inventory work with CDB_USERS.

10. Other Reasons a Database User Might Not Appear

Container context is a cause of missing-user confusion, but it is not the only possible explanation.

Incorrect username spelling

Oracle normally stores user identifiers in uppercase.

For example:


CREATE USER lab_reader NO AUTHENTICATION;

The name is generally stored as:


LAB_READER

A search that uses lowercase text may return no rows if the comparison is case-sensitive.

A diagnostic query can use:


SELECT username

FROM dba_users

WHERE UPPER(username) LIKE '%LAB%';

Be careful with quoted, case- user identifiers because applying UPPER() is not equivalent to an exact search.

Connected to the PDB service

A client may connect using an incorrect service name.

This can place the session in a PDB from the intended one.

Verify the container after connecting.

Account. Is locked

A locked account still exists in the data dictionary.

To review its status:


SELECT username,

account_status

FROM dba_users

WHERE 'LAB_READER';

An account marked LOCKED or EXPIRED is not the same as a missing account.

Avoid unlocking or changing authentication settings until the access requirement has been reviewed and approved.

dictionary privileges

A user may not have permission to query DBA_USERS or CDB_USERS.

The database may raise a privilege‑related error than displaying the expected information.

The solution is to use an account or request appropriately scoped dictionary access.

Broad roles such as DBA should not be granted merely to run a query.

Restricted container visibility

when a user can query CDB_USERS, the result may not contain rows from every PDB.

Oracles container-data security rules influence visibility.

A complete investigation may require an administrator to review those settings.

11. Security and Banking Database Considerations

Correctly identifying a users container is especially important in enterprise environments.

Database accounts should be managed according to the principle of privilege.

This means granting users the access necessary for their responsibilities.

In an environment, account reviews should also consider whether the privilege is local or common.

Some practical recommendations include:

  1. Identify the PDB before making account changes.

  2. Verify the accounts existence and status before recreating it.

  3. Avoid granting roles or system privileges.

  4. Confirm whether required privileges apply locally or across containers.

  5. Review account changes through authorized change‑management processes.

  6. Maintain audit records for administrative activity.

  7. Avoid sharing database usernames, credentials, connection details or infrastructure identifiers publicly.

When preparing technical articles, use fictional account names and laboratory environments.

The objective is to explain Oracle behavior without disclosing operational information.

12. SQL Troubleshooting Checklist

The following read‑only checks provide a starting point for investigating missing user accounts.

Check the container 


SELECT SYS_CONTEXT(

'USERENV',

'CON_NAME'

) AS current_container

FROM dual;

Check whether the target account exists in the container 


SELECT username,

account_status,

common

FROM dba_users

WHERE username = 'LAB_READER';

Search across containers

Run from the root with the required privileges:


SELECT con_id,

username,

Here is the text that the user provided:


account_status,

FROM cdb_users

WHERE username = 'LAB_READER'

ORDER BY con_id;

Map container IDs to container names 


SELECT con_id,

name,

open_mode

FROM v$containers

ORDER BY con_id;

Confirm the session user 


SELECT SYS_CONTEXT(

'USERENV',

'SESSION_USER'

) AS session_user

FROM dual;

Together, these checks together help figure out where the session is connected, whether the account is visible and which container should be examined next.

13. Suggested Original Screenshots

To give technical proof, a practical article should show screenshots from real Oracle SQL execution.

Screenshot 1. Current container

Display the result of SHOW CON_NAME or the equivalent SQL query.

Screenshot 2. Root DBA_USERS result

Display the result of searching for the account from CDB$ROOT.

Screenshot 3. CDB_USERS result

Display the account with its CON_ID value.

Screenshot 4. PDB DBA_USERS result

Display the local account found from the relevant PDB.

Screenshot 5. Comparison

If useful, include a concise table explaining the different results.

All screenshots should be laboratory execution evidence. Example outputs printed in this guide are illustrative. Are not substitutes for original screenshots.

14. Lessons Learned

This type of issue shows useful Oracle DBA principles.

First, always check the container.

A database user may exist in a PDB when a query against DBA_USERS in the root returns no rows.

Second, understand the purpose of each view.

DBA_USERS is useful for the container, while CDB_USERS supports container‑aware investigations from the root.

Third, understand common users.

A local account does not automatically exist in every PDB or in the root.

Fourth, verify visibility and privileges.

Access to dictionary information is controlled by Oracle security rules.

Fifth, avoid account changes.

Before creating a replacement user or granting privileges, establish whether the original user already exists in another container.

These principles can reduce troubleshooting errors. Support more consistent database administration.

Oracle Database 19c multitenant architecture introduces a distinction between database-wide administration and container‑specific user management.

When a database account appears to be missing, the first troubleshooting step should be to identify the container.

A local user may not appear in DBA_USERS when the DBA is connected to CDB$ROOT, even though the account exists in a PDB.

With privileges and container visibility, CDB_USERS can help identify the container associated with that account.

The main takeaway is simple:

Before concluding that an Oracle Database user does not exist, verify the container and investigate the account using the appropriate data dictionary views.

This approach supports troubleshooting, effective account administration and safer management of Oracle multitenant databases.

Official Oracle Documentation

1. Oracle Database 19c. Multitenant Architecture Overview

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/multi/overview-of-the-multitenant-architecture.html

2. Oracle Database 19c. Creating User Accounts

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/dbseg/creating-user-accounts.html

3. Oracle Database 19c. CDB Views

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/refrn/cdb_-views.html

4. Oracle Database 19c. DBA_USERS Reference

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/refrn/DBA_USERS.html

5. Oracle Database 19c. Monitoring CDBs and PDBs

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/multi/viewing-information-about-cdbs-and-pdbs-with-sql-plus.html

6. Oracle Database 19c. Schema- Accounts

https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/oracle-database/19/dbseg/schema-only-accounts.html

title: Inside V.E.T.O.R — Limbo Spider Boss Fight: Canvas Architecture, Hostage Risk & Synced Video Engine
description:
In boss fight design, challenge usually comes from boss health, attack patterns, and player reflexes. But what happens when the primary challenge is not destroying the creature, but preserving the living captive strapped to its body?

In this technical breakdown from V.E.T.O.R — A Ruptura, we examine the Limbo Spider encounter, focusing on how custom HTML5 Canvas rendering, synchronized video layers, and state tracking work together to create a high-stakes combat dilemma.

The Tactical Dilemma: Living Human Shield

The Limbo Spider does not fight alone—it carries an abducted living human trapped in a web cocoon positioned directly across its body. Every attack angle carries immediate consequences:

  • Zone-Aware Damage Detection: Strikes must be carefully calculated. Wide or mistimed combos can strike the hostage cocoon, resulting in mission failure if the captive dies before extraction.
  • Combat Timing vs. Tactical Pause: In this development footage, combat gameplay runs at 4x pace while tactical voice communications remain at 1x over the soundtrack. The UI is in Portuguese with in-game voice dialogue spoken in English.
  • Companion Robot Synergy: Working closely with the robotic companion V.E.T.O.R, players coordinate tactical pauses to draw the spider's attention, exposing weak appendages away from the cocoon.

Custom Engine Architecture: HTML5 Canvas + Synchronized Video

Building this encounter in a browser-based stack required avoiding conventional DOM-heavy rendering in favor of high-performance Canvas pipelines:

  1. Deterministic 60 FPS Loop: The combat state machine tracks creature coordinates, limb hitboxes, and hostage vulnerability frames on a discrete requestAnimationFrame loop.
  2. Synchronized Video Playback: High-fidelity creature textures and atmospheric dimensional rift effects are delivered via pre-rendered video assets synchronized directly to Canvas compositing layers.
  3. Decoupled Combat & Dialogue Logic: Pacing transitions smoothly between high-speed 4x kinetic exchanges and real-time 1x conversational tactical audio.

Project Status & Disclosures

  • Project: V.E.T.O.R — A Ruptura (Brazilian indie sci-fi action-RPG for PC/Windows, ~80% complete).
  • Playable Test Demo: Currently in preparation for internal testing (no public demo available yet).
  • Localization: The finished release will include complete localized voice dubbing across 7 languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Dutch).
  • Technology Disclosures: Development utilized OpenAI Codex for visual and structural code support, and Google Veo for selected pre-rendered cinematic background sequences.

Official Links

  • Official Website: vetorlogico.com
  • itch.io Devlog & Updates: jonie-magno-rangel.itch.io/vetor

title: Go Heartbeats over Logs for Silent Failures in Background Notification Tasks
description:
To track and report silent failures in background notification tasks, start with a page that identifies the batch without a confirmed outcome, the release that owns it, and whether replay is safe. For a B2B SaaS notification service, the least complex useful strategy is a scheduled heartbeat check paired with explicit task initiation and completion records. An exception counter alone cannot tell you that a worker never started.

Short answer: Track expected runs, record starts and terminal outcomes, and report overdue completion through a dedicated heartbeat service such as Healthchecks.io. Use execution-time and success-rate metrics to detect deterioration earlier, then preserve failure logs for investigation. Prefer heartbeats over error logs for detecting silent background task failures; keep both when deciding whether to roll back a notification release.

Consider a design example, not an incident report: a batch named renewal-notices belongs to release release-b, and its expected completion has passed. The page shows the batch identity and deadline, but no terminal outcome. Rolling back the worker changes future execution. It doesn't establish whether the previous worker already handed notifications to a delivery provider.

Preserve that distinction.

How should we track and report silent failures before a rollback?

Work backward from the decision the page demands. The responder needs evidence of a missing outcome, a way to locate the affected work, and an explicit replay policy; a graph of successful process exits is insufficient when the business requirement is that a notification reaches its intended delivery boundary. Define that boundary before choosing the chart. A worker finishing its function, a provider accepting a request, and a recipient receiving a message are different observations.

A useful run record connects the scheduled occurrence, batch identity, worker release, start time, and terminal result. These are application-owned design fields, not a monitoring vendor's request schema. A stable identity for each logical notification distinguishes a retry from new work, while an attempt identity preserves the history of repeated execution.

The earlier signal is overdue progress. If the scheduled occurrence never produces a start, investigate scheduling or dispatch. If a start has no terminal result before its deadline, investigate execution or the external handoff. If completion arrives but the service's chosen delivery boundary remains unconfirmed, keep that work unresolved. A heartbeat can expose missing activity; it cannot manufacture a delivery receipt.

Try Infrai for the diagnostic log-ingestion portion of this workflow if your team wants a plain REST API that the worker's existing HTTP client can call without installing a vendor SDK. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas and runnable examples, helping engineers check the integration contract before wiring it into a release. One key covers both log ingestion and metric reporting, reducing separate credential configuration at deployment; one bill also keeps those two diagnostic services together for platform accounting. Keep scheduled-run detection and paging with a dedicated monitoring service such as Healthchecks.io. That boundary gives each provider a specific job.

Set the SLO before setting the timeout

Define a notification SLO around a deadline and an observable outcome. For example, a proposed objective could require 99.9% of scheduled notification batches to reach their declared completion boundary within 10 minutes. Those numbers are design inputs for discussion, not measured service performance or a vendor guarantee. The denominator must include expected batches that never started.

Otherwise, missing work disappears.

Capacity planning belongs here because a timeout that ignores queueing will eventually describe demand rather than failure. As an illustrative load calculation, 600 notifications arriving per minute against capacity for 500 per minute add 100 pending notifications each minute while that imbalance persists. That arithmetic doesn't size a real worker fleet: task duration, retries, delivery-provider constraints, and concurrency still determine sustainable throughput. It does show why a healthy process can fall behind its delivery SLO without throwing an exception. A runtime metric begins at execution; the user's wait begins earlier.

Track queue wait separately from execution time where the application can observe both. Follow success rates alongside duration, and retain failed-task logs with the same logical identities so a responder can connect an overdue batch to its attempts. Report unresolved outcomes as unresolved rather than silently treating them as successful or definitively failed.

A transient slow attempt with ample deadline headroom may justify investigation, while a growing set of overdue batches may justify stopping a rollout. Neither observation proves that replaying every affected notification is safe.

Instrument the outcome before adding another dashboard

Record the start before attempting work, preserve an explicit error outcome when work fails, and record completion only after the application's declared success condition has been met. Keep the completion heartbeat aligned with that condition. Sending it from an unconditional cleanup block turns a failed task into apparent monitoring success.

Start records cannot detect a task that never launches.

For the diagnostic integration, Infrai's single API key and unified billing are a separate operating benefit from REST access. One API key covers the log and metric handoffs, so deployment configuration need not hold separate credentials for those two services. This does not remove the heartbeat specialist's configuration or the application's responsibility for run identity.

Keep lifecycle identities consistent when handing records to a log service, and use its documented schema rather than assuming that arbitrary local JSON fields can be posted unchanged. The following runnable Go program reads Infrai's public discovery schema for log ingestion, the contract-checking step before implementing that handoff. This public request needs no API key; authenticated ingestion belongs in a separate integration using a key read from the environment. The example performs no writes and prints the schema rather than inventing an ingestion payload.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func inspect() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/logs.ingest", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(deadline)
                if delay < 0 {
                    delay = 0
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := inspect(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Run this as a standalone Go program during integration review, outside the notification's execution path. Review the returned request schema before writing the authenticated sender. Discovery is a contract inspection tool, not a worker heartbeat. A single HTTP surface simplifies how diagnostic evidence enters a service; the scheduling contract and rollback decision still belong to the application and its monitoring workflow.

Buy missing-run detection and build the rollback contract

The buy-versus-build decision should follow the question the responder needs answered. Healthchecks.io, Prometheus, Grafana, and Datadog address different parts of the monitoring workflow. They aren't interchangeable answers to notification correctness.

Option Useful role in this workflow Operating responsibility and selection boundary
Healthchecks.io Heartbeat monitoring and notifications for task misfires Prefer it when the decisive question is whether expected work checked in; the application must define what a successful check-in means.
Prometheus with Alertmanager Metrics and alert rules for execution time, success rates, and overdue-work signals Prefer this path when the team can own metric design and alert operation; explicitly represent expected work so absent runs are detectable.
Grafana Alerting Evaluating alert rules and routing notifications from configured data sources Prefer it when those data sources and alert ownership are already established; a dashboard still needs a trustworthy task-outcome signal.
Datadog Managed monitoring with metric monitors Consider it when the team wants a managed monitoring workflow and accepts vendor-specific monitor configuration; business completion still needs instrumentation.
Infrai plus a heartbeat specialist Log ingestion through a plain REST interface alongside independent expected-run monitoring Use it when HTTP and a discoverable schema simplify the diagnostic handoff; choose the specialist for the missing-run page.
Application-owned run ledger Connecting scheduled work, attempts, release identity, and replay eligibility Build this contract when rollback safety depends on business outcomes; the team owns consistency, reconciliation, and retention decisions.

The trade-off is operational responsibility. Buying heartbeat monitoring removes a monitoring job from the platform roadmap, while running a metrics stack gives the team more control over signal design at the cost of operating that path. Infrai is not a replacement for a dedicated heartbeat monitor in this design; Healthchecks.io is the better choice for detecting that an expected run never checked in. Likewise, an established Grafana or Datadog monitoring workflow may be the better place to keep alert ownership rather than adding another handoff. No choice eliminates the application work needed to distinguish an accepted notification from an uncertain attempt.

For a small service whose immediate failure mode is a missed scheduled batch, begin with the heartbeat specialist. An existing metrics practice can justify expanding the signal set earlier. Keep the ledger's business meaning portable: provider-specific request shapes can live at the handoff, but the definition of a completed notification should survive a change of monitoring provider.

That is the part a rollback depends on.

Close the page without creating a second delivery incident

The useful incident report states which expected runs are overdue, which have explicit failures, which remain uncertain, and which release handled each attempt. Include the relevant time window and chosen success boundary. A success-rate chart helps prioritize investigation; a run-level history explains what can safely happen next.

Before replay, reconcile uncertain handoffs against whatever delivery evidence the application actually has. If a provider may already have accepted the notification, retry safety depends on the delivery integration's documented deduplication behavior or the application's own idempotency contract. A rollback is not evidence that an earlier side effect was undone. Preserve the original logical identity through recovery.

Finally, count the cost of a threshold that is too aggressive. As a hypothetical alert-budget calculation, a five-minute task has 288 scheduled runs in a day; if one out of every 100 runs is delayed beyond an overly tight threshold, that is about three late-run signals per day. This isn't a measured false-positive rate. It illustrates the investigation load a threshold can create before considering whether any delivery SLO was actually threatened.

Repeated unnecessary pages also create repeated opportunities for unsafe replay. Set the grace period against the completion objective and observed runtime variation, review alerts against actual outcomes, and tighten it only when the earlier signal changes a useful action. Aim for an actionable missing-outcome page with enough evidence to recover safely.

Further reading

References for the monitoring roles and implementation details discussed above:

  • Healthchecks.io documentation
  • Prometheus instrumentation guidance
  • Prometheus alerting overview
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Datadog metric monitors
  • Go HTTP client documentation

If the HTTP diagnostic handoff fits your service, start with the first-party Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery schema before connecting the worker.

title: Understanding Database Transactions: Why ACID Properties Matter
description:
A database transaction is a group of database operations treated as one logical unit of work.

Transactions are essential when multiple operations must succeed together. Without them, an application can end up with incomplete or inconsistent data.

Let's understand this with a practical example.

A real-world example

Imagine transferring $100 from Account A to Account B.

Two operations are required:

  1. Subtract $100 from Account A.
  2. Add $100 to Account B.

What happens if the first operation succeeds but the second fails?

Money could disappear from the system.

A database transaction helps prevent this situation.

Example using SQL 

BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE account_id = 1;

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 100
WHERE account_id = 2;

COMMIT;

If an operation fails, the application can roll back the transaction:

ROLLBACK;

The exact transaction behavior depends on the database engine, isolation level, and application logic.

Understanding the ACID properties

ACID describes four important properties of reliable database transactions.

1. Atomicity

A transaction is treated as one complete unit.

Either all its operations succeed, or none of them are committed.

2. Consistency

A transaction must preserve database rules and constraints.

For example, an application might enforce that an account balance cannot become negative.

3. Isolation

Concurrent transactions should not interfere with one another in ways that produce invalid results.

Database isolation levels determine how concurrent operations interact.

4. Durability

Once a transaction is committed, its changes should survive a system failure, subject to the database's durability guarantees.

Why developers should care

Transactions are useful in:

  • Banking and payment systems
  • E-commerce orders
  • Inventory management
  • Booking platforms
  • User account management
  • Financial record systems

Whenever multiple database operations depend on each other, transaction design matters.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Forgetting to roll back after an error.
  • Keeping transactions open longer than necessary.
  • Assuming every database uses identical isolation behavior.
  • Updating related records without considering concurrent requests.
  • Failing to test what happens when an operation fails halfway through.

Final thoughts

Database transactions are not just an advanced SQL feature. They are a fundamental part of building dependable software.

Understanding ACID helps developers create applications that protect data integrity, especially when multiple operations must work together.

Discussion: Have you implemented database transactions in a project? Which database did you use: MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or another one?

Database #SQL #BackendDevelopment #SoftwareEngineering #Programming #WebDevelopment

title: The Provider Said 'Already Charged'. Nothing Was Charged.
description:
Saturday morning, before coffee, a customer called Ana wrote in. She had tried to buy the $29 book twice, and twice my site told her she had already paid. Her bank showed nothing, and no order existed on my side. She asked whether I had taken her money and forgotten the book. I had not taken anything. My checkout had refused her money and then told her the refusal was her own history.

That email is the whole piece. A provider saying "already charged" is a rumour, not a receipt, and most payment code treats it as a verdict. It should not. On a first attempt the provider's word can be wrong in the direction nobody checks for: it can say the money moved when nothing moved at all. If your code believes it, you do something quieter than double-charging anyone. You turn away a customer who is trying to pay you, and no statement, no dashboard, no alert ever shows you did it.

ilragioniere put this to me in the comments, and he put it better than I could. He called it the false positive, and the quietest failure in the whole series: a provider that answers "already charged" when nothing was charged skips a real charge forever, and no statement ever shows it. His floor under it: the provider's own settlement report, a charge record nobody prunes, dated, independent of the key. Inside the lag, answer "unknown, hold" and let the file settle it when it lands. So I ran his shape. I built a small stand-in for the provider, one that lies on purpose, and I put two ways of handling a first attempt through the same 10 tries, twice over.

The stand-in answers "already charged" on every first attempt, even when no charge exists and no settlement line exists. That is the lie, stated plainly. The first handler is the three-line version: if the provider says already charged, skip. It never looks at the settlement file. The second handler reads the provider's answer and refuses to trust it. It says "unknown, hold", waits for the settlement file to land, and reads that instead. No line in the file means no settlement, and the charge goes ahead. A matching line means the charge is real, and nothing is charged twice.

The count is what makes this more than an opinion. Across 60 first attempts the stand-in said "already charged" 60 times, and in all 60 nothing had been charged. The trusting handler skipped 20 out of 20 real charges, $580 of payments refused, and never once looked at the file. The careful handler charged 20 out of 20 when the file held no matching line, $580 taken properly, and recognised the charge 20 out of 20 times when the file did hold one, with zero second charges. Same lie, same tries. The only difference was what each handler treated as evidence.

Five things I took away from that count.

  1. The lie leaves no trace. A double charge is loud. The customer sees $58 for a $29 book and asks for a refund. A skipped charge is silent. The provider took nothing, the file lists nothing, and the only record of the missing money is a customer deciding whether to write in or just leave. Ana wrote in. Most people do not; they assume the site is broken and buy the book somewhere else. Your numbers stay clean while sales quietly shrink, and nothing in your records can tell you why.

  2. The two mistakes are not the same size. A false "not charged" costs a double charge, a refund, and a thread with an unhappy customer. Somebody sees it the same day. A false "already charged" costs one charge nobody sees, found only if a customer complains. The loud error gets the guardrails and the late-night fixes. The quiet one gets trusted code and a shrug, because nobody has felt it yet. That is exactly backwards. The error you cannot see is the one you have to design against, not the one you will notice.

  3. The key cannot rescue this one. The key is a good tool for the job it does. If the charge landed and your own record of it did not, the key stops the retry from charging twice. But this failure happens before any of that. It is a first attempt. Nothing was charged, so there is no key entry worth asking about, and if the key was pruned it is gone anyway. A key proves a retry is the same request. It was never a receipt.

  4. The search lags, and the lag has a floor. The other place people look is the charge search: ask by your own order number instead of by key. It beats the key, and the previous piece showed it surviving a pruned key. But a search is not a read. It lags the charge by seconds, and inside those seconds the only honest answer is that you do not know yet. Code that cannot say "I don't know" fills the gap with whatever answer arrives first, usually the provider's confident one. The floor under the lag is the file: the settlement report lands on its own schedule, dated, and once it lands it does not change its mind.

  5. The file is the only thing nobody prunes. Keys get pruned, searches lag. The settlement file is the provider's own record of money that actually moved, written down after the fact, and it answers a different question from the other two: not "do you remember this request" but "did this money move". With the line absent, the careful handler's answer was not "already charged" but "no settlement", with the age of the attempt attached, and then it charged. With the line present, it said charged, and it was right. It is not fast or convenient. It is the one record that does not depend on the answer you are trying to check.

There is a limit to what this run can claim, and I would rather state it plainly. The provider here is a stand-in I built, not a real payment company, and the settlement file is one I wrote myself, landing a second after each attempt. The shape of the lie is real and the counts are real, but a real provider's file could arrive late, mangled, or not at all, and I did not measure that. The check that would close this properly needs a real sandbox account, a real charge, a pruned key, and both answers held up against the settlement line. I have not done that one, and I am not going to pretend the stand-in is the same thing. What it does prove is narrower: the three-line shortcut fails every time the provider is wrong, and the hold-and-read shape survives the same lie in both directions, twenty times out of twenty.

So here is where I land. Never let a provider's "already charged" be the last word on whether money moved. Read it, then check the record that does not depend on it. Inside the lag, say you do not know, wait for the file, and let the file decide. It costs a second and one extra read per attempt. The alternative costs customers you will never hear from, which is a strange price to pay for saving a second.

Has this one bitten you? As a buyer, were you ever told you had already paid when your bank said otherwise, and what did you do, write in or walk away? As a builder, what do you check first when a charge is in doubt, the provider's answer or your own records, and has the provider's answer ever been wrong for you? Tell me what you found. The quiet failures are the ones I only hear about when somebody says so out loud.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam
