title: Amazon S3 Annotations: Turning Object Storage into an AI-Ready Data Platform
description:
Imagine storing millions of documents, images, reports, and datasets in Amazon S3.

Your files are safe. Your storage is scalable. Your data lake is growing.

But there is a problem.

Your objects contain data, but do they contain enough context to explain what that data means?

Consider a file named:

report_2026_final_v3.pdf

From its filename, can you determine its owner, classification, approval status, customer, or business purpose?

Probably not.

Traditionally, applications solve this problem by maintaining separate metadata databases, custom tagging systems, and indexing pipelines.

But what if you could attach meaningful context directly to your S3 objects?

That is where Amazon S3 Annotations come in.

1. What Are Amazon S3 Annotations?

Amazon S3 Annotations provide a way to attach structured contextual information to S3 objects without modifying the original object content.

Think of annotations as an additional information layer associated with an object.

For example, a document stored in S3 could have contextual information like this:

{
  "document_type": "customer_contract",
  "department": "legal",
  "classification": "confidential",
  "customer_id": "CUST-1024",
  "processing_status": "reviewed",
  "summary": "Cloud infrastructure services agreement",
  "retention_years": 7
}

The original document remains unchanged, while the annotation provides useful business context.

This can help applications and data platforms discover and manage objects more intelligently.

2. Why Does This Matter?

Let's consider a typical enterprise data platform.

A company stores:

  • Customer contracts
  • Financial reports
  • Product images
  • Machine learning datasets
  • Application logs
  • Business documents
  • Compliance records

The challenge is not just storing these files.

The real challenge is discovering the right information when applications, analysts, and AI agents need it.

For example:

"Find all approved contracts belonging to customer CUST-1024."

A filename-based search is not enough.

The application needs structured information about the document type, customer, and approval status.

Annotations can help provide that context.

3. Building an AI-Ready S3 Architecture

Let's design a practical AWS architecture for an intelligent document processing platform.

Architecture flow

  1. Documents arrive through an application, API, or batch upload.
  2. Amazon S3 stores the original documents.
  3. S3 event notifications initiate processing.
  4. AWS Lambda orchestrates document-processing tasks.
  5. Amazon Textract extracts text and structured information from supported documents.
  6. Amazon Bedrock helps generate summaries and propose document classifications.
  7. The application validates the extracted information.
  8. The workflow attaches contextual annotations to the relevant S3 objects.
  9. Amazon S3 Metadata makes object metadata and annotations available through managed metadata tables.
  10. Amazon Athena queries the metadata for discovery and analytics.
  11. AI applications use the contextual information alongside an appropriate RAG retrieval pipeline.

Reference architecture 

       Enterprise Applications
                  |
                  v
             Amazon S3
            Original Files
                  |
                  v
        S3 Event Notifications
                  |
                  v
             AWS Lambda
                  |
          +-------+-------+
          |               |
          v               v
    Amazon Textract  Amazon Bedrock
    Text Extraction  AI Understanding
          |               |
          +-------+-------+
                  |
                  v
          Metadata Validation
                  |
                  v
         Amazon S3 Annotations
                  |
                  v
          Amazon S3 Metadata
                  |
                  v
             Amazon Athena
                  |
          +-------+-------+
          |               |
          v               v
       Analytics       AI / RAG Apps
                          |
                          v
                   Enterprise Agents

This is a reference architecture. The exact implementation depends on supported AWS APIs, event handling, annotation operations, and the application's retrieval design.

4. Annotations and RAG: A Powerful Combination

One of the most interesting applications is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

A typical RAG pipeline includes:

  1. Document ingestion
  2. Text extraction
  3. Chunking
  4. Embedding generation
  5. Vector indexing
  6. Similarity search
  7. Context retrieval
  8. LLM response generation

However, semantic similarity alone does not always provide enough business context.

Imagine asking:

"Find approved legal contracts for customer CUST-1024."

A vector database can find semantically similar content, but the application also needs structured filters.

For example:

SELECT
    object_key,
    document_type,
    customer_id,
    processing_status
FROM document_catalog
WHERE document_type = 'customer_contract'
  AND customer_id = 'CUST-1024'
  AND processing_status = 'approved';

This is a conceptual query against a metadata catalog or analytics table, not a direct SQL query against S3 object annotations.

The application can use the resulting object references to retrieve relevant document chunks from its vector index.

The important idea is combining:

  • Semantic search
  • Structured metadata filtering
  • Authorization checks
  • Context-aware generation

Annotations can help connect business context with AI retrieval.

They do not replace vector databases, embeddings, document chunking, or access-control systems.

5. How Can AI Agents Use S3 Annotations?

Imagine an enterprise AI agent that helps employees find internal documents.

A user asks:

"Find the latest approved security assessment reports for our production environment."

The agent could follow this workflow:

Step 1: Understand the request

Identify the document type, environment, approval status, and date requirement.

Step 2: Discover relevant objects

Query an appropriate metadata catalog using structured attributes.

Step 3: Verify permissions

Check whether the requesting user is authorized to access the matching documents.

Step 4: Retrieve content

Use the document-processing and RAG pipeline to retrieve relevant text and supporting evidence.

Step 5: Generate an answer

Use Amazon Bedrock to generate a response grounded in the retrieved information.

Step 6: Maintain traceability

Record the object references and versions used to produce the answer.

This architecture can make AI agents more context-aware without giving them unrestricted access to the storage environment.

6. Real-World Use Cases

Enterprise Document Intelligence

Attach document categories, ownership, approval status, and retention information to business documents.

AI-Powered Data Lakes

Add business context to datasets so analytics teams can discover information based on domain, owner, quality status, and processing stage.

Financial Services

Associate reports with reporting periods, business units, classification labels, and review status.

Healthcare Data Platforms

Attach operational context to supported healthcare data objects, while protecting sensitive information through appropriate security and governance controls.

Machine Learning Pipelines

Track dataset versions, validation status, processing stages, and model-training relevance.

7. Important Production Considerations

Before implementing this architecture, consider the following:

Security: Apply least-privilege IAM permissions and protect sensitive annotation information.

Data quality: Validate AI-generated classifications and summaries before treating them as trusted business information.

Versioning: Understand how annotations relate to object versions and explicitly handle new versions.

Governance: Define standard annotation schemas, field ownership, permitted values, and lifecycle rules.

Search: Annotations can support structured discovery, but semantic search requires an appropriate retrieval system.

Cost and performance: Evaluate annotation operations, metadata processing, query frequency, and downstream indexing costs.

8. The Bigger Picture

For years, cloud storage discussions focused on capacity, durability, availability, and cost.

Those things still matter.

But AI applications are changing what organizations expect from their data platforms.

They need to know:

  • What does this object represent?
  • Who owns it?
  • Can this user access it?
  • Is it approved for use?
  • Which business process does it support?
  • Is it relevant to the current AI task?

Amazon S3 Annotations offer another building block for answering these questions.

The opportunity is bigger than adding labels to files.

It is about connecting object storage with business context, metadata analytics, and intelligent applications.

The future of object storage is not just storing more data. It is making data easier to understand, discover, govern, and use.

References

  • Amazon S3 Annotations – AWS News Blog
  • Amazon S3 Annotations – AWS Documentation
  • Amazon S3 Metadata
  • Amazon Athena
  • Amazon Bedrock

This article describes a reference architecture. Check current AWS documentation for supported operations, regional availability, quotas, and pricing before deploying it in production.

title: Kiểm tra ngưỡng điểm từng kỹ năng của chứng chỉ B2 Aptis bằng Python
description:
Một số chứng chỉ ngoại ngữ không chỉ xét tổng điểm mà còn đòi hỏi từng kỹ năng đạt một ngưỡng tối thiểu. Với B2 Aptis ESOL, thông tin trên trang khóa ôn nêu mỗi kỹ năng thang 0–50, tổng tối đa 200, và để đạt B2 thí sinh thường cần khoảng 35–42 điểm ở mỗi kỹ năng, không kỹ năng nào dưới 35. Bài này viết một hàm Python nhỏ để kiểm tra điều kiện đó. Mã đã chạy thử trên Python 3.12. Các con số chỉ mang tính tham khảo theo thông tin khóa ôn, không phải quy định chính thức của đơn vị chấm thi.

Quy tắc cần mã hóa

  • Có bốn kỹ năng: Listening, Reading, Writing, Speaking, mỗi kỹ năng thang 0–50.
  • Điểm một kỹ năng dưới 35 thì chưa đạt B2, dù tổng điểm cao.
  • Tổng điểm thường nằm trong khoảng 140–165; nếu ngoài khoảng, ta chỉ ghi chú để người dùng kiểm tra lại.

Mã nguồn 

NGUONG_KY_NANG = 35          # moi ky nang can tu muc nay tro len de dat B2
TONG_KHOANG = (140, 165)      # khoang tong diem thuong gap (4 ky nang, toi da 200)
KY_NANG = ("Listening", "Reading", "Writing", "Speaking")

def kiem_tra_diem(diem):
    if set(diem) != set(KY_NANG):
        raise ValueError("Can du 4 ky nang: " + ", ".join(KY_NANG))
    for ten, v in diem.items():
        if not 0 <= v <= 50:
            raise ValueError(f"{ten}: diem {v} ngoai thang 0-50")

def danh_gia_b2(diem):
    kiem_tra_diem(diem)
    thap = [k for k, v in diem.items() if v < NGUONG_KY_NANG]
    tong = sum(diem.values())
    if thap:
        return {"ket_qua": "chua dat B2", "tong": tong, "ky_nang_duoi_nguong": thap}
    kq = {"ket_qua": "dat nguong B2", "tong": tong}
    if not TONG_KHOANG[0] <= tong <= TONG_KHOANG[1]:
        kq["ghi_chu"] = f"tong {tong} nam ngoai khoang tham khao {TONG_KHOANG}"
    return kq

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mau = [
        {"Listening": 38, "Reading": 40, "Writing": 36, "Speaking": 37},
        {"Listening": 42, "Reading": 44, "Writing": 34, "Speaking": 40},
        {"Listening": 50, "Reading": 50, "Writing": 50, "Speaking": 50},
    ]
    for m in mau:
        print(danh_gia_b2(m))
    try:
        danh_gia_b2({"Listening": 60, "Reading": 40, "Writing": 36, "Speaking": 37})
    except ValueError as e:
        print("LOI:", e)

Giải thích

Kiểm tra dữ liệu trước khi đánh giá. kiem_tra_diem bắt hai lỗi hay gặp: thiếu hoặc thừa kỹ năng, và điểm ngoài thang 0–50. Lỗi được báo bằng ValueError thay vì trả về kết quả sai.

Ưu tiên từng kỹ năng. danh_gia_b2 xét ngưỡng 35 cho từng kỹ năng trước, rồi mới nhìn tổng. Nhờ vậy trường hợp tổng cao nhưng một kỹ năng thấp vẫn bị nhận diện đúng.

Ghi chú thay vì từ chối. Khoảng 140–165 chỉ là mức thường gặp, nên mã không loại điểm nằm ngoài khoảng mà thêm ghi chú.

Kết quả chạy thử 

{'ket_qua': 'dat nguong B2', 'tong': 151}
{'ket_qua': 'chua dat B2', 'tong': 160, 'ky_nang_duoi_nguong': ['Writing']}
{'ket_qua': 'dat nguong B2', 'tong': 200, 'ghi_chu': 'tong 200 nam ngoai khoang tham khao (140, 165)'}
LOI: Listening: diem 60 ngoai thang 0-50

Mẫu thứ hai có tổng 160, nằm trong khoảng thường gặp, nhưng Writing chỉ 34 nên vẫn chưa đạt. Đây là điểm mà việc chỉ cộng tổng dễ bỏ sót.

Mở rộng

  • Đọc điểm từ file CSV cho nhiều thí sinh.
  • Thêm kiểm thử với unittest cho từng ngưỡng biên (34, 35).
  • Dùng dữ liệu Grammar & Vocabulary làm yếu tố phụ khi điểm kỹ năng sát ranh giới, nếu bạn có quy định cụ thể để mã hóa.

Dữ liệu mẫu trong bài do tự tạo, không phải kết quả thật của thí sinh.

title: AI Tokenomics: Why Cheaper Tokens Are Making Your AI Bill Bigger
description:
The price of a given level of AI capability is falling by roughly an order of magnitude every year. Yet companies are blowing through AI budgets, flat-rate AI plans are disappearing, and token spending keeps climbing. This is not a pricing anomaly. It is the economics of tokens working exactly as economics predicts. Here is what is happening on the supply side, the demand side, and in your budget, and the controls that actually keep AI spend under control.

Research checked November 21, 2026.

The Budget Was Gone by April

In June 2026, Fortune reported a detail that should make every engineering leader pause. Uber's chief operating officer said the company had used up its entire AI budget in the first four months of the year. Bloomberg later reported that Uber capped AI spending at $1,500 per employee per month.

Uber is not a company that misunderstands technology costs. And the tokens it was buying were getting cheaper the whole time.

The same Fortune piece cited the Silicon Data Token Expenditure Index: the price of a single token has dropped more than 90 percent since 2023, while spending on large language models has doubled since late 2025. Bain and Company analysts put it more bluntly in a brief quoted in the article:

"The models get cheaper. The usage gets heavier. The bill stays stubbornly high."

This looks like a paradox. It has a name, and it is more than 150 years old.

In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain's coal consumption. They increased it. Cheaper energy per unit of work made coal worth using for far more work.

Apollo's chief economist, Torsten Slok, applied the same idea to AI this year: "As tokens get cheaper, companies don't spend less but instead run more AI agents, automate more workflows."

That is AI tokenomics in one sentence.

Falling token prices do not shrink AI budgets. They expand what is worth automating. Vendors set the price of a token. Your architecture, your agents, and your incentives set how many tokens you use. The organizations that control AI spend will be the ones that govern demand, not the ones waiting for prices to fall.

TL;DR

  • Token prices are collapsing at fixed capability. Epoch AI estimates the cost of a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47 percent per quarter since 2023, or about 13x per year. MIT researchers estimate 5x to 10x per year for frontier-level benchmark performance.
  • Frontier costs are not falling the same way. The same MIT paper estimates the price of running frontier models is rising 3x to 18x per year, because of bigger models and larger reasoning demands.
  • Token volume is growing faster than prices fall. Google said at I/O 2026 that it processes 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month, up from 9.7 trillion two years earlier. Its model APIs alone reached nearly 32 billion tokens per minute in Q3 2026, more than four times a year earlier.
  • Spending is the product of both. Bain found token costs halved from December 2024 to December 2025 while tokens consumed grew 450 percent. Half the price times 5.5x the volume is 2.75x the spend.
  • Agents and reasoning are the multiplier. Anthropic reported that agents use about 4x more tokens than chat, and multi-agent systems about 15x. Reasoning tokens, longer contexts, and background agents push the number higher.
  • Cheaper tokens unlock new workloads. Each price drop moves more tasks above the break-even line, so total demand grows. This is the Jevons effect, and AI demand appears to be highly elastic.
  • Flat-rate AI is breaking. Pricing designed for chat cannot absorb agents that run for hours. Anthropic introduced weekly limits for Claude Code in 2025, and other AI coding tools have moved toward metered or capped pricing.
  • For AI product builders, demand is margin risk. If you charge per seat and your users adopt agents, your costs can grow faster than token prices fall.
  • For buyers, forecast volume, not price. A budget that assumes token prices will fall is the budget that runs out in April.
  • Govern demand. Budgets per agent and per employee, routing by task difficulty, caching, reasoning-effort tuning, loop caps, and cost attribution are the levers that work.

First, Separate the Prices of a Token

"Tokens are getting cheaper" and "AI is getting more expensive" are both true. They describe different numbers.

Number Direction What drives it Who controls it
Price per token at fixed capability Falling fast Better hardware, better algorithms, competition Vendors
Price per token at the frontier Flat or rising Bigger models, more reasoning, premium tiers Vendors
Tokens per task Rising Agents, reasoning, longer context, retries Your architecture
Tasks per month Rising New use cases, adoption, background automation Your organization
Total spend Usually rising All of the above multiplied together Mostly you

The core equation is simple:

AI spend  =  price per token  x  tokens per task  x  tasks

Vendors push the first term down. Almost everything about modern AI adoption pushes the second and third terms up.

When people say AI is getting cheaper, they are usually looking at the first row. When finance says AI is getting more expensive, they are looking at the last.

The Supply Side: Why Tokens Keep Getting Cheaper

The decline in token prices is one of the fastest cost curves in modern technology.

The measurements

Epoch AI published "The plunging price of thought" in September 2026. Its estimate: "The cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, or 13× per year."

The decline is not uniform over time. Averaging across five benchmarks, Epoch found cost falls "66% per quarter (75× per year) for performance that has just debuted as SOTA," and "two years later, prices fall half as fast, at 32% per quarter (4.7× per year)." New capability gets cheap fastest right after it arrives, then the decline slows.

a16z's Guido Appenzeller coined the term "LLMflation" in 2024: "For an LLM of equivalent performance, the cost is decreasing by 10x every year." He also cautioned that "its rate may slow down."

MIT researchers in "The Price of Progress" estimate that the price for a given level of benchmark performance has decreased "around 5× to 10× per year" for frontier models across knowledge, reasoning, math, and software engineering benchmarks. After removing the effects of competition and hardware price declines, they estimate algorithmic efficiency progress alone at "around 3× per year."

Different methods, different benchmarks, same conclusion: at a fixed level of capability, tokens get dramatically cheaper every year.

Tokens as a manufactured product

The supply side is also being reframed in industrial terms. NVIDIA now describes data centers as "AI factories," and its own materials treat tokens per megawatt as the measure that governs a factory's earning capacity. Power, not chips alone, is increasingly the constraint, so efficiency per watt becomes efficiency per dollar.

That framing matters for buyers. Tokens are becoming a manufactured commodity with a production cost, and production costs keep falling with each hardware generation.

The part that does not get cheaper

There is an important caveat in the MIT paper. While the price of a given level of performance falls, "the price of running frontier models is rising" between 3x and 18x per year "due to bigger models and larger reasoning demands."

That is the first half of the tokenomics paradox. Last year's capability gets cheap. This year's capability costs more. And most teams upgrade.

The Demand Side: Why Token Volume Is Exploding

If prices tell half the story, volume tells the rest.

Google's numbers

Google publishes some of the clearest public token data.

At Google I/O 2026 in May, Sundar Pichai described the growth in tokens processed across Google's surfaces: 9.7 trillion tokens per month two years earlier, about 480 trillion at I/O 2025, and "3.2 quadrillion tokens per month" at I/O 2026.

That is roughly a 330x increase in two years.

The API-only numbers, reported in Alphabet earnings remarks, show the same curve:

Period Google first-party model APIs
Q1 2026 About 16 billion tokens per minute
Q2 2026 (July 22) About 22 billion tokens per minute
Q3 2026 (October 28) Nearly 32 billion tokens per minute, "more than four times what we processed a year ago"

Google also reported internal developer usage rising from half a trillion tokens a day in March 2026 to more than 3 trillion a day by I/O in May.

These figures use different scopes and units, so they should not be stacked into one series. Together they show something unambiguous: token demand is compounding much faster than token prices are falling.

The enterprise numbers

Bain's analysis, as quoted by Fortune, found that token costs halved from December 2024 to December 2025, while tokens consumed grew 450 percent over the same period. Bain attributed part of the growth to companies upgrading to newer models rather than keeping existing ones and banking the savings.

Run the arithmetic:

price:   x 0.5
volume:  x 5.5   (450% growth)
spend:   0.5 x 5.5  =  x 2.75

Prices halved. The bill almost tripled.

What is driving demand

Five forces are multiplying tokens per task and tasks per month at the same time.

1. Agents. Anthropic reported in 2025 that "agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats." Every workflow that moves from chat to agent multiplies its token footprint.

2. Reasoning. Reasoning models spend tokens thinking before they answer. Those tokens are billed, even when you do not see them.

3. Longer context. Agents re-read growing histories, tool results, and documents on every step.

4. Background and proactive work. Agents that monitor inboxes, run scheduled routines, or work overnight consume tokens without a human prompt. As I wrote about Claude Duet, an agent that works while you sleep also spends while you sleep.

5. Upgrades. When a better model ships, teams switch to it, as Bain noted. The price drop on last year's model never reaches the budget.

The Jevons Mechanism in AI

The Jevons paradox happens when demand is elastic enough that a lower price increases total spending. In AI, three feedback loops make demand very elastic.

Loop 1: New use cases cross the break-even line

Every task has a value and an AI cost. When AI cost falls below the task's value, the task becomes worth automating.

worth automating  if  value of task  >  tokens per task x price per token

A tenfold price drop does not make existing tasks ten times cheaper and leave it there. It moves a whole new set of tasks above the line: summarizing every support call instead of a sample, reviewing every pull request instead of large ones, monitoring every log stream instead of alerts only. Each new category adds volume.

Loop 2: Savings are reinvested in quality

When a cheaper model can do last year's work, teams rarely pocket the savings. They use the headroom to run a stronger model, add a verification step, increase reasoning effort, or run a second agent to check the first. Quality improves. The token bill does not shrink.

Loop 3: Autonomy scales consumption

Cheaper tokens make longer agent runs affordable. Longer runs make agents more capable. More capable agents get assigned bigger tasks. Fortune's summary of the trend captures it: once a team believes AI can handle bigger tasks, it asks for more and uses more tokens.

Slok summarized the result: "Lower cost per interaction does not mean fewer interactions."

Who Pays: The End of Flat-Rate AI

Flat-rate AI pricing was designed for chat. A person types, the model replies, the person reads. Usage is bounded by human attention.

Agents removed that bound.

An agent can run for hours, spawn sub-agents, and work overnight. A single heavy user running agents can consume many times the tokens of a typical chat user on the same plan.

The industry is adjusting:

  • Anthropic introduced weekly rate limits for Claude Code subscribers in 2025, citing users who ran it continuously and saying the change would affect a small minority of users.
  • Other AI coding tools, according to 2026 trade coverage, have moved from unlimited plans toward token-based credits, metered billing, or tighter caps.
  • Enterprises are introducing their own caps, like Uber's reported $1,500 per employee per month.

None of this means AI is becoming unaffordable. It means the cost of agentic usage is becoming visible, and someone has to own it: the vendor, the employer, or the user.

What Tokenomics Means If You Build AI Products

If you sell an AI product, token demand is not just your customer's problem. It is your gross margin.

Here is an illustrative example. The numbers are assumptions, but the structure is common.

Year 1. You charge $30 per user per month. Most users chat; a few run agents.

User type Share of users Tokens per month Blended price per 1M tokens Token cost
Chat user 90% 2M $1.50 $3
Agent user 10% 60M $1.50 $90
Average $11.70

Average token cost is $11.70 per user. Gross margin on tokens is about 61 percent.

Year 2. Token prices halve. Good news. But 40 percent of users now run agents, and agent workflows have doubled in size.

User type Share of users Tokens per month Blended price per 1M tokens Token cost
Chat user 60% 2M $0.75 $1.50
Agent user 40% 120M $0.75 $90
Average $36.90

Average token cost is now $36.90 against $30 of revenue. Token prices halved, and gross margin went from about +61 percent to about -23 percent.

That is the tokenomics trap for product builders. Your costs are driven by your users' behavior, and agents change user behavior faster than vendors cut prices.

What I would design in from day one:

  • Metering everywhere. Know tokens per user, per feature, and per workflow.
  • Pricing that tracks usage or value. Seats plus usage, credits, or outcome-based pricing, rather than unlimited seats.
  • Model routing. Send easy work to cheap models, and keep frontier models for tasks that need them.
  • Caching and compaction. Reuse stable context instead of paying for it on every call.
  • Fair-use caps with clear communication. Limits users discover by surprise damage trust more than limits they understand.

What Tokenomics Means If You Buy AI

For engineering and finance leaders, the lesson is about forecasting.

Forecast volume, not price. A budget built on the assumption that token prices will fall 50 percent is likely to be wrong in the dangerous direction. Prices may fall. Usage will almost certainly rise faster.

Attribute every token. Spend that cannot be assigned to a team, product, workflow, or agent cannot be managed. Tag model calls with the owner and purpose.

Measure value per token, not tokens. In my previous article, I argued for cost per verified successful task as the core unit metric. Tokenomics is the organizational version of the same idea: total spend only matters relative to the value it produces.

Treat token budgets as product decisions. Deciding that an internal coding agent gets $500 per engineer per month, or that a support agent may spend up to $2 per resolved ticket, is a decision about what work is worth automating. It belongs with product and engineering leaders, not only finance.

Demand Governance: The Controls That Actually Work

If vendors control price and you control demand, these are the levers worth building.

1. Budgets at the right level

Set budgets per agent, per task, per team, and per employee, and enforce them in code, not in a spreadsheet. A task-scoped budget, like the spend envelopes I described for agent payments, stops runaway runs before they become monthly surprises.

2. Route by task difficulty

Most tasks do not need the frontier model. Route classification, extraction, and routing decisions to small models or decision models such as Jev, and reserve frontier models for work that measurably benefits.

3. Tune reasoning effort per step

Princeton's Holistic Agent Leaderboard found higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in the majority of its runs. Reasoning is a parameter to measure, not a dial to turn up by default.

4. Cache and compact

Cache stable prefixes such as system prompts, tool definitions, and reference documents. Compact long histories. These cut tokens without cutting quality.

5. Cap loops and tails

Set maximum steps, tokens, and wall-clock time per task. A small number of runaway agents can dominate a monthly bill.

6. Make background work earn its keep

Scheduled and proactive agents run without a human asking. Review what they produce. A daily briefing nobody reads is pure token spend.

7. Show people their usage

Engineers and teams make better decisions when they can see what their agents cost. Visibility changes behavior faster than policy documents do.

What Could Change the Curve

Tokenomics is a trend, not a law. Several things could bend it.

Price declines may slow. Epoch's own data shows the decline slowing as capability matures, and both a16z and Epoch warn against assuming the current pace continues indefinitely.

Power may set a floor. If electricity and data center capacity become the binding constraint, tokens per megawatt matters more than chip price, and token supply may not keep pace with demand.

Frontier costs may keep rising. If the best models keep getting bigger and reason longer, staying at the frontier will cost more each year, even as older capability becomes nearly free.

Subsidies may unwind. Some AI pricing has been set to win market share rather than to cover cost. The shift away from flat-rate plans suggests that correction has started.

Demand may saturate. At some point, organizations will have automated the obvious work. That point does not appear close.

I would not bet on any of these reversing the core dynamic in the next two years. I would plan for token demand to keep growing faster than token prices fall.

A Practical 30-Day Plan

Week 1: Baseline

  • Pull token usage and spend by model, team, product, and workflow.
  • Identify the top 10 workloads by spend.
  • Separate chat usage from agent and background usage.
  • Find any spend you cannot attribute to an owner.

Week 2: Unit economics

  • For the top workloads, calculate tokens per task and cost per successful outcome.
  • Identify which workloads use frontier models for work a smaller model could handle.
  • Measure what share of spend comes from the top 1 percent of tasks.

Week 3: Controls

  • Add budgets and caps for the highest-spend agents.
  • Route one high-volume workload to a cheaper model and compare outcomes.
  • Enable caching for stable prompt prefixes.
  • Review background and scheduled agents for value.

Week 4: Forecast

  • Build next year's forecast from expected task volume and tokens per task, not just expected price changes.
  • Model a scenario where agent adoption doubles.
  • Set budget owners and a monthly review.

At the end of 30 days, you should know where your tokens go, which ones produce value, and how fast demand is growing. That is more useful than any price prediction.

Seven Questions for Any AI Budget Owner

  1. What share of our token spend comes from agents and background work?
  2. How fast is token volume growing per team, and why?
  3. Which workloads use frontier models, and do they need to?
  4. What is our cost per successful outcome for the top five workloads?
  5. Which spend cannot be attributed to an owner?
  6. What happens to our budget if agent adoption doubles?
  7. If we sell AI features, what does our heaviest 10 percent of users cost us?

If your forecast assumes prices will fall and usage will stay flat, it is not a forecast. It is a hope.

Final Take: The Price of a Token Is Not the Price of Intelligence

Token prices are falling faster than almost any cost curve in technology. That is real, and it is good. It is why AI capability that was a research demo three years ago now costs fractions of a cent.

But cheaper tokens do not make AI cheap.

They make AI everywhere.

Every price drop moves more work above the break-even line. Every capable model invites bigger tasks. Every agent that can run longer will be asked to. That is how Jevons' coal story played out in the nineteenth century, and it is how tokenomics is playing out now.

The organizations that handle this well will not be the ones with the best vendor discount. They will be the ones that know what each token buys, decide deliberately what is worth automating, and enforce those decisions in their systems.

Vendors will keep making tokens cheaper.

Deciding how many you need is still your job.

Sources and Further Reading

  1. Fortune, Tokens are getting cheaper, but companies are spending even more on AI as a result, top economist warns (June 17, 2026): https://fortune.com/2026/06/17/why-is-ai-spending-increasing-as-tokens-get-cheaper-jevons-paradox/
  2. Bain & Company, How token economics will change opex: https://www.bain.com/insights/how-token-economics-will-change-opex/
  3. Epoch AI, The plunging price of thought (September 2026): https://epoch.ai/publications/the-plunging-price-of-thought
  4. Gundlach, Lynch, Mertens, and Thompson, The Price of Progress: Price Performance and the Future of AI (MIT; November 2025, revised March 2026): https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.23455
  5. a16z, Welcome to LLMflation: LLM inference cost is going down fast (November 12, 2024): https://a16z.com/llmflation-llm-inference-cost/
  6. Google, Q2 2026 earnings call: Remarks from our CEO (July 22, 2026): https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/message-ceo/alphabet-earnings-q2-2026/
  7. Google, Q3 2026 earnings call: Remarks from our CEO (October 28, 2026): https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/message-ceo/alphabet-earnings-q3-2026/

title: Part 32: Data residency and on-prem runtimes compared
description:
Part 32 · One Agent, Five Platforms

Regulated? Then where the agent and its data run matters as much as what it does. An invoice agent reads supplier bank details, approval history and amounts. A security or data protection review will ask three questions before it asks anything about prompts:

  • Runtime: where does the agent itself run, and can it run in our own infrastructure?
  • Model: where are prompts and completions processed?
  • Logs: where do traces, conversation history and audit records end up?

Part 30 flagged residency as the control with the most gaps. This part answers the three questions for each platform, from vendor documentation I read on 20 November 2026. Like the builds, it's documentation-only, and the gaps are stated rather than filled.

MuleSoft

  • Runtime. Agent networks deploy to a CloudHub 2.0 shared or private space, or a Runtime Fabric target. Runtime Fabric runs on infrastructure you manage, so it's the customer-hosted option (Part 11). The control planes overview lists agent network projects and the LLM gateway as available on the EU control plane. Since 16 November 2026, the release notes also list Hyperforce as a target for version 2.0 agent networks.
  • Model. The broker calls an LLM provider you configure, through the gateway. I found no statement about where those calls are processed. That depends on the provider and region you choose.
  • Logs. Traces and logs go to Anypoint Monitoring, and the EU control plane lists log search, raw log data and a telemetry exporter. Retention and storage location weren't on the pages I read.

Boomi

  • Runtime. The runtime clouds page lists four Boomi-managed clouds: US East, UK, Japan and Australia. There's still no EU cloud; the UK one is outside the EU. A self-hosted Flex runtime "runs in your own infrastructure" but is in early access, as it was in Part 15.
  • Model. The Boomi AI FAQ says agents use models through Amazon Bedrock, and that each runtime runs the model, prompts and responses "in the selected region". You can also connect your own Anthropic, OpenAI or Google account, in which case prompts go to that provider. On Flex, "only the model prompt leaves your network".
  • Logs. Audit trace logs are in Agent Control Tower, without a stated retention period. Chat sessions are kept until a user deletes them. Two exceptions matter for residency: glossary and knowledge base content is stored in the platform's region, so a North America customer running agents in the UK, Japan or Australia retrieves it from the US.

SAP

  • Runtime. The Business AI reference architecture says the platform is "SAP-managed by default", with SAP AI Core running on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. SAP Learning's data residency lesson describes locally hosted AI, SAP Sovereign Cloud and an EU AI Cloud with "AI infrastructure hosted within Europe". I found no on-premises option for Joule agents, and no availability dates for those offerings.
  • Model. Models come through the generative AI hub, from SAP and partners such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral and Cohere. The lesson says processing "may occur on SAP-managed infrastructure or approved external model providers, depending on the use case and configuration". I found no way to pin Joule's model calls to a region.
  • Logs. Not covered in what I read, as in Part 18. The architecture mentions agent session telemetry going to SAP Cloud ALM, but not where it's stored or for how long.

Azure

  • Runtime. Foundry Agent Service endpoints are regional, and the FAQ says "data is stored in the same region as the endpoint". In the standard setup, threads, files and vector stores go to your own Cosmos DB, Storage and AI Search resources. Agents can run in your virtual network, on a delegated subnet in the same region. There's no on-premises option on these pages.
  • Model. This is where Azure is clearest. The deployment types page defines three levels:
    • Global: may be processed in any Azure region.
    • Data Zone: processed only within the US, EU or APAC zone. The EU zone is the EU Data Boundary.
    • Standard (regional): processed within the geography you choose. In every case, "data stored at rest remains in the designated Azure geography". So the deployment type you pick is a residency decision, not just a pricing one.
  • Logs. Traces go to an Application Insights resource in your own subscription (Part 22).

AWS

  • Runtime. AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Identity and Observability are available in seven European regions, according to the regions page: Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain and Stockholm. Milan and Spain don't have Memory or Runtime Instances yet. The runtime can attach to your VPC (Part 25). There's no on-premises option.
  • Model. Bedrock's geographic cross-Region inference keeps EU requests within EU regions. But prompts and results "might move outside of your source Region", and any abuse-detection copies are stored in the destination region. On the AgentCore side, the cross-Region inference page says Memory, Policy and Evaluations use it. From the EU regions it stays in Europe. From some other source regions, Policy and Evaluations use global routing that can leave the geography.
  • Logs. Observability writes to CloudWatch in your account (Part 25). The cross-Region page warns that CloudWatch and CloudTrail logs "won't specify the AWS Region in which data inference occurs".

What the builds could and could not show

  • Could: where each vendor says the runtime runs, which regions exist, and which platforms offer a customer-hosted runtime. MuleSoft has Runtime Fabric, and Boomi has Flex in early access.
  • Could not: where model calls actually land for MuleSoft and SAP, and log retention on most of them. Those need the vendor's trust documentation or contract terms, and a hands-on build that checks the traces.
  • For an EU-only requirement: Azure's Data Zone and AWS's EU regions are the most explicit in the docs. MuleSoft can keep the runtime and control plane in the EU but leaves model location to your provider. Boomi has no EU-managed cloud. SAP describes an EU AI Cloud without dates I could find.

The policy from Part 30 still holds: classify the data first, then pick the runtime, model deployment and log store that keep each class where it's allowed.

Where must your agent data stay?

This series describes a reference build on a fictional company. This part is based only on vendor documentation read on 20 November 2026 and the documentation-only builds in Parts 11 to 30; no hands-on build has been run yet. It's not legal or compliance advice. Views are my own.

title: Healthtech Background Job Queue: Fixing Malformed 256KB JSON Payloads
description:
Short answer: keep the renewal command small, validate the serialized bytes and schema in both the Node.js producer and consumer, and store the large health record outside the queue behind a stable reference. The 256 KB ceiling is a contract boundary, not a retryable incident; malformed JSON and schema failures should be quarantined with an audit record, while a delayed reminder should be recoverable through idempotent consumer state.

This matters when a healthtech business wants to delay a renewal reminder until a contract or business deadline. The reminder is time-sensitive, but its payload should not become a copy of the subscription, patient, or billing aggregate. A queue message should say what must happen, when the decision was made, and where the worker can obtain the minimum authorized input.

How should a background job queue reject malformed 256KB payloads?

Treat the producer and consumer as two independent contract boundaries. The producer creates an explicit envelope, serializes it once, measures the resulting byte length, and refuses a message above 256 KB. The consumer performs the same byte check before parsing, then parses JSON, validates the schema, checks domain rules, and only then starts the reminder workflow. Repeating validation is deliberate: a delayed message may outlive a deployment, and another publishing path may not share the producer's assumptions.

The order prevents confusing failures. A byte-limit violation is not a JSON parse error. A malformed document is not a schema violation. A syntactically valid object can still lack a message ID, a deadline, a schema version, or the reference needed to decide whether a reminder is still appropriate. Log those classifications separately; otherwise an operations dashboard will describe three different contract failures as one mysterious retry spike.

The practical envelope for this scenario is small:

type RenewalReminder struct {
    SchemaVersion int    `json:"schema_version"`
    MessageID     string `json:"message_id"`
    AccountID     string `json:"account_id"`
    Deadline      string `json:"business_deadline"`
    Subscription  string `json:"subscription_ref"`
    Template      string `json:"template_version"`
}

The reference is not automatically harmless. In a healthtech system, an account ID or subscription reference can still be personal data, so it belongs in the deletion inventory and access-control model. GDPR Article 17 does not stop applying because the identifier moved from an HTTP request into a queue or a database table.

The architecture decision record: where does recovery stop?

The decision is to use a versioned command envelope, a durable inbox, and a separate source for large objects. The invariants are more important than the queue brand:

  • A message is accepted only if its serialized bytes are at or below 256 KB.
  • The schema version, command identity, business deadline, and reference are required.
  • The consumer records the message ID before the reminder side effect, using a uniqueness constraint in the same transaction as the business state transition.
  • An acknowledgement follows the committed transaction, not the moment the worker begins processing.
  • A permanent contract failure is recorded and quarantined; a transient delivery failure can be retried within a bounded policy.

This is an exactly-once mindset applied where it can actually be enforced. A queue may deliver a message more than once. The application can still make the business effect happen once by putting the inbox insert and the reminder-state update in one database transaction. If the worker crashes after the transaction commits but before acknowledgement, redelivery finds the existing message ID and does not send a second reminder.

The audit row should include the message ID, schema version, correlation ID, disposition, timestamp, and a digest of the received bytes. It generally should not include the raw health record or the entire JSON body. A digest lets an investigator connect a repeated failure to an input without spreading another copy of regulated data through logs.

Recovery becomes much clearer when the producer's refusal and the consumer's quarantine are treated as different observations. A producer can reject a message before it leaves the application, which is the cheapest place to expose a growing payload and the best place to return a useful validation error to the caller. A consumer, by contrast, has to assume that the message may have been emitted by an older release, replayed from a redrive tool, or produced by a second service that did not share the current schema package. It therefore records what it actually received, including the byte count and digest, rather than copying the producer's explanation. During an investigation, those two records answer different questions: did the publishing path understand the contract, and did the worker enforce the contract at the point of side effect? Keeping both answers makes an audit trail useful without making the queue a second patient-record system. It also gives an operator a controlled repair path: correct the producer, deploy the schema change, inspect quarantined IDs, and redrive only messages whose business deadlines and authorization still make them valid.

Keep it boring.

Decision area Compact command envelope Full aggregate in the message
Size control Easy to measure before publish Can cross 256 KB as fields grow
Schema change Versioned command contract Couples the worker to unrelated fields
Privacy Keeps routine copies out of the queue Replicates sensitive fields into queue retention
Recovery Redrive one command after fixing the cause Reconstruct and re-authorize a large object
Appropriate use Renewal decision and stable reference A small, self-contained, non-sensitive object

The rejected option is compression as the primary fix. Compression may reduce transport bytes, but it does not solve schema coupling, retention, access control, or a consumer that parses an unexpected version. Fragmenting one large object is worse for recovery: now operators must reconcile missing pieces, duplicate fragments, ordering, expiration, and authorization at assembly time.

There is a valid use for the full-object design. Use it when the object is demonstrably below the limit, has a stable versioned schema, contains no separately governed data, and has idempotent processing. That is a reasonable choice for a compact internal command. It is a poor default for an evolving healthtech aggregate.

A Go reference implementation for the producer-consumer boundary

The following sample shows the critical path without pretending that an in-memory map is a production inbox. The production version should put the uniqueness check, renewal-state change, and outbox or send decision under the database's transaction rules. The sample's useful property is its failure classification: oversize, malformed JSON, and invalid schema do not enter an endless retry loop.

package main

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

const maxMessageBytes = 256 * 1024

type RenewalReminder struct {
    SchemaVersion int    `json:"schema_version"`
    MessageID     string `json:"message_id"`
    AccountID     string `json:"account_id"`
    Deadline      string `json:"business_deadline"`
    Subscription  string `json:"subscription_ref"`
    Template      string `json:"template_version"`
}

func validate(job RenewalReminder) error {
    if job.SchemaVersion != 1 {
        return fmt.Errorf("unsupported schema version: %d", job.SchemaVersion)
    }
    if job.MessageID == "" || job.AccountID == "" || job.Deadline == "" ||
        job.Subscription == "" || job.Template == "" {
        return errors.New("message_id, account_id, deadline, subscription_ref, and template_version are required")
    }
    return nil
}

func encodeForPublish(job RenewalReminder) ([]byte, error) {
    if err := validate(job); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("schema rejected before publish: %w", err)
    }
    payload, err := json.Marshal(job)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("JSON encoding failed: %w", err)
    }
    if len(payload) > maxMessageBytes {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("permanent size failure: %d bytes exceeds %d", len(payload), maxMessageBytes)
    }
    return payload, nil
}

func consume(payload []byte, inbox map[string]string) error {
    if len(payload) > maxMessageBytes {
        return fmt.Errorf("permanent size failure: %d bytes exceeds %d", len(payload), maxMessageBytes)
    }

    var job RenewalReminder
    if err := json.Unmarshal(payload, &job); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("permanent JSON failure: %w", err)
    }
    if err := validate(job); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("permanent schema failure: %w", err)
    }

    if priorDigest, exists := inbox[job.MessageID]; exists {
        fmt.Printf("duplicate %s; prior digest=%s\n", job.MessageID, priorDigest)
        return nil
    }

    digest := sha256.Sum256(payload)
    inbox[job.MessageID] = hex.EncodeToString(digest[:])
    fmt.Printf("renewal reminder accepted for %s by %s\n", job.AccountID, job.Deadline)
    return nil
}

func main() {
    job := RenewalReminder{
        SchemaVersion: 1,
        MessageID:     "renewal-20260811-001",
        AccountID:     "acct-4821",
        Deadline:      "2026-08-15T17:00:00Z",
        Subscription:  "sub-2048",
        Template:      "renewal-v3",
    }

    payload, err := encodeForPublish(job)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    inbox := map[string]string{}
    if err := consume(payload, inbox); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if err := consume(payload, inbox); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The real Node.js implementation should preserve the same sequence even if its validation library differs: use a byte measurement of the encoded Buffer, not a character count; reject unknown schema versions; and keep the producer's error response distinct from the consumer's quarantine disposition. A JavaScript string length is not a reliable proxy for UTF-8 bytes when the payload contains non-ASCII data.

One subtle healthtech rule belongs after validation but before sending: re-read the subscription state and compare it with the stored deadline and template policy. A renewal can be cancelled, paid, or moved while the message waits. The worker should record that decision as a normal terminal disposition, not send an old reminder because the queue message was technically valid.

How can operators distinguish retryable delivery failures from contract failures?

Use a small state machine rather than one generic failed flag. published means the producer passed local validation. received means the consumer obtained bytes. quarantined means the bytes or schema cannot produce a valid command. ready means the inbox transaction committed and the reminder is eligible for the deadline policy. sent means the external notification outcome was recorded. A separate cancelled or superseded state handles a subscription that changed while work was waiting.

The retry rule follows the state, not the emotional urgency of the reminder. A broker connection interruption, temporary database unavailability, or notification provider timeout may be retriable with a finite attempt budget. Invalid JSON, an unsupported schema version, a missing reference, and a 256 KB violation are deterministic; retrying them creates noise and can delay valid work behind a poisoned message. A dead-letter or quarantine record should retain the message ID, error class, schema version if parseable, byte count, digest, and the producer release identifier.

RabbitMQ's consumer acknowledgement documentation is useful here because acknowledgement timing is an explicit part of delivery semantics. A worker should acknowledge after durable application state is committed, and it should expect redelivery when the process ends before acknowledgement. The acknowledgement is not an audit record and cannot substitute for an inbox constraint.

For a delayed reminder, recovery also requires visibility into time. Measure queue age, time until business deadline, quarantine count by error class, redelivery count, inbox duplicates, and the number of reminders superseded before sending. Alert on a deadline approaching with no ready state, not only on worker crashes. A healthy process can repeatedly reject every message and still look green if the only metric is process uptime.

I once assumed the parse-error rate was the important signal in this class of system. It wasn't. The more useful question was how many valid reminders had less than an hour before their business deadline while waiting behind invalid work. That metric changed the recovery conversation from “the queue is noisy” to “these 18 accounts need an operator decision.”

When is a different queue architecture the right choice?

The compact command pattern is not a universal answer. A queue is a poor source of truth for compliance evidence, and a short retention window is not a replay archive. If the business requires long-lived event replay, independent consumer groups, or historical reconstruction, use an event-log design with explicit retention and deletion controls. If the workflow has many durable steps, timers, joins, or human approvals, a workflow engine may express recovery more clearly than a hand-built retry table.

Stay with a simple queue when the job is one bounded command, the consumer owns an idempotency boundary, and operators can redrive quarantined messages after correcting the producer. Choose a workflow or event-log architecture when recovery requires reconstructing a sequence rather than repeating one command. The catch is operational ownership: each broader model adds retention, replay, permissions, and audit decisions that the team must test and document.

The final decision rule is narrow. Put only the renewal intent and a controlled reference on the queue; make byte size and schema validation executable at both ends; commit idempotent state before acknowledgement; and keep compliance evidence in a durable system designed for audit and erasure. That's enough architecture to make a 256 KB failure boring, which is exactly what an operator needs at a business deadline.

References

  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • GDPR Article 17, Right to erasure: https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/

title: TOTP second factor, optional per user and required by role
description:
This week the security news is full of authentication being bypassed rather than broken. Hacker News on 20 November 2026 carries Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, an OpenJDK Base64 decoder heap overflow reachable without credentials), Ruby2Shell (a one-byte heap overflow in string case conversion reachable on stock Rails without authentication), two critical Nginx RCEs (CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both unauthenticated and HTTP/2 specific), and a VMware vCenter authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123890, CVSS 9.8). On dev.to the trending MFA cluster for the same week is the same problem from the other side: CVE-2026-107145 (a Roundcube TOTP plugin that did not restrict repeated attempts), CVE-2026-107146 (a session that survived failed verification), CVE-2026-107147 (a whitelist bypass through spoofed client headers), and device code phishing that completes the real MFA prompt on the real Microsoft page. The common thread is that a second factor is only as strong as the checks around it.

artivisi/balaka#60, merged 18 November 2026, is one concrete example of putting those checks in place. It adds a TOTP second factor to the balaka finance application: self-service and optional per user, forced by role through app.mfa.required-roles, with attempt limits, replay protection, and hashed single-use recovery codes. The change is 27 files, +2681, -1, with 13 controller tests and a 62-test functional suite that includes a Playwright flow.

What the feature does

TOTP per RFC 6238: HMAC-SHA1, 6 digits, 30 second period, one step of drift for clock skew. The otpauth URI states the algorithm, digits, and period, so authenticator apps produce codes the service accepts. Enrolment is self-service and optional; app.mfa.required-roles forces it per role, and a user is asked to verify before other pages open.

The parts that map onto the bypasses above:

  • Attempt limit with a time window. A durable record of failed verification attempts, so the budget cannot be reset by changing session or connection state. This is the control CVE-2026-107145 was missing.
  • Replay protection by remembering the last accepted step. A code that was already used is rejected even if it is still inside its 30 second window.
  • Single-use recovery codes, stored hashed.
  • Refusal to enrol when the encryption key is missing, so a shared secret is never stored in plaintext.

Why it is one PR and not five

The PR is the fifth and last of the focused PRs requested in balaka issue #42, and it replaces PR #59, which was closed by mistake and could not be reopened because the branch was deleted. The work was resubmitted from the same branch and rewritten to the review notes rather than ported. The original branch forced enrolment on everyone, took the secret from the request, used HMAC-SHA256, and had no attempt limit, no replay protection, and no recovery path. The merged version is the opposite on every point: optional per user, server-generated secret, HMAC-SHA1 per RFC 6238, and the four controls above.

Tests that had to be fixed before they could run

Two test classes were fixed so they actually exercise the code, and the PR documents each failure mode:

  • @WithUserDetails resolved principals before @BeforeEach created the users, with random names, so every annotated test failed with "User not found". Users are now seeded once per class under the names the annotations use, and re-read per test so a previous method's in-memory MFA flag does not leak.
  • MockMvc was built without CspNonceFilter, which the layout requires, so every page render failed with "CSP nonce missing".
  • The shared test profile sets app.mfa.enabled=false, so enrolment threw; these two classes now enable it for themselves.
  • The unauthenticated cases assert the 401 the security chain returns, instead of the older redirect expectation.
  • The "MFA not required" case used the enrolled admin, so it could never test the redirect; it now uses a non-enrolled staff user.

Verification run locally with Maven 3.9 and Temurin 25 in Docker, PostgreSQL through Testcontainers:

  • MfaControllerTest and MfaVerifyControllerTest: 13 tests, 0 failures.
  • MfaLoginFunctionalTest and SecurityRegressionTest together: 62 tests, 0 failures, Playwright flow included.

The flow

Enrolment and login verification. The attempt limit and replay check live in the verify step, not in the session.

Why this matters this week

The honest link is narrow. The news cycle this week is about MFA being bypassed: replayed or unlimited verification attempts, sessions that survive a failed check, and proxies that complete a real MFA prompt on the user's behalf. None of those are fixed by adding TOTP alone. What fixes them is the verifier refusing to accept a reused code, counting attempts in a durable store, and destroying the session on failure. The balaka PR is the implementation of those three checks in one Spring Boot application, behind a feature flag (app.mfa.enabled) and a role list (app.mfa.required-roles), with 75 tests. It is a small answer to a large problem, and it is the kind of answer that can be read line by line.

Sources checked on 20 November 2026: trendshift.io/weekly, github.com/trending, news.ycombinator.com (front page), dev.to/trending.

The rule to carry

When a second factor is added, the verifier has to enforce the assumptions the factor depends on: a durable attempt counter that survives session changes, replay rejection by step, and single-use recovery codes stored hashed. A TOTP implementation that generates codes but does not limit attempts or reject replays gives the appearance of MFA without the property. This PR is 27 files to get those four controls right, and 75 tests to keep them right.

title: Your sales webhook fires twice, and your spreadsheet believes it
description:
I run a small shop that sells digital files. Two platforms, one local checkout, and a spreadsheet
that I update by hand — which is fine until a payment webhook times out, gets retried, and the same
sale lands twice. You notice it on your best day, three weeks later, when the monthly total looks
better than your bank account does.

So the ledger I run now is one SQLite table. Two decisions do most of the work.

1. Let the database refuse duplicates

Every webhook carries an id from the platform. Make (platform, external_id) unique and the second
delivery fails at the constraint:

CREATE TABLE sales (
    id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    platform    TEXT NOT NULL,
    external_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    product     TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount      TEXT NOT NULL,
    currency    TEXT NOT NULL,
    occurred_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE(platform, external_id)
);

Then the insert handler is boring, which is what you want:

def record(conn, platform, external_id, product, amount, currency="USD"):
    try:
        conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO sales (platform, external_id, product, amount, currency, occurred_at)"
            " VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,datetime('now'))",
            (platform, str(external_id), product, str(amount), currency),
        )
        conn.commit()
        return True          # baru
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
        return False         # sudah pernah diterima — bukan error

Two details that matter more than the code:

Still return HTTP 200 on the duplicate. A sender that receives an error retries with backoff, so
"smart" duplicate handling that returns 409 turns one retry into ten. The duplicate is your problem,
not theirs.

Deduplicate on the platform's id, not on your own timestamp. Two genuine sales of the same
product by the same buyer can happen in the same minute; one delivery delivered twice cannot.

2. Never let a float touch an amount

0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. In a revenue report that becomes a discrepancy you cannot
explain to yourself at 11pm. Store money as Decimal and persist it as text:

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def money(value) -> str:
    return str(Decimal(str(value)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))

SQLite has no decimal type, so text is the honest choice. Sum with CAST(amount AS REAL) only for
display, or convert to Decimal in code when the number will be used for anything that matters.

3. Do not add currencies together

A $29 sale and a Rp30.000 sale are not 29,030 of anything. Group by currency:

SELECT platform, product, currency, COUNT(*), SUM(CAST(amount AS REAL)) AS gross
FROM sales
GROUP BY platform, product, currency
ORDER BY gross DESC;

If you must show one number, convert explicitly with a rate you recorded, and label the line with the
rate and the date. Silent conversion is how a report becomes a fiction.

4. Roll up on the sale's timestamp, not on insert time

received_at is when your server heard about it — useful for debugging, wrong for accounting. A sale
that happened at 23:58 on 31 January and arrived at 00:03 on 1 February belongs to January. Keep both
columns; group by occurred_at.

The whole thing

The lite version of the ledger is MIT-licensed, standard library only, ~100 lines:
github.com/shitpicious666-spec/sales-ledger-lite
— includes a selftest.py that proves the duplicate rejection and the monthly isolation against an
in-memory database.

I also ship a paid version with per-platform fee profiles (so the report shows net, not gross), an
HTTP receiver and a daily digest; it is linked from the README. The lite version is enough if all you
need is "do not count twice", and I would rather you read the code than take my word for it.

If you have solved refunds in an append-only ledger differently, I would like to hear it — right now
I record a negative row with its own id, which keeps the history honest but makes "revenue this
month" a sum instead of a constant.

title: Verify Webhook Signatures in Node.js: Fix the Raw-Body Bug
description:
Originally published on Extenify.

To verify webhook signatures in Node.js, you hash the request body with a shared secret and compare the result to a header. It looks like five lines of code, yet the top Stripe error, "No signatures found matching the expected signature for payload", has close to 90,000 views on Stack Overflow, and the cause is nearly always the same: you hashed the wrong bytes. Here is what to get right, and how GitHub, Stripe and Standard Webhooks (used by Polar) differ.

The signature covers bytes, not data

Anyone who knows your webhook URL can POST to it. So the provider signs each delivery with HMAC-SHA256 using a secret only you two share. You recompute the value and compare.

The catch: HMAC works on exact bytes. If your framework parses the JSON and you call JSON.stringify on it, whitespace, escapes and number formatting can change, and the check fails even though the data looks identical. In the original tests, a re-stringified Stripe payload failed the official library's check with exactly the error above.

The three schemes differ in what they sign and how they encode it:

Provider Header Signed content Encoding
GitHub X-Hub-Signature-256 raw body hex
Stripe Stripe-Signature (t=, v1=) timestamp.body hex
Standard Webhooks (Polar) webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, webhook-signature id.timestamp.body base64

If a provider ships an SDK verifier, such as Stripe's constructEvent() or Polar's validateEvent(), use it. Write your own when there is no SDK, when you want one verifier for several providers, or when you need to understand why the SDK rejects a request.

Get the raw body first

In Express, put express.raw() on the webhook route only, and register it before any global express.json(). Stripe's troubleshooting page gives the same advice. In a Next.js App Router handler, read the body as bytes and parse it yourself afterwards:

export async function POST(request) {
  const raw = Buffer.from(await request.arrayBuffer()); // not request.json()
  if (!isValid(raw, request.headers)) {
    return new Response('invalid signature', { status: 401 });
  }
  const event = JSON.parse(raw.toString('utf8'));
  return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
}

Also check what sits in front of Node. A proxy or gateway that re-encodes or trims the body breaks the signature just as a JSON parser does.

Compare in constant time

A plain === returns at the first differing character, which leaks timing. Use crypto.timingSafeEqual, but compare lengths first: it throws ERR_CRYPTO_TIMING_SAFE_EQUAL_LENGTH when the buffers differ in size. The header is attacker-controlled, so without that check a short signature turns a 401 into a 500.

import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';

function githubOk(raw, header, secret) {
  const want = Buffer.from('sha256=' + createHmac('sha256', secret).update(raw).digest('hex'));
  const got = Buffer.from(String(header ?? ''));
  return want.length === got.length && timingSafeEqual(want, got);
}

GitHub publishes a test vector worth pinning in a unit test: secret It's a Secret to Everybody, payload Hello, World!, expected signature 757107ea0eb2509fc211221cce984b8a37570b6d7586c22c46f4379c8b043e17.

Mind the key format

Most "it never matches" bugs after the raw body are key mistakes:

  • Stripe: the key is the whole whsec_... string as text.
  • Standard Webhooks: the key is the base64-decoded part after whsec_.
  • Stripe rotation: while an old secret stays active (up to 24 hours), Stripe sends one v1 signature per secret, so accept a match on any of them. Ignore every scheme that is not v1, which blocks downgrade attacks.
  • Standard Webhooks rotation: webhook-signature can hold several space-separated entries, so try each key against each entry.

Polar added a twist. Secrets generated on or after 8 September 2026, 00:00 UTC follow Standard Webhooks. Older secrets use the full whsec_... string's UTF-8 bytes as the key. Polar SDKs 1.0.0-alpha.19 and later try both. A custom verifier that only decodes base64 keeps working for old secrets, then rejects every delivery the day you create a new one. The fix is to pass both keys and accept a match on either.

Stop replays and slow endpoints

A valid signature proves who sent a message, not that it is new. Two defences work together:

  1. Time window. The timestamp is part of what Stripe and Standard Webhooks sign, so an attacker cannot edit it. Stripe's libraries default to 5 minutes, and Stripe warns that a tolerance of 0 disables the check. Keep your server clock on NTP.
  2. Deduplication. Store the delivery or event ID (webhook-id, Stripe's event ID, GitHub's X-GitHub-Delivery) with a unique index, and answer duplicates with a 2xx so the provider stops retrying. GitHub sends no timestamp, so for GitHub this is the only replay defence.

Then answer fast. Polar times out after 10 seconds, recommends a response within 2, and disables an endpoint after 10 consecutive failed deliveries. Verify, deduplicate, enqueue, return 204, and do the real work in a background job.

Debug a mismatch in this order

  1. Print the first characters of the secret you load and compare them with the dashboard. A secret from stripe listen differs from the dashboard endpoint secret.
  2. Log Buffer.isBuffer(body). If it is an object, a parser ran first.
  3. Check the key encoding for the provider.
  4. Read headers in lowercase (req.headers['webhook-signature']).
  5. If only some deliveries fail, compare the header timestamp with your server time.
  6. Look for a proxy, CDN or middleware that changes the body.

Key takeaways

  • Hash the raw bytes, never re-serialized JSON.
  • Check lengths, then use crypto.timingSafeEqual.
  • Keys differ per provider: text for Stripe and GitHub, base64-decoded for Standard Webhooks.
  • Reject stale timestamps and deduplicate on the delivery ID.
  • Return 2xx quickly and process in the background.
  • Polar secrets created before 8 September 2026 need a different key rule, so try both.

The original guide has the complete tested verifier for all three schemes, plus replay and duplicate handling, in verifying webhook signatures in Node.js with Stripe, GitHub and Polar. If you also track app and extension store data, Extenify's cross-platform store dashboard polls Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Google Play and App Store listings for you.

Which provider's webhook signature has cost you the most debugging time, and was it the raw body, the key format or something else?
