title: Merchant Sending Domain Endpoint in 2026: DNS Plus Mail Evidence Boundaries
description:
A merchant's request to use a sending domain is intent. The published DNS records and the mail provider's verification result are the evidence. An e-commerce onboarding endpoint has to connect those things before it marks the merchant ready to send order confirmations or account codes. Otherwise, a successful configuration write can quietly become permission to send from an unverified domain.

TL;DR: expose one internal endpoint that adds the zone, upserts the three configured TXT records, requests sending-domain verification, and returns the resulting verification status. Keep the merchant pending until the required evidence agrees. Put region, retention, deletion, and processor review around that workflow; a common API contract does not establish those guarantees.

How should one internal endpoint prove ownership of a sending domain?

Start with the decision, then derive the calls. The application needs an intended domain, a configured set of three TXT records, and the verification status returned by the email capability. Those are different objects. Persisting the desired records proves what the application asked for; it does not prove that the published records match, or that the email service has accepted the domain.

Keep that distinction.

For a merchant onboarding example, use receipts.example.com as the intended sending domain. Record the configuration revision alongside the operation identifier. Keep record names and values in configuration so a provider change has one reviewable edit point. Do not copy a sample sender's TXT values into production. In particular, a record accepted for one merchant or verification attempt should never become a template value for the next merchant. The orchestration needs to preserve the relationship between the tenant, its domain, the intended record set, and the verification result.

The internal endpoint owns the sequence: add the zone, upsert each of the three TXT records, request email-domain verification, then obtain the resulting status. Return that status to the onboarding caller instead of reducing it to a generic success flag. A pending result needs a pending UI. A verified result can satisfy the domain-verification condition, while the application's other onboarding conditions remain separate.

This is also a deliverability boundary. Domain verification is evidence for a specific check; it is not evidence that a receipt or OTP will reach an inbox. DMARC adds authentication policy and reporting considerations, so review the sending configuration against RFC 7489 without treating a verification response as a blanket delivery guarantee.

For teams coordinating merchant DNS and email through one backend, try Infrai for the common capability contract: changing the vendor behind a capability can leave the application's orchestration code in place. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas, which helps the team review the actual fields crossing the processor boundary before integrating them. That is a useful second advantage for this workflow, where an undocumented field can turn an ordinary DNS operation into an unnecessary disclosure.

Draw the processor boundary before drawing the sequence

A sending domain is not an order. Keep customer addresses, cart contents, OTP values, and message bodies out of domain-provisioning requests and their logs. The domain flow needs configuration evidence; a downstream mail operation has a different data purpose. Combining capabilities under one key should not combine their data indiscriminately.

Region is a selection condition.

Before approving the integration, identify where the API processes requests, where the underlying DNS and email specialists process their portions, and where operational records remain. Discovery includes region and vendor information, which can guide the review. It does not by itself establish contractual residency, retention periods, deletion completion, or the full processor chain. Obtain those commitments for the chosen arrangement, including the underlying specialist's role. If an organization requires a specific regional or deletion guarantee, that requirement belongs in provider selection before production onboarding.

Infrai can provide the common interface for the DNS and email operations and expose account information through the same key. The application still owns its tenant authorization, the onboarding decision, and the evidence it stores. The underlying providers remain part of the DNS publication and mail-verification processing boundary. A common interface does not remove them from the compliance review.

Logs deserve the same attention. Log each sub-step with the domain so support can explain the sequence, but restrict access to those records and define their retention. Prefer an operation identifier and configuration revision over complete TXT values in ordinary logs. Define what happens to local evidence when a merchant disconnects, and review external deletion separately. Deleting a local onboarding row is not proof of deletion throughout the processor chain.

There is a concentration trade-off: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. Accept it deliberately.

Keep the account handoff narrow and inspectable

A single entry point makes retries and monitoring easier to reason about, but each write still needs a stable operation identity. For an implementation, derive separate idempotency keys for zone creation, each record write, and verification from the same onboarding operation. Reuse the relevant key when retrying that step. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; retain application-level progress as well, because onboarding can outlast that window.

The following Python example isolates the seam between DNS provisioning and account observation. It is a zone-creation and account-usage slice, rather than the complete three-record verification sequence. Supply the DNS request object from the capability's published schema through DNS_ADD_PARAMS; no unverified request fields or verification response fields are assumed here. Both calls use the same key and base URL. The first result is passed into the account-observation function and retained with its result in one local evidence object.

Account usage is account-level context. This example does not attribute that usage to the domain or treat it as verification evidence.

import json
import os
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime

BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
OPERATION_ID = os.environ["ONBOARDING_OPERATION_ID"]

def request(method, path, payload=None, idempotency_key=None):
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}
    body = None
    if payload is not None:
        headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
        body = json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    if idempotency_key is not None:
        headers["Idempotency-Key"] = idempotency_key

    for attempt in range(5):
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            BASE_URL + path, data=body, headers=headers, method=method
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            delay = float(2 ** attempt)
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after:
                try:
                    retry_delay = float(retry_after)
                except ValueError:
                    retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                    retry_delay = (
                        retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)
                    ).total_seconds()
                delay = max(delay, retry_delay)
            time.sleep(delay)

def attach_account_observation(domain_result):
    account_result = request("GET", "/account/usage")
    return {
        "operation_id": OPERATION_ID,
        "domain_result": domain_result,
        "account_observation": account_result,
    }

def main():
    params = json.loads(os.environ["DNS_ADD_PARAMS"])
    if not isinstance(params, dict):
        raise ValueError("DNS_ADD_PARAMS must contain a JSON object")
    domain_result = request(
        "POST", "/dns/domain/add", params, OPERATION_ID + ":zone"
    )
    evidence = attach_account_observation(domain_result)
    print(json.dumps(evidence, indent=2))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The example allows 5 attempts and sets a 30-second request timeout. That's a bounded retry policy, not a delivery deadline. Run this only where the output can be handled as operational evidence. Printing full provider responses is useful for a controlled integration check; production logging should apply the narrower policy above. Keep ONBOARDING_OPERATION_ID stable across retries of the same operation and allocate a new value for a new operation.

The complete endpoint still has to execute the configured record writes and email verification, using their discovered request and response contracts. Keep that work in the same orchestration record. Account observation should be independently retryable so a failure to retrieve account context cannot erase an already completed DNS step.

Do not derive a completion callback from an account read. Getting told when verification finishes requires an explicitly documented completion mechanism, or an application-owned reconciliation policy. Keep that distinction in the design review: consolidating credentials reduces integration work, while the verification status remains the evidence for the onboarding decision.

Compare the alternatives at the trust boundary

Choose the system that makes the required evidence and processor commitments easiest to inspect. The following are real alternatives or components of an alternative stack, rather than interchangeable end-to-end products.

Option Fit for this workflow Boundary to evaluate
Infrai A common contract across DNS, email, and account capabilities, with one API key Review the intermediary and the selected underlying providers; keep verification distinct from account context
Cloudflare for SaaS Evaluate when custom-hostname onboarding is the central problem Custom hostnames and sending-domain verification answer different questions; retain the mail integration and its evidence
Amazon Route 53 Evaluate when the team wants to own the DNS integration directly The application coordinates DNS changes with a separate email-verification step
Amazon SES Evaluate when the team wants a direct specialist relationship for sending identities DNS publication and the internal onboarding decision remain part of the application's integration

For the Cloudflare for SaaS plus in-house poller alternative, count the boundaries explicitly. With no existing accounts, Cloudflare and a separate mail provider mean two external signups and at least two credential sets. The poller is code the team owns: schedule checks, preserve tenant authorization, correlate a check with the intended configuration, and prevent a stale response from advancing a newer onboarding attempt. Hosting that poller may add another account or credential set depending on the deployment. Do not count it as a free integration.

Direct Route 53 and SES integrations can be the better choice for a team already organized around those services, particularly when a direct specialist relationship is a requirement. Cloudflare for SaaS deserves consideration for a custom-hostname requirement. Infrai fits the team that wants the shared capability contract and accepts the associated processor review. None of those choices makes intended DNS state equivalent to published evidence.

Roll out against drift, then expand

Start with one merchant cohort and a fixed configuration revision. Exercise three cases: the published records agree with intent, one configured record differs, and verification remains pending. These are rollout checks, not claims about measured provider behavior. In each case, the caller should receive the actual verification status and the application should apply its onboarding rule consistently.

Also replay the same operation identifier after a completed zone step. Confirm that the application resumes from its recorded progress and preserves the domain evidence even if account observation must be repeated. Then change the configured record set and confirm that evidence for the older revision cannot complete the newer attempt. That is the drift trap worth catching before a merchant relies on the domain for order mail.

Expand only after the support team can explain a domain's state from the sub-step history and the data owners have approved retention, deletion, region, and processor responsibilities. The useful result is an explainable onboarding decision.

Sources

References for the capability contract, mail policy, and alternative integration boundaries:

  • RFC 7489, DMARC
  • Cloudflare for SaaS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide
  • Amazon SES verified identities

If this boundary fits your onboarding system, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: AI Image Generation Pipeline: 5 Queue Tests for 429 Object Storage Upload Retry Backoff
description:
Short answer: Put generated report images in private object storage, but make generation and upload separate queue states; persist the generated bytes before upload, retry a 429 with bounded backoff, and derive the object key from the job ID so every retry targets the same object.

For a logistics system serving generated reports to authenticated customers, retention is part of correctness. The report preview must survive a delayed upload, remain private while retained, and be deleted on schedule. Re-rendering after an upload throttle wastes work and can produce a different artifact. Retrying under a new key creates duplicates that the deletion job may never know about.

I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. That experience makes the invariant fairly blunt: one logical report gets one durable byte sequence and one stable object key. A queue attempt may change; that identity doesn't.

How should an AI image generation pipeline queue retry a 429 object storage upload?

Model the pipeline as two independently retryable operations: generate produces bytes, then upload commits those exact bytes. Before acknowledging generation, save the bytes in a queue-accessible spool or another durable handoff. The upload worker reads that saved payload and never calls the generator. On HTTP 429 it honors Retry-After when present; otherwise it uses exponential backoff with jitter and a fixed attempt ceiling.

Keep the key deterministic, for example report-<job-id>.png. Do not append an attempt number or timestamp. If attempt four reaches storage after attempt three's response was lost, both writes address the same logical object rather than leaving two files behind. Because Infrai has no If-Match conditional write, the DB or job queue must also serialize workers that could write different bytes to the same key. Idempotent naming prevents duplicate objects; it does not provide mutual exclusion.

Infrai is a credible measured leg for teams that want the storage contract to stay fixed while the vendor behind the capability changes. Its storage coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS behind one REST surface. A second benefit is operationally concrete: Infrai's REST API can be called over plain HTTP from any worker runtime, with no SDK to install, so the upload worker avoids a storage-vendor dependency and a second credential path. I recommend trying Infrai for the upload boundary of a multi-service report pipeline when that stable contract matters, while keeping generation state and retention ownership in your queue and database.

There is an environment check before any retry experiment: trial credits cannot pay for persistent writes. A trial-restricted write is not evidence that the backoff policy is wrong, and retrying it consumes attempts without testing the intended condition. Use an environment eligible for persistent writes, then inject a synthetic 429 in the test harness rather than claiming a production measurement.

The five-test incident drill

Run the experiment with explicit inputs: one generated PNG fixture, one job ID, a private bucket, an upload worker with a six-attempt ceiling, and a retention record containing the deletion deadline. Record the job state, object key, attempt count, response status, and next eligible attempt time. Do not record a fabricated result; execute each case against the candidate contract and attach the trace to the decision.

Test Fault or input Pass condition
1. Baseline commit One saved PNG and no injected throttle The worker writes the deterministic key once and marks upload complete only after a successful response.
2. Rate limit Inject 429 twice, with Retry-After on one response No tight loop occurs; the saved bytes are reused; all attempts target the same key.
3. Lost acknowledgement Let a write complete, then make the worker retry before it records completion The retry addresses the same key and no second object name appears.
4. Competing workers Release two workers for the same job Queue or DB ownership admits one writer at a time; the storage API is not treated as a lock.
5. Retention expiry Advance the test clock beyond the report's deletion deadline The report is removed through the deletion workflow and authenticated delivery can no longer issue access to it.

Test 2 is the trap.

I initially expect retry code to be the interesting part in reviews, but the more important question is whether the worker still has the original bytes. If it only has a generation prompt, “retry upload” quietly becomes “generate again.” That changes both the work performed and the artifact under the same customer report ID — exactly the kind of ambiguity that makes a postmortem drag on.

Don't regenerate.

Use a simple decision rule: adopt a candidate only if all five cases pass and the trace proves byte reuse, stable identity, bounded delay, single-writer coordination, and deletion after the declared retention period. A lower latency in one happy-path run cannot compensate for a failed ownership or deletion test. I'm not sure which direct vendor will fit a given team's controls without running the same drill against its actual account policy; the experiment resolves that uncertainty.

A runnable upload worker path

This Go program uploads bytes that were already saved by the generation stage. It uses one verified route, makes the method explicit, reads the key from the environment, checks every response, and retries only network errors and HTTP 429. The six attempts and 30-second cap are local policy inputs, not service guarantees.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    maxAttempts = 6
    maxBackoff  = 30 * time.Second
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("REPORT_BUCKET")
    jobID := os.Getenv("REPORT_JOB_ID")
    if apiKey == "" || bucket == "" || jobID == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, REPORT_BUCKET, and REPORT_JOB_ID are required")
    }
    if strings.ContainsAny(jobID, "/\\") {
        panic("REPORT_JOB_ID must not contain path separators")
    }

    png, err := os.ReadFile("generated-report.png")
    if err != nil {
        panic(fmt.Errorf("read saved generation output: %w", err))
    }
    objectKey := "report-" + jobID + ".png"

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 3*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 45 * time.Second}
    rng := rand.New(rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano()))

    if err := upload(ctx, client, rng, apiKey, bucket, objectKey, png); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("uploaded %s (%d bytes)\n", objectKey, len(png))
}

func upload(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, rng *rand.Rand, apiKey, bucket, key string, body []byte) error {
    const endpointTemplate = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    endpoint := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket),
        "{key}", url.PathEscape(key),
    ).Replace(endpointTemplate)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("build upload request: %w", err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if ctx.Err() != nil {
                return ctx.Err()
            }
            if attempt == maxAttempts-1 {
                return fmt.Errorf("upload transport error after %d attempts: %w", maxAttempts, err)
            }
            if err := wait(ctx, backoff(attempt, rng)); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            continue
        }

        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 64<<10))
        closeErr := resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil || closeErr != nil {
            return errors.Join(readErr, closeErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return fmt.Errorf("upload returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(responseBody)))
        }
        if attempt == maxAttempts-1 {
            return fmt.Errorf("upload remained rate limited after %d attempts", maxAttempts)
        }

        delay := retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), time.Now())
        if delay <= 0 {
            delay = backoff(attempt, rng)
        }
        if delay > maxBackoff {
            delay = maxBackoff
        }
        if err := wait(ctx, delay); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return errors.New("upload attempts exhausted")
}

func backoff(attempt int, rng *rand.Rand) time.Duration {
    base := time.Second << attempt
    if base > maxBackoff {
        base = maxBackoff
    }
    return base/2 + time.Duration(rng.Int63n(int64(base/2)+1))
}

func retryAfter(value string, now time.Time) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil && deadline.After(now) {
        return deadline.Sub(now)
    }
    return 0
}

func wait(ctx context.Context, delay time.Duration) error {
    timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
    defer timer.Stop()
    select {
    case <-timer.C:
        return nil
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

The bucket must remain private or signed-only. Authenticated delivery should issue a short-lived presigned URL after the application verifies the customer and retention record; the API Authorization header must never be forwarded to that returned URL. Keep authorization in the application even when object access is delegated for a short window.

Where this design stops fitting

The catch is retention granularity and storage governance. The lifecycle minimum is one day, so this layer is not suitable when generated artifacts must expire automatically within hours. Run an explicit deletion job for shorter application retention, or choose a specialist whose native policy matches the requirement. It also has no object versioning or object lock, so use a direct specialist such as AWS S3 when recoverable overwrite history or WORM controls are mandatory. Static website hosting and permanent public image links are out too: there is no public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null.

The abstraction also omits automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration, and its vendor coverage does not include Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2. Stick with GCS or B2 directly when either is a fixed platform requirement. Browser-direct upload is another poor fit when the team must self-manage CORS, because an independent CORS route is not available. Metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and strict same-key exclusion still belongs in the queue or DB.

Candidate What this experiment measures Decision signal
Unified REST layer over R2, S3, OSS, or COS One REST contract while the backing vendor can change Choose when contract stability and plain HTTP matter, and all five tests pass within the stated limits.
AWS S3 direct The native integration as a specialist leg Prefer when required storage governance exceeds the abstraction's supported controls.
Cloudflare R2 direct A second native contract under the same injected faults Prefer when the team has already standardized on its direct operational boundary.
Alibaba Cloud OSS direct A native option for teams committed to that provider Prefer when provider-specific integration is intentional rather than something the team plans to swap.
Tencent Cloud COS direct Another native option covered by the same pass/fail trace Prefer when direct provider ownership is the requirement.

This comparison is deliberately not a winner-by-feature-count exercise. Deletion correctness, concurrency ownership, and recovery from 429 are gates. Everything else is secondary.

References

  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • FedRAMP: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai storage retry guide and run the five cases against your own queue trace.

title: Stop regex-ing the LLM's prose
description:
Ask an LLM a question and it hands you back prose. Lovely to read, miserable to program against. You wanted the one number buried in the middle of it, and now you're writing a regular expression to fish a word out of three well-written paragraphs that phrase themselves slightly differently every single time you run them.

There's a much better way, and it's the difference between forever interpreting an LLM and actually building on one.

The problem with a paragraph

You ask an LLM to analyse a log file and tell you the severity of what it found and a suggested fix. It comes back with three well-written paragraphs. Somewhere in there is the word "critical", and somewhere is the fix.

Your program now has to extract those two facts from prose, and prose has no contract. The next run, the model phrases it differently. It leads with a caveat. It says "severe" where last time it said "critical". It puts the fix first. Anything that worked by finding "critical" in the text is now quietly wrong, and you didn't change a line. Parsing free text for structured facts is a game you lose slowly.

What you actually wanted was never a paragraph. It was a value: a thing with a severity field and a fix field, that you can branch on and store and pass around like any other.

Ask for the struct, not the prose

go-tool-base's chat package draws the line with two methods. Chat gives you text. Ask gives you a struct.

You define the Go type you want back:

type Analysis struct {
    Severity string `json:"severity"`
    Fix      string `json:"fix"`
}

var result Analysis
err := client.Ask(ctx, "Analyse this log file: "+logText, &result)

The framework generates a JSON Schema from that struct, sends it to the model as the required response format, and unmarshals the reply straight into result. You never lay a finger on the prose. You get result.Severity and result.Fix, typed, ready to use. If you want the model's answer to drive a switch statement, this is the method that lets it.

The struct is the schema is the contract

The detail that makes this hold up over time: you don't write the schema. The struct is the schema.

The framework derives the JSON Schema from your type. In go-tool-base that's GenerateSchema[T](); in rust-tool-base the schema comes from your Rust type through schemars. (Yes, there's a Rust sibling now. I'll introduce it properly in a few weeks, but it keeps gatecrashing these posts because the two frameworks deliberately share ideas.) Either way there's one definition, your type, and the schema is just a projection of it.

That matters, because otherwise two things have to agree. There's the schema you tell the model to obey, and there's the type you unmarshal the answer into. Hand-write the schema and those two can drift: add a field to the struct, forget to add it to the schema, and the model is never told to produce it, so it silently never appears. Deriving the schema from the type collapses the two into one. They can't disagree, because there's only one of them.

Both frameworks, with one extra step in Rust

go-tool-base does this with Ask and a ResponseSchema set on the client config. rust-tool-base does it with chat_structured::<T>, where T is any type that's both deserialisable and JsonSchema.

rust-tool-base adds one step worth calling out. Before it deserialises the model's reply into your T, it validates the raw response against the schema with a JSON Schema validator. That splits the failure into two distinct, named cases: the response didn't match the schema, or it matched the schema but still wouldn't deserialise. A model that returns subtly wrong JSON fails loudly and specifically, with an error that tells you which of those happened, instead of quietly handing you a zero-valued struct that you end up debugging an hour later.

When you'd reach for it

The line is simple, and it's about who reads the answer.

If a human reads the answer, prose is right. Chat, free text, let the model write well. A summary, an explanation, an interactive reply: leave all of those as prose.

If a program consumes the answer, you want a value. Classification, extraction, a code review scored out of a hundred with a list of issues, a yes-or-no with reasons: anything where the next thing that happens is your code branching on the result. There, Ask and chat_structured turn the LLM from something you have to interpret into something that returns a value, and a typed value is a thing you can actually build on.

To sum up

An LLM returns prose by default, and prose has no contract, so a program that picks structured facts out of it breaks the moment the model rephrases.

Structured output asks for the value instead. You define a struct, the framework derives a JSON Schema from it, the model is constrained to that shape, and you get a typed result. go-tool-base's Ask and rust-tool-base's chat_structured both work this way, with the schema derived from your type so the schema and the type can't drift; rust-tool-base additionally validates the response against the schema before deserialising. Use it whenever the answer feeds code rather than a human. It's one of the four methods that make up go-tool-base's small chat interface, and it's the one that makes an LLM safe to program against.
