title: 5 Marketplace Backup Controls: Private Object Storage Lifecycle Retention After 30 Days
description:
Short answer: keep marketplace receipt backups in a private object store, record the intended expiry beside each object, and let one accountable deletion control remove them after 30 days. Use bucket access policy to prevent public reads; use observability to prove the retention clock actually ran.

A receipt archive is not ordinary application media. A seller may need the original file for an audit, support may need a short restore window, and the same document can contain names, addresses, and order details. The least complex useful design is a private bucket with a 30-day retention rule, an immutable-looking receipt key, and a daily check that compares the inventory with the deletion outcome. No public URLs. No vague ownership of the expiry clock.

Control Pick this when What to observe
Object-store lifecycle rule The store can enforce expiry from object age and the policy is the source of truth policy revision, objects reaching 30 days, deletion counts
Application deletion worker Expiry depends on receipt state or a legal hold stored by the app eligible records, delete attempts, retry queue, object-not-found results
Hybrid catalog plus lifecycle rule You need audit evidence without making the app responsible for every delete catalog-to-object matches and daily aged-object totals

The lifecycle rule is usually the right default for a fixed 30-day window. An application worker earns its complexity only when its decision needs business data. The catch is that a fixed rule cannot express a case-specific hold unless the storage policy and object layout provide a separate path for those records.

The expiry clock needs one owner.

1. What should a private backup lifecycle delete after 30 days?

Delete the receipt object, its temporary derivatives, and any catalog entry whose only purpose is to locate that object. Keep a separate, minimal audit event if the business needs evidence that deletion occurred; do not keep another copy of the original receipt by accident. This distinction matters: deleting receipts/ while leaving exports/ or an event attachment untouched turns a 30-day promise into a naming convention.

Use a key that makes the retention scope obvious to humans and automation. For example, receipts/2026/09/merchant_42/order_9182/original.pdf exposes the class of data without placing a customer name in the path. A bucket policy should deny anonymous reads and grant the receipt-processing identity only the actions it needs for the relevant prefix. The OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet recommends storing uploads outside the webroot or on a separate host and controlling access rather than exposing uploaded files directly.

The policy choice is simple, but the clock is not. Define whether the 30 days start at upload completion, receipt issuance, or successful processing. Pick one timestamp, write it to the catalog, and use the same interpretation in tests and dashboards. If a regulator or contract sets a different retention period, the policy owner needs to resolve that requirement before deployment; an engineer cannot infer it from the object creation date.

2. How should a Node.js application choose the deletion clock owner?

A storage lifecycle rule is a good fit when every receipt archive has the same 30-day lifetime. It keeps deletion close to the bytes, so a missed application deployment does not automatically create an immortal archive. Treat the rule as infrastructure configuration: review it, version it, and alert when the deployed policy differs from the approved 30-day rule.

Choose an application worker when deletion depends on a hold, a dispute, or a receipt that has not yet completed processing. The worker must be idempotent. A second delete request should converge on the same desired state, because retries and duplicate scheduler runs are normal operating conditions.

Use a hybrid approach when auditors need a readable trail. The object store owns age-based deletion, while a small catalog records objectKey, receivedAt, expiresAt, and a deletion observation. The catalog is evidence, not a second archive.

Here is a TypeScript shape for the catalog check. It deliberately uses an interface rather than pretending every object store has the same SDK or policy syntax.

interface ReceiptArchive {
  objectKey: string;
  receivedAt: Date;
  expiresAt: Date;
  deletionObservedAt?: Date;
}

interface ObjectStore {
  exists(key: string): Promise<boolean>;
}

export async function observeExpiry(
  archive: ReceiptArchive,
  store: ObjectStore,
  now: Date,
): Promise<ReceiptArchive> {
  if (now < archive.expiresAt) return archive;

  const stillExists = await store.exists(archive.objectKey);
  if (stillExists) return archive;

  return { ...archive, deletionObservedAt: now };
}

This check does not delete anything. It answers a different operational question: did the retention control produce the expected state? That separation keeps a monitoring job from quietly becoming a second, competing deletion system.

3. Make the private bucket policy narrow enough to review

A private bucket is not a bucket with an obscure name. Public access must be disabled, and the processing identity should receive a narrow allow-list: write the receipt at intake, read it only for authorized processing or restore, and remove it only through the selected retention control. Avoid broad wildcard permissions that make every service in the account a receipt reader.

For an app-owned worker, the policy intent can be reviewed as typed configuration before it is translated into a platform-specific policy document:

type Capability = "write" | "read" | "delete";

const receiptPolicy = {
  bucket: "marketplace-receipt-archive",
  publicAccess: false,
  grants: [
    { identity: "receipt-ingest", prefix: "receipts/", capabilities: ["write"] },
    { identity: "receipt-restore", prefix: "receipts/", capabilities: ["read"] },
    { identity: "retention-controller", prefix: "receipts/", capabilities: ["delete"] },
  ] satisfies Array<{ identity: string; prefix: string; capabilities: Capability[] }>,
};

void receiptPolicy;

Keep backup restoration off the normal download path. An authorized service can create a short-lived, logged retrieval path after it has checked the request. The exact mechanism depends on the chosen object store, so review that platform's access-control documentation instead of copying a policy from a different provider.

4. Test the expiry boundary and alert on the gap

The dangerous test is the one that only uploads and downloads a file. Test the boundary at 29 days, at the selected 30-day expiry moment, and after the storage platform's documented lifecycle evaluation window. The retention control may be scheduled rather than instantaneous; an alert should account for that documented window instead of flagging every object at the first second past expiresAt.

Track four numbers daily: receipt objects older than their configured expiry, catalog rows without an object, objects without a catalog row, and deletion observations. A sudden rise in any one of them gives the operator a concrete investigation path. A dashboard that only charts total bytes does not prove a deletion policy is working.

Make the daily check usable during an ordinary on-call shift. Start with the count of objects that are past expiresAt, then sample their catalog records rather than opening receipt files. If the catalog says an object is expired but the object remains, first check the deployed lifecycle policy revision and the provider's documented evaluation window. If the object is gone but the catalog is still live, mark the deletion observation and investigate why reconciliation lagged. If objects lack catalog rows, identify the writer identity and the prefix involved; this often points to a bypass of the normal intake path, which is a more useful finding than a generic retention alert. Record the query time, policy revision, count, and resulting ticket or change record. The resulting dashboard tells an operator where the gap is: policy, catalog, object inventory, or authorization. It also gives a reviewer evidence that the 30-day rule is operating as designed without exposing the receipts themselves.

For the worker option, emit an event with the object key's non-sensitive identifier, the scheduled expiry, the attempt time, and the result class. Do not log receipt contents or signed retrieval URLs. OWASP's guidance on file uploads is a useful reminder that file handling includes storage and access controls, not only input validation.

One small test catches a common mistake: force a duplicate run and assert that the catalog ends with one deletion observation. Another tests a missing object. Both outcomes are expected states in a distributed system, not excuses to skip reconciliation.

5. Limits: when a 30-day private archive is the wrong choice

Thirty days is unsuitable when accounting, tax, dispute, or contractual rules require a longer hold. In that case, keep the bucket private but use the approved retention schedule and document the policy owner. A lifecycle rule should not override a legal obligation just because it is easy to configure.

A single shared bucket can also be the wrong boundary for a marketplace with strong tenant isolation requirements. Separate prefixes and carefully scoped identities may be sufficient for some teams; separate buckets or accounts can make isolation and review clearer for others, with more operational overhead.

Finally, do not use a backup archive as a general document store. A receipt processing system needs a clear source of truth, a restoration procedure, and a deletion record. The archive is there for a bounded audit purpose.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob

title: Budgeting 3 Recovery Boundaries for Shared Chat Viewers (Subscribe-Only Token Scope)
description:
A Node.js chat room can reconnect successfully and still leave viewers on a shared channel looking at an incomplete conversation. A read-only token must preserve their subscription rights during recovery. The operational constraint is recovering missing messages without granting permission to write, then proving recovery worked without retaining a second copy of the conversation in telemetry.

Short answer: issue subscribe-only viewer tokens scoped to one shared channel. Keep publication on the trusted backend. Treat reconnect and backfill as an application contract with three observable boundaries: token authorization, durable message handoff, and recovery completion. Publish rights belong in the token; hiding a send button cannot enforce them.

The useful optimization is bounded evidence. A delivery system needs enough information to distinguish an authorization failure from unfinished backfill, but it does not need every viewer identifier attached to every metric. Start there before choosing a transport.

A stable capability interface also fixes the integration boundary: vendor switching should leave the application's calls unchanged. Unified credentials reduce administration across backend services; they don't prove that a disconnected viewer recovered the conversation. Keep that distinction explicit when evaluating a unified API.

How should a read-only token scope viewers on a shared channel?

Consider a proposed developer-tools room carrying release discussion alongside live build scores. Contributors publish updates; viewers watch the shared feed. A viewer reconnecting after an interruption needs the missing conversation and current score, with the original permission boundary intact. These are design requirements, not claims that a subscription token supplies storage or replay.

Separate the room's durable identity from its event channel. An application might associate a release discussion with one event-specific channel and retain its conversation independently. Rotating that channel for the next event limits the usefulness of an old token: it grants access to the old channel rather than the new event. It does not retroactively erase information a viewer already received.

Scope matters first.

In an Express application, the backend should authorize the viewer before issuing a token and grant subscription rights only for the intended shared channel. Publishers need their own trusted authorization path. On reconnect, recheck the viewer's entitlement before restoring access; possessing a recovery cursor should never grant permission to read another room. An application-level message identifier and cursor are proposed contract fields here, not vendor API parameter names.

A score can often be represented by its latest state, while a conversation contains distinct messages that a viewer may need to read in order. A recovery policy must say which records it preserves. Otherwise, a dashboard can report a healthy connection while the application silently substitutes a current snapshot for missing discussion.

Count evidence at 3 boundaries

At the authorization boundary, record the outcome and intended scope class: viewer or publisher.

Never retain the token itself.

A successful token request alone does not demonstrate that attempted publication is denied. That needs a separate acceptance check.

At the durable handoff boundary, distinguish a record accepted for later delivery from a socket publish accepted now. These receipts represent different events. Preserve a stable message identity across the handoff so a retry can be recognized, and define when a worker may acknowledge queued work. For standard queues, assume at-least-once delivery and require consumer idempotency. A duplicate delivery must not create a duplicate chat message.

Recovery completion is the third boundary. Define completion against the application's expected position in the conversation, rather than merely against a connected socket. Useful aggregate outcomes include caught up, authorization denied, and recovery window exceeded. Keep the categories small and explicit.

Here is an illustrative cardinality budget, not a benchmark: 4 outcome classes multiplied by 3 deployment environments gives 12 possible label combinations before other dimensions. Adding 10,000 room identifiers expands that upper bound to 120,000. Adding viewer identifiers expands it again. The arithmetic explains why room and viewer identity belong in a deliberately limited diagnostic record rather than in every time series.

Count before collecting.

Retention deserves the same treatment. Assume, solely for planning, 100,000 diagnostic events per day at 300 bytes each. Seven days retains 210,000,000 raw bytes; 30 days retains 900,000,000. Neither figure includes indexes, replication, compression, or storage overhead. Replace those assumptions with measured event sizes before procurement. The multiplication already exposes the consequence of retaining every successful reconnect.

The trade-off is explicit: choose complete aggregate counts over exhaustive successful-session traces because the operating question is how often recovery fails, while a full trace archive multiplies retained records by viewer activity. Sampling ordinary successes reduces retained evidence, but it also reduces detail available for reconstructing a particular viewer's session. Preserve aggregate counts independently of sampled diagnostic records. Record permission denials and recovery-window failures through a bounded diagnostic policy, and avoid copying message bodies into those records. The resulting telemetry can explain recovery without becoming an unplanned archive of the room. Make this choice explicit in the support policy: an operator may be able to count successful recovery without reconstructing every successful session.

Put the durable handoff inside the recovery contract

A queue and a socket solve different parts of this workflow. Persist the notification for later processing, then let a worker attempt delivery under a stable message identity. A viewer that was offline still needs an authorized retrieval path when it returns.

Acceptance is not receipt.

A queued publish by itself does not establish that the viewer received or read a message.

That distinction determines what output should cross the boundary. The application needs a durable acceptance reference associated with its message identity before treating notification work as safely handed off. The worker uses that identity for deduplication, and recovery uses the authoritative conversation position to identify what remains missing. These are application acceptance criteria; they should not be inferred from an HTTP success response or from two services sharing credentials.

For deferred recovery work, a cron trigger can schedule a queue worker. Keep cron execution within 900 seconds and move longer processing into the worker. Standard queue consumers must remain idempotent, delays must stay within 604,800 seconds, and queue retention must stay within 30 days. A conversation retention policy may require a separate durable store beyond that queue window.

The contract also needs an explicit gap response. If the viewer's cursor precedes retained history, return an authorized snapshot or require a fresh view under a documented application policy. Silently skipping the gap produces attractive success metrics and an incomplete conversation. That is the pitfall the third telemetry boundary should expose.

Compare authorization and recovery obligations

Evaluate products against the same experiment: a viewer subscribes, attempts an unauthorized publish, disconnects while messages arrive, and returns with its last acknowledged position. These products occupy different parts of that experiment. Verify the exact plan and protocol behavior before implementation.

Option Relevant mechanism Application obligation
Ably Token capabilities distinguish subscription and publication permissions. Match channel scope and recovery behavior to retention and entitlement policies.
Pusher Channels Channel authorization controls private subscriptions. Distinguish subscription authorization from client-event permissions; design durable recovery separately.
Socket.IO Connection state recovery addresses temporary disconnections within documented conditions. Implement viewer authorization, check adapter support, and retain a recovery path when recovery does not succeed.
Amazon SQS alongside a realtime service A queue supplies a separate durable work handoff. Connect consumption to socket delivery, handle duplicate work, and implement viewer-facing backfill.

Ably merits evaluation when explicit token capabilities are central to the security review. Pusher Channels merits evaluation when its channel model fits and the team accepts a separate history design. Socket.IO merits evaluation when the team wants control over server behavior and accepts recovery and adapter decisions. SQS addresses queued work, so pairing it with a realtime product still leaves conversation recovery to the application. None of these names alone proves complete delivery.

Infrai provides a single API key, a single bill, and a unified REST API: no SDK required. Switch vendors without changing code at the capability boundary. This is useful when the room belongs to an application with several backend services, because one credential covers 295 routes across 20 modules rather than separate provider integrations. The API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. For this workflow, its consistent per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata supplies a second advantage: accounting for recovery operations without logging conversation bodies. The application must still establish durable acceptance and authorized backfill. A stable call contract does not establish equivalent history retention or recovery semantics across providers; those remain acceptance criteria for any switch.

Before implementing viewer issuance, inspect the public capability manifest with curl. Set the environment variables to the provider's documented versioned API base and your API key. This read-only preflight retrieves the capability paths, allowing an implementer to identify token issuance before inspecting its request schema. It does not mint a viewer token or demonstrate backfill.

curl --request GET \
  --url "${INFRAI_BASE_URL:?Set the documented versioned API base}/discovery" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${INFRAI_API_KEY:?Set the API key}" \
  --fail-with-body \
  --retry 5 \
  --retry-max-time 120 \
  --output capability-manifest.json

The discovery request requires no credential; the header demonstrates environment-based authentication for protected calls. Send it only to the documented API base. The failure flag surfaces HTTP errors, while bounded retries back off on transient failures, including HTTP 429, and honor Retry-After. Because this request reads metadata, retrying it cannot duplicate a message. Do not infer token permission field names from the route name: inspect the request schema before implementing the Express handler.

For a new Pusher plus SQS deployment, the alternative involves two provider onboarding processes and two credential systems: Pusher application credentials and AWS credentials. The team writes glue mapping queued notifications to channels, retrying delivery, recognizing duplicate work, and correlating receipts. Existing accounts can shorten onboarding, but they do not remove that integration boundary. A common interface reduces that integration surface; it doesn't remove the recovery contract.

Roll out with bounded recovery evidence

Start with one event channel and two roles: publisher and viewer. Before moving traffic, verify that a viewer can subscribe, cannot publish, and cannot use its cursor to retrieve another room's history. Rotate the event channel and confirm that the previous event's token does not authorize the new channel.

Then interrupt a viewer while messages arrive. Require the returning view to account for the missing interval, including an explicit outcome when retained history cannot cover it. Retry the handoff deliberately and check that the conversation contains one logical message per stable message identity.

Finally, compare aggregate recovery outcomes with the diagnostic sample. Keep room IDs, viewer IDs, credentials, and conversation bodies out of metric labels. Set retention before widening the rollout. The acceptance criterion is a complete, authorized view with bounded operational evidence; a connected socket is only one input to that decision.

Sources

References for evaluating the authorization and recovery mechanisms discussed above:

  • Ably token capabilities
  • Pusher Channels authorization
  • Pusher client events
  • Socket.IO connection state recovery
  • Amazon SQS at-least-once delivery
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0, for distinguishing a communications standard from application recovery policy

title: Background Job Queue Push Subscriber: Public HTTPS 429 Rate-Limit Backoff
description:
Short answer: for a fintech renewal reminder that must wait until a business deadline, accept the webhook into durable storage first, then let a bounded worker queue handle delivery, 429 responses, Retry-After, and idempotent replay. The public HTTPS endpoint and its framework are transport details; the delivery guarantee is the design decision.

This distinction matters because a reminder is often attached to a financial state change. A duplicate notification is noisy, but a duplicate renewal command can create a ledger discrepancy. A missed reminder can also make a later reconciliation difficult to explain. The subscriber therefore needs a small, explicit state machine: received, durably accepted, scheduled, attempted, delivered, or dead-lettered for review.

The deadline belongs to the business operation, not to the HTTP request. If the request arrives early, store the target time and acknowledge the delivery after the write commits. If the downstream service is throttling, schedule another attempt without holding the inbound connection open. That arrangement keeps the push edge responsive while the worker spends the dependency's rate budget deliberately.

Renewal deadlines define the queue invariant

A 429 Too Many Requests says that the recipient cannot accept work at the current rate. It does not say that the original webhook was lost, and it does not justify returning success before the job is durable. There are two independent acknowledgements to reason about:

  1. The push subscriber acknowledges responsibility for the incoming message.
  2. The worker records whether the business operation was delivered to its downstream target.

The first acknowledgement should happen only after authentication, schema validation, deduplication, and a durable enqueue have completed. A persistence failure should produce a retryable response, so the sender can try again. A successful enqueue should produce a success response, even if the downstream API is temporarily rate-limited; that later condition belongs to the job state.

I keep the distinction visible in the data model. For each renewal reminder, the unique key is the business operation key, such as account-1842:renewal:2026-09-30, while each delivery attempt receives its own audit record. The unique key prevents two workers from creating two financial effects. The attempt records preserve enough evidence to answer who scheduled the reminder, which deadline was used, what response arrived, and when the next attempt was due.

No durable acceptance, no acknowledgement.

It failed.

The retry delay should use Retry-After when the recipient supplies a valid value. Otherwise, use exponential backoff with a maximum delay and bounded jitter. A worker should also stop after a policy-defined deadline or attempt budget and move the job to a reviewable terminal state. Retrying forever is not a delivery guarantee; it is an unbounded liability.

Can a background job queue webhook push subscriber acknowledge early?

Node.js and Express can provide the HTTP edge, but neither one changes the queue contract. The deployed listener must be reachable through public HTTPS, terminate TLS correctly, validate the sender's authentication mechanism, and apply request limits before parsing unnecessarily large bodies. A localhost test proves only that a process is listening on a developer machine.

The handler should do as little synchronous work as the acceptance contract permits. Parse the envelope, derive a stable operation key, write the inbox record and queue entry in one transactional boundary where possible, and return success. Do not call the payment provider, send the email, or wait for a rate-limited subscriber inside that request. The queue exists to separate the sender's delivery timeout from the worker's business timeout.

The following Go handler shows the boundary without binding it to a commercial queue or a particular framework. An Express implementation should preserve the same ordering: the storage interface is the important part, not the language.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Reminder struct {
    ID          string    `json:"id"`
    Operation   string    `json:"operation"`
    Deadline    time.Time `json:"deadline"`
    AccountID   string    `json:"account_id"`
}

type Inbox interface {
    Accept(context.Context, Reminder) error
}

func subscriber(inbox Inbox) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
            return
        }

        var reminder Reminder
        if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&reminder); err != nil ||
            reminder.ID == "" || reminder.Operation == "" || reminder.AccountID == "" {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }

        if err := inbox.Accept(r.Context(), reminder); err != nil {
            if errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) {
                w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "5")
            }
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }

        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
    })
}

The Accept operation must be idempotent. A repeated message with the same delivery ID may be harmlessly recognized as already accepted, while a repeated business operation must not create a second ledger effect. Those are different keys and should not be collapsed into one field merely because both are called an ID.

Retry policy is a deadline invariant

The worker needs three clocks. The first is the recipient's requested delay, represented by Retry-After when it is valid. The second is the queue's visibility or lease interval, which must be long enough for one attempt but short enough to recover a crashed worker. The third is the business deadline after which a reminder is stale or must be escalated. A correct scheduler compares all three rather than blindly adding seconds to the current time.

Keep it bounded.

For example, if a renewal notice is due on September 30 but the downstream endpoint returns 429 with a delay of 120 seconds, the next attempt can be scheduled at the later of the requested retry time and the operation's permitted retry floor. If that time would cross a contractual cutoff, the job should be marked for review according to the business policy. The right action might be a different channel or a manual reconciliation; it is not safe to assume that another HTTP attempt preserves the same meaning.

Consider a business account whose annual service renews at midnight in its billing region. The reminder is created three days early, but the account owner has asked for delivery after an internal approval deadline. At 09:00 the worker sends the reminder and receives 429 with Retry-After: 120; at 09:02 the provider still rejects the request, and at 09:15 a deployment restarts the worker while its lease is active. A queue that stores only a payload cannot explain whether the reminder was waiting for approval, waiting for the provider, or waiting for lease recovery. A queue record with available_at, deadline_at, attempt, lease_expires_at, last_status, and the operation key can. On restart, the worker can reclaim an expired lease, compare the next permitted attempt with the business deadline, and either send once or create a review task. The audit trail then shows the original acceptance, both rate-limit responses, the lease recovery, and the final decision. This is the useful meaning of delivery guarantees in a fintech system: the transport may deliver several times, but the business state has one accountable transition. The extra fields are not ornamental telemetry; they are the evidence needed when a support request arrives after the reminder window has closed.

Backoff is also a concurrency control. A queue with 500 ready jobs and 50 workers can reproduce the same overload every few seconds if all workers retry together. Jitter spreads the attempts, while a per-destination concurrency limit prevents one provider's quota from consuming capacity needed by other operations. Record the chosen delay and the source of that delay, because an operator should be able to distinguish an explicit recipient instruction from a local fallback.

The Retry-After header can carry a delay in seconds or an HTTP date. A parser should reject negative, malformed, or unreasonably distant values and apply a configured cap. The cap is a policy boundary, not a claim that every provider behaves identically. I'm not sure any static retry number survives every settlement calendar; your mileage may vary with quotas, cutoffs, and contractual service levels.

This is the compact scheduling rule I use in a worker, with the transport-specific parsing kept separate from the queue adapter:

package retry

import (
    "math/rand"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func Delay(retryAfter string, attempt int, cap time.Duration) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        delay := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if delay < cap {
            return delay
        }
        return cap
    }

    if attempt < 0 {
        attempt = 0
    }
    base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<min(attempt, 6))
    if base > cap {
        base = cap
    }
    jitter := time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(base/4 + time.Millisecond)))
    if base+jitter > cap {
        return cap
    }
    return base + jitter
}

func min(left, right int) int {
    if left < right {
        return left
    }
    return right
}

This function is not an exactly-once guarantee. Exactly-once business effect requires an idempotent consumer and a uniqueness constraint around the effect, with an audit trail that survives process restarts. At-least-once delivery is the usual queue assumption; design the financial operation so repeated delivery is safe under that assumption.

Choose the queue by failure ownership

The comparison should start with failure ownership. A managed push queue can handle message retention and redelivery, but your service still owns authentication, idempotency, downstream rate limits, and reconciliation. A self-hosted Redis-backed worker can offer familiar job APIs, but the team then owns durability, failover, ingress, and observability. A cloud-native topic and subscription model can help with fan-out, but adds concepts that may be unnecessary for one renewal stream.

Design Useful when What your team still owns Main limitation
Managed push queue A public subscriber and durable redelivery are the primary needs Inbox idempotency, worker policy, audit, and reconciliation It does not turn an at-least-once transport into an exactly-once financial effect
Cloud topic plus subscription Several independent consumers need the same event Topic policy, subscription operations, consumer idempotency, and quotas More operational objects and fan-out semantics than a single reminder flow needs
Self-hosted Redis worker The team already operates Redis and wants application-level job control Redis durability, failover, ingress, queue metrics, and retry policy The HTTP edge and persistence guarantees remain application responsibilities
Database-backed outbox and worker Auditability and transactional coupling to the business record dominate Polling, lease recovery, throughput tuning, and outbound delivery High-volume fan-out can require more careful partitioning and capacity work

The catch is that no design is suitable when the business requires a multi-step workflow with human approval, joins, or compensation across many systems and the queue offers only delayed messages. In that case, choose a workflow engine or implement the state machine explicitly around the ledger. Stay with the simpler outbox and worker when the job is one bounded reminder whose durable state can be queried and reconciled.

Price should not decide this architecture. The meaningful questions are who owns the retry policy, how the audit record is queried, what retention is required, and how a failed delivery is escalated before the deadline.

Release by replaying the failures

Start with a test matrix that treats the delivery boundary and the business effect as separate assertions. Send a valid payload, the same payload twice, a malformed payload, a persistence failure, and a downstream 429 both with and without Retry-After. Verify that only durable acceptance returns success, that duplicate operation keys produce one business effect, and that a retry cannot be scheduled past the operation's final allowed time without an explicit review state.

Then test recovery rather than just throughput. Stop a worker after it acquires a lease; confirm that another worker can recover the job after the visibility interval. Rebuild a reminder's history from the audit records. Observe queue age, attempt count, destination-specific concurrency, retry reason, and the number of jobs approaching their deadline. A dashboard showing only HTTP success rates hides the failure that matters.

I have found the most useful failure injection to be deliberately boring: one expired lease, one duplicate operation key, and one response carrying 429 with a five-second delay. Those cases expose ordering mistakes quickly. They also keep the review grounded in the invariant that matters: one financial intent, one explainable outcome, however many transport attempts were required.

Roll out with a small worker concurrency, a bounded retry horizon, and a reconciliation query that can find every reminder by operation key. Increase throughput only after queue age and deadline slack remain within policy during a synthetic burst. The endpoint may be public, but the decision to send a reminder is still a controlled accounting event.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html

Further reading

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html

title: SMS One-Time Passwords: A Guide to Auditable Fintech API Integration
description:
Choose an SMS integration that can explain why a fintech login message was sent, what happened afterward, and why another attempt was blocked. A successful send response is insufficient evidence for that decision.

TL;DR: For generating and sending one-time passwords via a Node.js API integration, use cryptographically secure randomness, apply recipient suppression before dispatch, and correlate sending with operational evidence. The minimal implementation below uses Go, with the same application responsibilities a Node.js service needs. It demonstrates the send-to-audit handoff without inventing provider request fields.

For a platform team already buying several backend services, Infrai combines one key and one bill with a single REST API, plain HTTP and no SDK required, a self-describing public discovery surface, and runnable examples in 10 languages, reducing credential sprawl while letting reviewers inspect request and response schemas before wiring the send-to-evidence handoff. The shared interface covers 295 routes across 20 modules, including communication and observability, so both steps can use the same HTTP client. Those conveniences matter only if the resulting evidence meets the institution's requirements.

What proves that an OTP reached the right recipient?

Separate three claims: the provider accepted a send request, the recipient received a message, and the login service accepted a valid challenge response. They require different evidence. Treating the first as the third can produce an attractive delivery dashboard while leaving the authentication decision unexplained, particularly when retries and recipient suppression are involved.

Acceptance proves less.

For this runbook, use a proposed test fixture with 3 recipient states: eligible, temporarily blocked, and suppressed after an invalid-destination decision. These are application policy states, not asserted API response values. An eligible recipient may receive a challenge; a blocked recipient needs the policy-defined review or cooldown; a suppressed recipient must fail the eligibility check before another request leaves the application. Keep a reason and an evidence reference with each transition, including any later reinstatement.

The fintech job includes email bounces when email is used as a fallback. Don't turn an email bounce into an assertion that a telephone number is invalid, or let an SMS failure erase an unrelated email suppression decision. Each channel needs its own recipient identity and classification rules, with a shared login-attempt reference connecting the decisions. A fallback that ignores the email suppression record merely moves the invalid-recipient problem to another transport.

The combined service's event workflow uses polling, so delivery-event freshness depends on the polling interval, backlog, and processing time. Define separate SLOs for send acceptance and evidence ingestion. Neither is a measured delivery guarantee.

Capacity planning starts with the outstanding-message population. If N messages each need one status request every T seconds, the initial polling load is roughly N/T requests per second before retries; a hypothetical 6,000 messages at a 30-second interval implies 200 requests per second. This is sizing arithmetic, not a vendor limit or benchmark. Leave recovery headroom, because a poller restart can turn a tolerable steady-state load into a backlog that competes with authentication traffic.

Buy versus build around the evidence boundary

Compare the responsibility the platform team accepts. The following are architecture choices and evaluation criteria, rather than claims that any product alone satisfies a financial-services compliance obligation.

Option Buy versus build Fit and limitation
Twilio plus Datadog Buy communication and observability separately; build their evidence mapping Fits teams selecting those systems independently, but the platform owns correlation, replay, and partial completion across them.
Vonage Evaluate a communication API; retain application policy A candidate when choosing a dedicated messaging supplier; validate its SMS contract against required suppression states and evidence before selection.
Amazon SNS Evaluate SMS within an AWS-oriented architecture A candidate for an existing AWS operating model; cloud familiarity does not establish authentication correctness or regulatory suitability.
Application-owned challenge service Build challenge lifecycle, suppression policy, and evidence mapping around a transport Gives direct control over decision records, while adding storage, concurrency, recovery, and on-call work to the roadmap.

A straightforward Twilio plus Datadog setup requires 2 service signups and 2 sets of credentials. Existing enterprise accounts can reduce signup work. The glue still needs an owner: preserve the communication request identifier, translate delivery events into the team's evidence model, and send the corresponding records to observability without confusing a replay with a new authentication attempt.

A combined API reduces that integration surface, but it means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. If independent communication and monitoring ownership is a hard requirement, the separate stack is a better fit despite the glue. Procurement convenience isn't compliance evidence.

How should code connect sending one-time passwords via SMS to audit evidence?

Check suppression eligibility before generating a code. A Node.js application should use the cryptographic randomness facilities in node:crypto; the Go program below uses crypto/rand to generate a six-digit value without modulo bias. Six digits is an example choice, not a complete authentication policy. Expiry, verification limits, resend rules, protected challenge storage, geographic restrictions, and country-based spending circuit breakers need explicit application decisions.

This standard-library Go program takes configuration through environment variables. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL, using the service's documented HTTPS API base with its version suffix. Set SMS_JSON_TEMPLATE and LOG_JSON_TEMPLATE to request bodies checked against the selected capabilities' public discovery schemas. Put {{OTP}} inside the intended SMS message string and {{SMS_RESPONSE_SHA256}} inside a string field supported by the logging schema. No provider payload fields are assumed here.

Both writes use the same key and base URL. The send response feeds log ingestion through a SHA-256 fingerprint, demonstrating the handoff without copying the complete response into monitoring. This is acceptance evidence; delivery events must subsequently be polled and correlated. A production record should also retain the documented message identifier and the application's attempt reference. Keep the OTP and full recipient address out of the log template.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/rand"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/big"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func required(name string) string {
    value := os.Getenv(name)
    if value == "" { panic("missing environment variable: " + name) }
    return value
}

func post(c *http.Client, base, key, path, id string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, base+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", id)
        resp, err := c.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1048576))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<uint(attempt))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(deadline)
                if delay < 0 { delay = 0 }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func run() error {
    key := required("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    base := strings.TrimRight(required("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    smsTemplate := required("SMS_JSON_TEMPLATE")
    logTemplate := required("LOG_JSON_TEMPLATE")
    if !strings.Contains(smsTemplate, "{{OTP}}") ||
        !strings.Contains(logTemplate, "{{SMS_RESPONSE_SHA256}}") {
        return fmt.Errorf("templates must contain their substitution markers")
    }
    n, err := rand.Int(rand.Reader, big.NewInt(1000000))
    if err != nil { return err }
    smsBody := []byte(strings.ReplaceAll(smsTemplate, "{{OTP}}", fmt.Sprintf("%06d", n.Int64())))
    if !json.Valid(smsBody) || !json.Valid([]byte(logTemplate)) {
        return fmt.Errorf("templates must be valid JSON")
    }
    seed := make([]byte, 16)
    if _, err := rand.Read(seed); err != nil { return err }
    attemptID := hex.EncodeToString(seed)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    sent, err := post(client, base, key, "/sms/send", attemptID+"-send", smsBody)
    if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("send: %w", err) }
    digest := sha256.Sum256(sent)
    logBody := []byte(strings.ReplaceAll(logTemplate, "{{SMS_RESPONSE_SHA256}}", hex.EncodeToString(digest[:])))
    if _, err := post(client, base, key, "/logs/ingest", attemptID+"-audit", logBody); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("send accepted; evidence write needs reconciliation: %w", err)
    }
    fmt.Println("Send accepted; evidence submitted. Delivery remains unconfirmed.")
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The explicit POST method, response checks, stable keys within each retry loop, and bounded backoff are intentional. The error includes the provider's response body; redact sensitive values before making that error broadly visible. Check each capability's idempotency declaration before relying on provider-side deduplication. A header alone cannot establish the guarantee.

There is a trap at the process boundary. If sending succeeds and logging fails, restarting this program creates a new code and identifier. Don't use a whole-program retry as the recovery mechanism: a production service needs a durable attempt record and an outbox that retries the evidence write independently, preserving the original identifier and payload across restarts. A transport error also leaves acceptance potentially ambiguous, which is why this example stops rather than automatically generating a replacement challenge.

Generating and sending a code does not implement verification. Persist protected challenge state before dispatch and implement the verification policy separately; this sample is limited to the communication-to-observability handoff.

Verify suppression, then rehearse recovery

Use controlled recipients in a policy-approved environment. For each of the 3 application states, check the eligibility decision, the presence or absence of a send attempt, and its evidence record. A suppressed recipient should produce a blocked decision with a reason, rather than a provider send. Replay a delivery event and then deliver an older event after a newer decision; an old success must not silently reactivate a suppressed destination.

Next exercise partial completion: an accepted send followed by an unavailable evidence sink. Recovery should finish the missing evidence write without generating another code or dispatching another message. Compare durable send-attempt records with ingested evidence, measure the age of the oldest unreconciled item, and alert against a declared freshness SLO. Delivery events and the application's operational records then meet in the same evidence workflow, instead of requiring an operator to join a carrier dashboard against logs by hand.

Email fallback deserves a separate test. Process bounce evidence, apply suppression before the next email attempt, and retain the reason for manual reinstatement. SPF describes sender authorization; it doesn't establish recipient validity, delivery, or fintech compliance. Evaluate jurisdiction, retention, access control, and vendor evidence independently of the number of API keys.

Rollback should pause new sends through the changed integration while retaining suppression decisions and outstanding challenge state. Resume evidence reconciliation independently. Reverting code must not restore a stale recipient list or clear a suppression decision made during deployment; if rollback switches providers, carry those decisions across before enabling traffic.

Keep the evidence.

The release criterion is a traceable chain from eligibility through sending, event ingestion, and authentication, with missing links visible to an operator. Consolidated services fit when they shorten that chain without weakening its records.

References

  • Node.js cryptography API: https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html
  • Go cryptographic randomness: https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/rand
  • Twilio messaging documentation: https://www.twilio.com/docs/messaging
  • Datadog log collection documentation: https://docs.datadoghq.com/logs/log_collection/
  • Vonage SMS API documentation: https://developer.vonage.com/en/messaging/sms/overview
  • Amazon SNS SMS documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-mobile-phone-number-as-subscriber.html
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208

title: Delivery Guarantees for Game Watch Parties Under Host Authority and Peer Consensus
description:
Consider a proposed page for a gaming watch party: playback acknowledgments have stopped advancing for part of the room, while chat still shows typing indicators and read receipts. The on-call sees active connections and a healthy transport dashboard. Neither answers the useful question: which viewers applied the latest playback command? This is a diagnostic scenario, not a report of a production incident.

Short answer: use host-authoritative playback when one designated controller should decide the room's timeline; consider peer consensus when the room must agree on control changes without that single decision point. In either design, specify delivery and recovery separately. Agreement about a command does not demonstrate that every viewer received it, and a typing indicator cannot serve as a playback acknowledgment.

For a server application, including one implemented in Node.js, that distinction belongs in the event contract before the transport choice. The examples below use Go to make the state transitions explicit.

What page fired when the room still looked connected?

Start with the page definition. In this proposed design, the page concerns eligible viewers whose applied playback sequence remains behind the room's committed sequence beyond a chosen recovery budget. Eligibility must be explicit: a viewer who has left the room should not remain in the denominator, and a newly joining viewer needs a defined catch-up period. The budget is a service objective the team must choose from its viewing requirements, not a universal timeout supplied by a protocol.

Distrust the dashboard.

A count of open connections can help locate a failure, but the proposed service promise concerns applied state. Work backward from an affected viewer: did the client receive the command, accept its authority, update playback, and report the resulting state? Those are separate steps. Instrument them separately, because an acknowledgment sent on receipt would make the dashboard report success even if the client later rejected the command as stale.

Use an illustrative room called arena-final with playback sequence 104 already applied. Its next command is sequence 105. A read receipt for chat message 900 does not establish anything about playback sequence 105; even a receipt from the same viewer belongs to a different state machine. This is the concrete trap in a watch party that adds social features: visible activity can distract from a stalled control path, particularly when the dashboard aggregates all room events into a single success count.

The earlier signal should therefore be divergence between committed playback state and client-applied playback state. Connection counts are supporting evidence. They should not be the proof that closes the incident.

How do host-authoritative playback and peer consensus affect fan-out?

Host authority and peer consensus answer a control question. Fan-out answers a distribution question. For this design, treat a playback command as an authority term, a sequence within that term, an intended playback state, and a room identifier. The term identifies a particular grant of control; it is an application field, not a transport feature. On an authority change, establish the new term through the chosen control mechanism and reject commands from superseded terms.

With host authority, the designated controller proposes playback changes and the service validates that controller before committing them. The attraction is a clear place to ask why a pause or seek was accepted. The operational burden is deciding what happens when that controller disappears: freeze control, appoint a replacement through a trusted coordinator, or require an explicit room action. Make that policy visible to viewers. Silent competing controllers would undermine the authority rule the design was meant to provide.

Peer consensus becomes relevant when participants must agree on the accepted control history or its successor authority. Its trade-off is a protocol to specify and operate: membership, the conditions for accepting a decision, behavior during disconnection, and recovery after rejoining. A majority of playback acknowledgments is not, by itself, such a protocol. It merely says that some clients reported applying something. Do not invent a consensus algorithm by renaming those acknowledgments votes.

Neither choice eliminates delivery work.

For typing, propose replaceable state with an expiry rather than a replayable history of every keystroke. A missed update can then resolve through expiry or a newer update. For read receipts, propose a monotonic watermark over an ordered chat stream, scoped to the participant and room; the watermark represents the greatest message position that participant has acknowledged as read under the application's definition. Playback needs its own reconciliation contract because an old seek delivered after a new pause could otherwise undo the room's intended state. These are proposed application semantics, not guarantees inherited from the wire.

The transport specification helps establish that boundary. W3C WebRTC 1.0 defines data-channel configuration for ordered delivery and retransmission constraints through ordered, maxPacketLifeTime, and maxRetransmits. Those controls describe channel behavior. They do not define room membership, an authoritative host, a chat read watermark, or an application commit point. Inspect the actual configuration, then supply the missing application rules.

Replace aggregate success with evidence of application

The instrumentation change is to attach a common command identity to the control decision, distribution attempt, and client application acknowledgment. Record the room's committed term and sequence, the viewer's last applied term and sequence, and the age of unresolved divergence. Retain a distinction between a transmission attempt and a client report. A transport send completing must not advance the viewer's applied watermark in this design.

Keep per-viewer detail in diagnostic records, with appropriate retention and access controls, and use bounded aggregate dimensions for the alert. The responder needs to find affected viewers without turning every participant identifier into a metric dimension. This is an operational design choice: aggregate data makes the page manageable, while sampled or retained event detail makes it explainable.

The following reducer illustrates the acknowledgment boundary for playback. It assumes the caller has authenticated the viewer, authorized room membership, loaded that viewer's watermark, and supplied the room's current committed position. It handles one command stream; chat receipts require their own stream and state.

package playback

type Position struct {
    Term uint64
    Seq  uint64
}

func ApplyAck(committed, previous, incoming Position) (Position, string) {
    if incoming.Term != committed.Term {
        return previous, "term_mismatch"
    }
    if incoming.Seq > committed.Seq {
        return previous, "ahead_of_commit"
    }
    if previous.Term > incoming.Term {
        return previous, "stale_term"
    }
    if previous.Term == incoming.Term && incoming.Seq <= previous.Seq {
        return previous, "duplicate_or_stale"
    }
    return incoming, "advanced"
}

This function returns a candidate state, not a durable receipt. Serialize or transactionally compare updates for the same viewer before persisting the result; otherwise two workers can read the same previous value and write their results in the wrong order. Emit the advancement event after that state change succeeds. Also define sequence numbers as contiguous positions within an authority term if subtraction will be used to calculate command lag. A counter with unexplained gaps cannot safely double as a count of missed commands.

An acknowledgment remains a client claim.

It doesn't prove that a human watched the frame or read the chat message. Keep that limitation in the service language and incident notes.

Exercise recovery before choosing the paging budget

Use the illustrative sequences 104 and 105 to test the contract. Disconnect a viewer before 105, reconnect it, and verify that it reconciles to the current authoritative state. Then deliver the acknowledgment for 105 twice and deliver an acknowledgment for 104 afterward. The persisted watermark should remain at 105 within the same term. Test a host change separately: a command from the old term must not regain authority just because it arrives late. Make the concurrency trap concrete in the test harness as well: let worker A read position 104, let worker B read that same position, have B persist an acknowledgment for 106, and then let A attempt to persist 105. The storage boundary must reject A's regression or serialize the operations so that the final watermark is 106. The reducer alone cannot enforce that boundary. These are synthetic inputs, not measured failures; their value is that a passing happy-path demonstration would miss precisely the ordering error the exercise introduces.

Test social features under the same interruption, but judge them by their own promises. An expired typing indicator should disappear under the proposed expiry rule. A chat read watermark should survive duplicate or out-of-order receipt reports without moving backward. A client that never reports reading a message must not be counted as having read it merely because the playback channel recovered.

For a consensus design, add a partition exercise and document which participants can make progress under the actual agreement protocol. For a host design, exercise host departure and replacement.

Recovery still needs testing.

Both exercises should include recovery fan-out to returning viewers; changing the authority mechanism does not answer how a disconnected client acquires current state.

Roll out the instrumentation before enabling its page. Observe divergence during joins, reconnects, and control changes, and compare the traces with the intended service objective. This requires engineering time and diagnostic storage, but it gives the responder evidence for distinguishing normal recovery from a room that cannot converge. No measurement results are assumed here.

A threshold can create its own incident load

Close the proposed incident only when the affected eligible viewers converge, or when the team explicitly accounts for viewers outside the recovery promise. A green send counter is insufficient. The incident record should say which page fired, which earlier signal was missing, and what action the new signal enables.

Set the threshold too close to ordinary reconnect behavior and the page repeatedly asks someone to investigate successful recovery; set it beyond the useful response window and the alert arrives after viewers have already abandoned the session. That false-positive cost belongs in the decision alongside delivery guarantees. Prefer a page tied to sustained, actionable divergence, with diagnostic evidence available when it fires.

Choose host authority for an explicit controller policy, and peer consensus for an explicit agreement requirement. Then verify the same uncomfortable detail in either case: which viewer applied which committed command, under whose authority, and how will a viewer who missed it recover?

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0, particularly RTCDataChannel and RTCDataChannelInit for ordering and retransmission configuration: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

Further reading

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0, the transport specification cited in References: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: CSS page breaks for HTML-to-PDF: tables, headers, margins and backgrounds
description:
These rules work in Chromium-based renderers: Chrome's Print to PDF, Puppeteer, Playwright and APIs built on them, including SlipKiln. Older engines like wkhtmltopdf support less of this.

Tables split across pages

Long tables get rows cut in half at the page edge, and the header row appears only on page one. Two rules fix both:

/* Keep each row whole and repeat the header row on every page */
tr      { break-inside: avoid; }
thead   { display: table-header-group; }
tfoot   { display: table-footer-group; }

Chromium repeats a <thead> on every printed page, so make sure your header row is actually in a <thead>, not the first <tr> of the body. A break-inside: avoid row that is taller than a whole page still has to break somewhere; keep rows short.

Controlling where pages break 

/* Start each section on a new page */
.section       { break-before: page; }
.section:first-child { break-before: auto; }

/* Don't split cards, figures or signature blocks */
.card, figure, .signature { break-inside: avoid; }

/* Don't leave a heading alone at the bottom of a page */
h2, h3 { break-after: avoid; }

/* At least 3 lines of a paragraph on each side of a break */
p { orphans: 3; widows: 3; }

The older page-break-before, page-break-after and page-break-inside properties still work as aliases. New code should use break-*.

Page size and margins 

@page {
  size: Letter;          /* or A4, A5, "Letter landscape" */
  margin: 18mm 16mm;
}
@page :first { margin-top: 30mm; }   /* extra room for a letterhead */

Watch out: many HTML-to-PDF tools pass a paper size to the renderer, and in Chromium that overrides your CSS size unless the tool sets preferCSSPageSize. With SlipKiln, set the size with options.format (A4, A5, Letter, Legal) and options.landscape, and margins with options.margin, so your PDF comes out the same every time.

Backgrounds and colors disappear

Browsers drop backgrounds when printing to save ink. SlipKiln turns print_background on by default; in your own Chromium pass printBackground: true. For individual elements:

/* Keep background colors and shaded rows in the PDF */
* { -webkit-print-color-adjust: exact; print-color-adjust: exact; }

Fonts and images

A server-side renderer only has the fonts installed on that machine, so text falls back to a default face. Embed fonts with @font-face and a base64 data: URL, and do the same for logos. SlipKiln requires this because its renderer has no network access; it also means your PDF never depends on a CDN being up.

Checklist

  • Header row inside <thead>; tr { break-inside: avoid }
  • break-before: page for sections, break-after: avoid on headings
  • Page size and margins set where your renderer actually reads them
  • Backgrounds on, print-color-adjust: exact for shaded rows
  • Fonts and images inlined

Want to try your HTML? The free plan renders 50 PDFs a month with no card: POST /v1/render/html.

Originally published on slipkiln.com. We build SlipKiln, an API that turns HTML or JSON into PDFs.

title: Why a 25-second answer box does not need an account
description:
This is a companion note about PlayKrillion, a free independent Krillion-inspired browser trivia game. It is not affiliated with krillion.io. It describes behaviour published on the official site, not unpublished source code, video features, or a claimed tech stack.

A daily dive is seven open-answer prompts. Each prompt has a three-second preview, then 25 seconds to type one answer and submit with Enter or Dive. A rejected answer can be changed while time remains. If the timer ends with text already in the box, that text is still checked.

Those constraints matter more than a backend account. The useful state is local: streaks and the logbook are stored in the browser you played in. There is no account-based cross-device sync. Private browsing or clearing site data can therefore change what history is visible. That is a product limit, not a hidden login.

Daily and practice games do not call a generative model. Answers are checked against a prepared list, with conservative typo matching described on the site. Rarity is not a live vote; accepted answers already sit in tiers of 10, 15, 30, 60, 85 or 100 points.

If you are adding a similarly short timer to a web form, the official mobile note is practical: on a phone the answer box should open the keyboard, and the keyboard Send key should submit. There are no movement keys. If the page fails to load, the site recommends a hard refresh, a private window, and checking whether an extension is blocking scripts — not a workaround for a network that is meant to block it.

Further reading, from the site itself:

  • Phone and browser behaviour: PlayKrillion's mobile note
